summary.scope: Remaining unique canonicalDifficulty=medium questions marked unknown in the saved review queue; automated indicators are screening candidates, not final editorial findings.

items.stem: The posted price is held below equilibrium, but buyers wait in long lines. What policy most likely caused this?
options: A binding price ceiling
A binding price floor
A tax on sellers
An outward PPF shift
items.feedback: A binding price ceiling creates a shortage, so nonprice rationing like waiting can appear.

items.stem: A rent ceiling is set above the equilibrium rent. What is the likely result?
options: The ceiling is not binding and has no effect
The ceiling creates a shortage
The ceiling creates a surplus
The ceiling shifts supply right
items.feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium does not prevent the market price from reaching equilibrium.

items.stem: A binding price ceiling tends to reduce the quality of rental housing because:
options: Landlords have less incentive to maintain units when price cannot rise
Tenants always demand less housing at lower prices
Quantity supplied rises above quantity demanded
The ceiling is above equilibrium
items.feedback: A binding ceiling can create shortages and reduce incentives to maintain quality.

items.stem: A government policy keeps apartment rents below equilibrium. Which outcome is most likely over time?
options: Shortages and nonprice rationing
Surpluses and unsold apartments
A rightward supply shift caused by lower rent
An increase in quantity supplied
items.feedback: A binding rent ceiling creates shortages, so apartments may be rationed through waiting, search costs, or other nonprice methods.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At a price ceiling of $20, what is quantity demanded?
options: 250 units
150 units
200 units
300 units
items.feedback: At $20, the demand curve shows quantity demanded of 250 units.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At a price ceiling of $20, what is quantity supplied?
options: 150 units
250 units
200 units
100 units
items.feedback: At $20, the supply curve shows quantity supplied of 150 units.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $40, what is the most likely result?
options: The price ceiling is not binding
A shortage of 100 units occurs
A surplus of 100 units occurs
The equilibrium quantity falls to 150
items.feedback: A price ceiling above equilibrium is not binding. Since $40 is above the $30 equilibrium price, it does not affect the market.

items.stem: At the $1,000 rent ceiling, what shortage is shown?
options: 50 apartments
200 apartments
150 apartments
300 apartments
items.feedback: Read quantity demanded and quantity supplied at the $1,000 ceiling and subtract: 250 − 50 = 200 apartments.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the binding $1,000 rent ceiling, what is the maximum number of apartments that can be rented if transactions cannot exceed the number landlords offer?
options: 150 apartments
200 apartments
50 apartments
250 apartments
items.feedback: At $1,000, quantity supplied is only 50 apartments. Even though 250 are demanded, actual transactions cannot exceed the 50 units offered.

items.stem: Equilibrium rent is $1,400. A ceiling is set at $1,550. What is the immediate market effect?
options: Shortage: the ceiling is binding
Surplus: the ceiling is binding
No effect: the ceiling is nonbinding
Tax wedge: the difference is $150
items.feedback: A ceiling above equilibrium does not constrain the market price.

items.stem: A government wants to make a good affordable, so it imposes a price ceiling. Which condition must hold for the policy to actually affect the market?
options: The ceiling must be below equilibrium price
The ceiling must be above equilibrium price
The ceiling must equal quantity demanded
The ceiling must be imposed on sellers only
items.feedback: A price ceiling only binds if it is below the equilibrium price.

items.stem: A binding rent ceiling is imposed below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 1,200 apartments and quantity supplied is 850. What is the shortage?
options: 350 apartments
850 apartments
1,200 apartments
2,050 apartments
items.feedback: Shortage is Qd - Qs: 1,200 - 850 = 350 apartments.

items.stem: A rent ceiling is set below equilibrium. Quantity demanded is 900 apartments and quantity supplied is 600. What occurs?
options: A shortage of 300 apartments
A surplus of 300 apartments
A shortage of 1,500 apartments
No effect because ceilings are minimum prices
items.feedback: The shortage is quantity demanded minus quantity supplied: 900 - 600 = 300.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price ceiling at $20, what shortage results?
options: 100 units
50 units
150 units
400 units
items.feedback: At $20, quantity demanded is 250 and quantity supplied is 150. The shortage is 250 - 150 = 100 units.

items.stem: A minimum wage is set below the equilibrium wage. What is the likely result?
options: The minimum wage is not binding
It creates unemployment
It creates a labor shortage
It shifts labor demand right
items.feedback: A price floor below equilibrium does not prevent the market wage from reaching equilibrium.

items.stem: A binding price floor in an agricultural market may lead to:
options: Unsold surplus output
A shortage of the crop
A lower legal price
A movement down the demand curve caused by lower price
items.feedback: A binding price floor keeps price above equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

items.stem: A price floor above equilibrium and a price ceiling below equilibrium both cause problems because:
options: They prevent the market price from adjusting to equilibrium
They eliminate all gains from trade immediately
They make demand and supply irrelevant
They always increase the quantity traded
items.feedback: Binding price controls prevent price from moving to equilibrium, creating shortages or surpluses.

items.stem: The graph shows a $40 price floor. Which statement correctly classifies the policy and identifies the competitive equilibrium price?
options: Binding: the equilibrium price is $30, so the legal level is above equilibrium.
Binding: the equilibrium price is $35, so the legal level is above equilibrium.
Nonbinding: the equilibrium price is $30, so the market still clears at that price.
Nonbinding: the equilibrium price is $35, so the market still clears at that price.
items.feedback: The demand and supply curves intersect at $30. The legal minimum of $40 is a price floor. It is above equilibrium, so it prevents the market from clearing at $30 and is binding.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At a price floor of $40, what is quantity demanded?
options: 150 units
250 units
200 units
300 units
items.feedback: At $40, the demand curve shows quantity demanded of 150 units.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At a price floor of $40, what is quantity supplied?
options: 250 units
150 units
200 units
100 units
items.feedback: At $40, the supply curve shows quantity supplied of 250 units.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the $10 minimum wage, what labor surplus results?
options: 75 thousand workers
100 thousand workers
350 thousand workers
150 thousand workers
items.feedback: At $10, labor supplied is 250 thousand workers and labor demanded is 100 thousand, so the labor surplus is 150 thousand workers.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the binding $10 minimum wage, how many workers are employed?
options: 100 thousand workers
150 thousand workers
175 thousand workers
250 thousand workers
items.feedback: At $10, firms demand 100 thousand workers. The larger 250-thousand labor supply does not force firms to hire beyond their quantity demanded.

items.stem: A government wants to raise producer income, so it imposes a price floor. Which condition must hold for the policy to actually affect the market?
options: The floor must be above equilibrium price
The floor must be below equilibrium price
The floor must equal zero
The floor must reduce supply
items.feedback: A price floor only binds if it is above the equilibrium price.

items.stem: At a price floor of $18, quantity supplied is 900 units and quantity demanded is 550 units. Which answer best states the result?
options: A surplus of 350 units
A shortage of 350 units
A surplus of 550 units
A shortage of 900 units
items.feedback: Surplus equals quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 900 - 550 = 350.

items.stem: A binding price floor is imposed above equilibrium. Quantity supplied is 700 and quantity demanded is 460. What is the surplus?
options: 240 units
460 units
700 units
1,160 units
items.feedback: Surplus is Qs - Qd: 700 - 460 = 240 units.

items.stem: A minimum wage is set above equilibrium. Labor supplied is 120,000 and labor demanded is 80,000. What is the labor surplus?
options: 40,000 workers
80,000 workers
120,000 workers
200,000 workers
items.feedback: The surplus is quantity supplied minus quantity demanded: 120,000 - 80,000 = 40,000.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. If the government sets a price floor at $40, what surplus results?
options: 100 units
50 units
150 units
400 units
items.feedback: At $40, quantity supplied is 250 and quantity demanded is 150. The surplus is 250 - 150 = 100 units.

items.stem: The market begins where SL0 and DL intersect. A licensing reform lets more trained healthcare workers enter the occupation. At $20, how many workers are available before and after the change? Does this show a supply shift or movement along a curve?
options: Supply changes from 3,000 to 7,000 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 8,000 workers; this is movement along a fixed supply curve caused solely by wage.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 8,000 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 3,000 to 7,000 workers; this is movement along a fixed supply curve caused solely by wage.
items.feedback: At $20, SL0 gives 4,000 workers and SL1 gives 8,000. Easier entry expands the quantity available at each wage. A wage change by itself moves along a supply curve rather than relocating it.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. By how much does the equilibrium healthcare wage decline?
options: $2 per hour
$15 per hour
$5 per hour
$20 per hour
items.feedback: The wage falls from $20 to $15 per hour, a $5 decline.

items.stem: Labor supply shifts from SL0 to SL1. What are the new wage and employment? Does the adjustment shift labor demand or move the market along it?
options: $30 and 1,000 workers; the market moves along labor demand.
$25 and 2,000 workers; the market moves along labor demand.
$25 and 2,000 workers; the wage change itself shifts labor demand.
$30 and 1,000 workers; the wage change itself shifts labor demand.
items.feedback: The new intersection is $25 and 20 hundreds of workers. Supply shifts, while the wage change produces movement along unchanged demand. It does not itself shift labor demand.

items.stem: Construction labor supply shifts from SL0 to SL1, with DL unchanged. How many fewer workers are employed at the new equilibrium?
options: 200 workers
4,000 workers
6,000 workers
2,000 workers
items.feedback: Employment falls from 4,000 to 2,000 workers, a decline of 2,000.

items.stem: Construction labor supply shifts from SL0 to SL1, with DL unchanged. How much higher is the new equilibrium hourly wage?
options: $2 per hour
$20 per hour
$5 per hour
$25 per hour
items.feedback: The wage rises from $20 to $25 per hour, an increase of $5.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. How many workers seek restaurant jobs at the minimum wage?
options: 600 workers
2,000 workers
6,000 workers
4,000 workers
items.feedback: The $20 line intersects labor supply at 60 hundreds of workers, or 6,000 workers.

items.stem: Compared with competition in the graph, what wage and employment prevail under the minimum wage, and which side of the market limits actual hiring?
options: $25 and 1,000 workers; firms’ demand limits employment.
$20 and 2,000 workers; firms’ demand limits employment.
$20 and 2,000 workers; the number wanting work determines employment regardless of firms’ demand.
$25 and 1,000 workers; the number wanting work determines employment regardless of firms’ demand.
items.feedback: The $20 floor is above the $15 equilibrium. At $20 firms demand 20 hundreds, so 2,000 are employed despite 6,000 willing workers. Actual trade is limited by the short side, labor demand.

items.stem: How far is the legal minimum below the market-clearing wage? Does this minimum wage create a surplus of workers?
options: $10; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
$5; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
$10; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
$5; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
items.feedback: Equilibrium is $15 while the legal minimum is $10. Paying the market wage already complies with the floor. The $5 gap therefore creates neither a forced wage reduction nor policy-induced excess supply.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Which change would make the wage floor binding, holding the curves fixed?
options: Lower it below $10
Move it to zero
Raise it above $15 per hour
Keep it at $10
items.feedback: A floor affects the competitive outcome only when it is set above the $15 market-clearing wage.

items.stem: With equipment and floor space fixed, marginal output at an apple orchard falls from 16 to 11 crates as another worker joins. What principle is operating?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 11 crates, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 16 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: With equipment and floor space fixed, marginal output at a construction crew falls from 10 to 7 wall sections as another worker joins. What principle is operating?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 7 wall sections, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 10 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: A repair shop expands its crew. The latest worker adds 5 repairs, down from 8 for the worker before. How should the manager interpret this?
options: Total product must be falling
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 5 repairs, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 8 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: The solar installation crew still produces more after hiring, but the added output falls from 7 to 4 arrays. Which conclusion follows?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 4 arrays, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 7 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: With equipment and floor space fixed, marginal output at a coffee roastery falls from 14 to 9 batches as another worker joins. What principle is operating?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 9 batches, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 14 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: A worker at a bakery adds 6 loaves per hour, each worth $8. The wage is $42. What should the competitive firm do?
options: Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $48 per hour (6 × $8). Because $48 exceeds $42, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: At a car wash, one additional worker washes 3 more cars per hour. Each wash sells for $15. Should the firm hire this worker at a wage of $40 per hour?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $45 per hour (3 × $15). Because $45 exceeds $40, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: The landscaper's next worker has an MPL of 4 lawns, and output sells for $14 per unit. At a $60 wage, is the hire profitable?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Do not hire the worker because VMP is below the wage
Compare total output with the wage instead
Hire because any positive VMP raises profit
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $56 per hour (4 × $14). Because $56 is below $60, the worker costs more than the added output value.

items.stem: A worker at a repair shop adds 2 repairs per hour, each worth $35. The wage is $72. What should the competitive firm do?
options: Do not hire the worker because VMP is below the wage
Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Hire because any positive VMP raises profit
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $70 per hour (2 × $35). Because $70 is below $72, the worker costs more than the added output value.

items.stem: A worker at a catering firm adds 5 orders per hour, each worth $11. The wage is $58. What should the competitive firm do?
options: Do not hire the worker because VMP is below the wage
Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Hire because any positive VMP raises profit
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $55 per hour (5 × $11). Because $55 is below $58, the worker costs more than the added output value.

items.stem: At a laundry service, the marginal worker produces value from 8 extra loads sold for $5 apiece. How does a $44 wage affect the hiring decision?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Hire because any positive VMP raises profit
Do not hire the worker because VMP is below the wage
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $40 per hour (8 × $5). Because $40 is below $44, the worker costs more than the added output value.

items.stem: The nursery's next worker has an MPL of 6 flats, and output sells for $9 per unit. At a $60 wage, is the hire profitable?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Do not hire the worker because VMP is below the wage
Compare total output with the wage instead
Hire because any positive VMP raises profit
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $54 per hour (6 × $9). Because $54 is below $60, the worker costs more than the added output value.

items.stem: A bakery increases labor from 4 to 5 workers, and output rises from 120 to 138 loaves. What is MPL over this change?
options: 18 total additional loaves
138 total loaves
18 loaves per added worker
27.6 loaves per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (138 − 120) ÷ (5 − 4) = 18 loaves per added worker.

items.stem: A printer increases labor from 3 to 4 workers, and output rises from 72 to 84 jobs. What is MPL over this change?
options: 12 total additional jobs
12 jobs per added worker
84 total jobs
21 jobs per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (84 − 72) ÷ (4 − 3) = 12 jobs per added worker.

items.stem: The greenhouse adds 1 worker and gains 14 flats of output. What is the marginal product per worker?
options: 14 total additional flats
264 total flats
24 flats per worker
14 flats per added worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (264 − 250) ÷ (11 − 10) = 14 flats per added worker.

items.stem: The furniture shop adds 2 workers and gains 26 chairs of output. What is the marginal product per worker?
options: 26 total additional chairs
106 total chairs
13 chairs per added worker
17.7 chairs per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (106 − 80) ÷ (6 − 4) = 13 chairs per added worker.

items.stem: A solar crew increases labor from 5 to 6 workers, and output rises from 24 to 30 installations. What is MPL over this change?
options: 6 total additional installations
30 total installations
6 installations per added worker
5 installations per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (30 − 24) ÷ (6 − 5) = 6 installations per added worker.

items.stem: A farm crew increases labor from 9 to 12 workers, and output rises from 270 to 306 bins. What is MPL over this change?
options: 36 total additional bins
12 bins per added worker
306 total bins
25.5 bins per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (306 − 270) ÷ (12 − 9) = 12 bins per added worker.

items.stem: The packing plant adds 2 workers and gains 46 boxes of output. What is the marginal product per worker?
options: 46 total additional boxes
676 total boxes
42.3 boxes per worker
23 boxes per added worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (676 − 630) ÷ (16 − 14) = 23 boxes per added worker.

items.stem: A clinic hires more physicians, which makes each medical technician more productive. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: Physicians and technicians are complements, raising technician demand
All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
items.feedback: Physicians and technicians are complements, raising technician demand. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: A construction boom increases firms' use of both cranes and crane operators. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: Output expansion raises derived demand for complementary capital and labor
All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
items.feedback: Output expansion raises derived demand for complementary capital and labor. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: A hotel opens another building and needs more housekeepers and maintenance workers. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: All factors must be substitutes
Expanded productive capacity raises demand for multiple complementary inputs
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
items.feedback: Expanded productive capacity raises demand for multiple complementary inputs. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: A city attracts many licensed nurses from other regions. What happens to labor supply?
options: There is movement along an unchanged labor-supply curve
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Nursing labor supply shifts right
Worker productivity must fall
items.feedback: This nonwage determinant changes how many workers are willing or able to work at a given wage, shifting labor supply.

items.stem: A neighboring industry raises wages while local factory wages are unchanged. What happens to labor supply?
options: There is movement along an unchanged labor-supply curve
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Factory labor supply shifts left
Worker productivity must fall
items.feedback: A change in the occupation's wage causes movement along its labor-supply curve.

items.stem: Many construction workers retire and few replacements enter. What happens to labor supply?
options: There is movement along an unchanged labor-supply curve
Construction labor supply shifts left
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Worker productivity must fall
items.feedback: This nonwage determinant changes how many workers are willing or able to work at a given wage, shifting labor supply.

items.stem: Childcare becomes less available for local workers. What happens to labor supply?
options: There is movement along an unchanged labor-supply curve
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Worker productivity must fall
Labor supply may shift left when fewer people can take jobs
items.feedback: This nonwage determinant changes how many workers are willing or able to work at a given wage, shifting labor supply.

items.stem: An influx of qualified nurses increases nursing labor supply. With labor demand unchanged, what happens to the equilibrium wage and employment?
options: Both wage and employment rise
Both wage and employment fall
The equilibrium wage falls and nursing employment rises
The wage changes but employment cannot change
items.feedback: A labor-supply increase moves wage and employment in opposite directions when labor demand is unchanged.

items.stem: A training subsidy expands the supply of technicians. With labor demand unchanged, what happens to the equilibrium wage and employment?
options: Both wage and employment rise
Both wage and employment fall
Technician wages fall and employment rises
The wage changes but employment cannot change
items.feedback: A labor-supply change moves wage and employment in opposite directions when labor demand is unchanged.

items.stem: Better scheduling software complements nurses and raises their productivity. What is the labor-demand effect?
options: Only movement along the original demand curve occurs
Labor supply must shift in the same direction
Demand for nurses shifts right
Labor demand cannot respond to product markets
items.feedback: Complementary scheduling software raises nurses’ productivity and value of marginal product, shifting labor demand right.

items.stem: A subsidy makes forklifts cheaper, and forklifts complement warehouse labor. How does this affect demand for warehouse labor?
options: Firms use more forklifts, warehouse-worker MPL rises, and labor demand shifts right
Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
items.feedback: Firms use more forklifts, warehouse-worker MPL rises, and labor demand shifts right. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: More irrigation equipment raises the productivity of farm labor. How does this affect demand for farm labor?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
Farm labor demand rises because complementary capital raises MPL
items.feedback: Farm labor demand rises because complementary capital raises MPL. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: Skilled technicians are needed to operate new diagnostic machines. How does this affect demand for skilled technicians when more diagnostic machines are installed?
options: More machines can raise demand for complementary technicians
Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
items.feedback: More machines can raise demand for complementary technicians. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: A construction boom raises demand for cranes. How does this affect demand for crane operators?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
Demand for complementary crane operators is also likely to rise
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
items.feedback: Demand for complementary crane operators is also likely to rise. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: More chefs make existing kitchen stations more productive. How does this affect demand for kitchen stations?
options: Demand for complementary kitchen capital can rise
Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
items.feedback: Demand for complementary kitchen capital can rise. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: Automated checkout substitutes for cashiers but requires maintenance technicians. How does this affect demand for cashiers and maintenance technicians?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
Cashier demand can fall while technician demand rises
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
items.feedback: Cashier demand can fall while technician demand rises. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: More classrooms raise the productivity of teachers when space was the bottleneck. How does this affect demand for teachers?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
Demand for teachers can rise because classroom capital complements labor
items.feedback: Demand for teachers can rise because classroom capital complements labor. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: A warehouse packing line expands its crew. The latest worker adds 19 orders, down from 24 for the worker before. How should the manager interpret this?
options: Total product must be falling
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 19 orders, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 24 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: The bakery still produces more after hiring, but the added output falls from 20 to 14 trays. Which conclusion follows?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 14 trays, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 20 is diminishing marginal product.
