options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 17 cases, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 25 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: A hotel housekeeping team expands its crew. The latest worker adds 8 rooms, down from 11 for the worker before. How should the manager interpret this?
options: Total product must be falling
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 8 rooms, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 11 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: Output at a warehouse rises from 210 to 234 orders when staffing rises from 6 to 7. Calculate marginal product per added worker.
options: 24 total additional orders
234 total orders
33.4 orders per worker
24 orders per added worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (234 − 210) ÷ (7 − 6) = 24 orders per added worker.

items.stem: Output at a machine shop rises from 90 to 99 parts when staffing rises from 5 to 6. Calculate marginal product per added worker.
options: 9 total additional parts
99 total parts
9 parts per added worker
16.5 parts per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (99 − 90) ÷ (6 − 5) = 9 parts per added worker.

items.stem: Output at a restaurant rises from 160 to 180 meals when staffing rises from 7 to 8. Calculate marginal product per added worker.
options: 20 total additional meals
20 meals per added worker
180 total meals
22.5 meals per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (180 − 160) ÷ (8 − 7) = 20 meals per added worker.

items.stem: Output at a catering firm rises from 96 to 118 orders when staffing rises from 8 to 10. Calculate marginal product per added worker.
options: 22 total additional orders
118 total orders
11.8 orders per worker
11 orders per added worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (118 − 96) ÷ (10 − 8) = 11 orders per added worker.

items.stem: Output at a coffee roastery rises from 48 to 55 batches when staffing rises from 3 to 4. Calculate marginal product per added worker.
options: 7 total additional batches
55 total batches
7 batches per added worker
13.8 batches per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (55 − 48) ÷ (4 − 3) = 7 batches per added worker.

items.stem: Healthcare labor supply shifts from SL0 to SL1, with DL unchanged. How many additional workers are employed at the new equilibrium?
options: 200 workers
4,000 workers
6,000 workers
2,000 workers
items.feedback: Employment rises from 4,000 to 6,000, so 2,000 additional workers are employed.

items.stem: Labor supply changes from SL0 to SL1. A student says this shows only the effect of a change in wages. Compare labor supplied on the two curves at $20. Does that comparison support the claim?
options: Supply changes from 5,000 to 1,000 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 0 workers; the demand curve must also shift left by 4,000 at every wage.
Supply is lower at $20, so the new curve shows less willingness to work caused solely by a lower construction wage.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 0 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
items.feedback: At $20, SL0 gives 4,000 workers and SL1 gives 0. Worker exit reduces the quantity available at each wage. A wage change by itself moves along a supply curve rather than relocating it.

items.stem: The landscaping crew still produces more after hiring, but the added output falls from 9 to 6 yards. Which conclusion follows?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 6 yards, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 9 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: The machine shop still produces more after hiring, but the added output falls from 6 to 3 parts. Which conclusion follows?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 3 parts, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 6 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: A landscaping crew increases labor from 3 to 5 workers, and output rises from 42 to 58 yards. What is MPL over this change?
options: 16 total additional yards
58 total yards
11.6 yards per worker
8 yards per added worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (58 − 42) ÷ (5 − 3) = 8 yards per added worker.

items.stem: A farm loses irrigation capacity, reducing what its field workers can harvest. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: All factors must be substitutes
Less complementary capital lowers worker MPL and labor demand
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
items.feedback: Less complementary capital lowers worker MPL and labor demand. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: A new training program lowers the cost of becoming an electrician. What happens to labor supply?
options: There is movement along an unchanged labor-supply curve
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Worker productivity must fall
Electrician labor supply shifts right over time
items.feedback: This nonwage determinant changes how many workers are willing or able to work at a given wage, shifting labor supply.

items.stem: Many electricians retire, reducing labor supply. With labor demand unchanged, what happens to the equilibrium wage and employment?
options: Both wage and employment rise
Both wage and employment fall
The wage changes but employment cannot change
The equilibrium wage rises and electrician employment falls
items.feedback: A labor-supply decrease moves wage and employment in opposite directions when labor demand is unchanged.

items.stem: A machine replaces routine packaging tasks. What is the labor-demand effect?
options: Only movement along the original demand curve occurs
Labor supply must shift in the same direction
Labor demand cannot respond to product markets
Demand for packaging labor shifts left when capital substitutes for labor
items.feedback: When capital substitutes for routine packaging labor, firms demand fewer packaging workers at each wage, shifting labor demand left.

items.stem: A catering company expands its crew. The latest worker adds 9 events, down from 13 for the worker before. How should the manager interpret this?
options: Total product must be falling
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 9 events, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 13 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: The bottling line adds 2 workers and gains 50 cases of output. What is the marginal product per worker?
options: 50 total additional cases
25 cases per added worker
550 total cases
45.8 cases per worker
items.feedback: MPL is the change in output divided by the change in labor: (550 − 500) ÷ (12 − 10) = 25 cases per added worker.

items.stem: Self-checkout machines replace routine cashier tasks. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
Capital substitutes for cashier labor and reduces cashier demand
items.feedback: Capital substitutes for cashier labor and reduces cashier demand. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: Remote-work options make software jobs more attractive to qualified workers. What happens to labor supply?
options: There is movement along an unchanged labor-supply curve
Labor supply to those jobs shifts right
Labor demand necessarily shifts in the same direction
Worker productivity must fall
items.feedback: This nonwage determinant changes how many workers are willing or able to work at a given wage, shifting labor supply.

items.stem: Stricter licensing reduces the supply of dental assistants. With labor demand unchanged, what happens to the equilibrium wage and employment?
options: Both wage and employment rise
The wage rises and employment falls
Both wage and employment fall
The wage changes but employment cannot change
items.feedback: A labor-supply decrease moves wage and employment in opposite directions when labor demand is unchanged.

items.stem: The selling price of solar installations falls. What is the labor-demand effect?
options: Only movement along the original demand curve occurs
Installer labor demand shifts left, other things equal
Labor supply must shift in the same direction
Labor demand cannot respond to product markets
items.feedback: A lower price for solar installations reduces the value of installers’ marginal product, shifting installer labor demand left, other things equal.

items.stem: Supply shifts from SL0 to SL1 while DL is unchanged. The wage initially remains $20. How large is the labor surplus, and which way will it push wages?
options: A 4,000-worker surplus, putting downward pressure on wage.
A 2,000-worker surplus, putting downward pressure on wage.
A 4,000-worker surplus, but this is the number employed after wages finish adjusting.
An 8,000-worker surplus, because all workers willing to work at $20 are surplus workers.
items.feedback: At $20, new supply is 8,000 and demand is 4,000, so excess supply is 4,000. This creates downward wage pressure; the gap is not employment after adjustment.

items.stem: Supply shifts from SL0 to SL1 while DL is unchanged. The wage initially remains $20. How large is the shortage of labor, and which way will it push wages?
options: A 4,000-worker shortage, putting upward pressure on wage.
A 2,000-worker shortage, putting upward pressure on wage.
A 4,000-worker shortage, which means 4,000 workers are unemployed at this wage.
No shortage, because the plotted quantity of labor supplied at $20 is zero.
items.feedback: At $20, demand is 4,000 and new supply is zero. The 4,000-worker shortage is unmet demand for labor, putting upward pressure on wages; it is not unemployment.

items.stem: Why is the minimum wage in the graph binding, and how far above the competitive wage is it?
options: $5 above it; the legal lower bound prevents adjustment to the market-clearing wage.
$10 above it; the legal lower bound prevents adjustment to the market-clearing wage.
$5 above it; a lower bound binds because any positive minimum wage fixes all wages.
$10 above it; a lower bound binds because any positive minimum wage fixes all wages.
items.feedback: The minimum is $20 and equilibrium is $15, a $5 gap. A floor above equilibrium rules out the wage that would clear the market; positivity alone does not make it binding.

items.stem: The monopsonist has chosen to hire 4,000 nurses. In the graph, what hourly wage does it pay, and which curve determines that wage?
options: $20, read from labor supply.
$25, read from labor supply.
$20, read from marginal factor cost.
$30, the marginal cost of hiring the last nurse.
items.feedback: At 4,000 nurses (40 hundreds), labor supply shows $20 per hour. The $30 MFC includes the extra wage expense associated with expanding employment; it is not the wage paid.

items.stem: Labor supply shifts from SL0 to SL1. What are equilibrium employment before and after the shift? Does this adjustment shift labor demand or move the market along it?
options: 3,000 and 5,000; both equilibria lie on the same demand schedule.
4,000 and 6,000; a lower wage by itself creates a different demand schedule.
3,000 and 5,000; a lower wage by itself creates a different demand schedule.
4,000 and 6,000; both equilibria lie on the same demand schedule.
items.feedback: The equilibria at 40 and 60 hundreds both lie on DL. Supply changes, while the wage decline produces a change in quantity demanded along that single demand curve.

items.stem: Many construction workers leave the region. At $20, how many workers are available on each supply curve? Does this represent a supply shift or movement along a curve?
options: Supply changes from 5,000 to 1,000 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 0 workers; this is movement along a fixed supply curve caused solely by wage.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 0 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 5,000 to 1,000 workers; this is movement along a fixed supply curve caused solely by wage.
items.feedback: At $20, SL0 gives 4,000 workers and SL1 gives 0. Worker exit reduces the quantity available at each wage. A wage change by itself moves along a supply curve rather than relocating it.

items.stem: The market begins where SL0 and DL intersect. Better jobs in another industry draw workers away from construction. At a construction wage of $20, how many workers are available before and after this change? What does that comparison tell us?
options: Supply changes from 5,000 to 1,000 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 0 workers; availability changes at a given wage, shifting supply.
Supply changes from 4,000 to 0 workers; this measures the final decline in employment after wages adjust.
Construction supply shifts left, so the graph proves total employment across all industries falls by 4,000.
items.feedback: At $20, SL0 supplies 4,000 workers and SL1 supplies zero. Better alternatives reduce construction labor supply at any given wage. This fixed-wage gap is not the eventual employment change and does not measure employment in other industries.

items.stem: Compare the legal minimum with the market-clearing wage. How large is the gap, and will this policy create a labor surplus?
options: $10; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
$5; the floor is nonbinding, so it does not create a labor surplus.
$5; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
$10; a legal minimum requires pay to fall to that minimum and creates a labor surplus.
items.feedback: Equilibrium is $15 while the legal minimum is $10. Paying the market wage already complies with the floor. The $5 gap therefore creates neither a forced wage reduction nor policy-induced excess supply.

items.stem: How many nurses will the monopsonist hire, and which marginal comparison determines that choice?
options: 3,000 nurses; equate marginal factor cost with marginal revenue product.
4,000 nurses; equate the wage on supply with marginal revenue product.
3,000 nurses; equate the wage on supply with marginal revenue product.
4,000 nurses; equate marginal factor cost with marginal revenue product.
items.feedback: MFC and MRP intersect at 40 hundreds, or 4,000 nurses. A monopsonist compares the extra hiring expenditure with the extra revenue generated; supply = MRP is the competitive benchmark instead.

items.stem: With equipment and floor space fixed, marginal output at a bottling line falls from 35 to 27 cases as another worker joins. What principle is operating?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
Average product must equal marginal product
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 27 cases, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 35 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: For the next worker, a cabinet shop estimates 2 additional cabinets at $28 each. Compare that contribution with the $50 hourly wage.
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Hire the worker because VMP exceeds the wage
Do not hire because the wage is a fixed cost
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $56 per hour (2 × $28). Because $56 exceeds $50, the added value is greater than labor cost.

items.stem: The market wage for landscapers rises. How should the firm's labor-demand response be represented?
options: A shift of labor demand
A shift of labor supply
Movement up the landscaper demand curve
No change in the firm's labor choice
items.feedback: The wage is the price of labor, so changing it changes quantity of labor demanded along the existing curve.

items.stem: A firm can use either paralegals or document-review software for the same task. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: The scenario identifies software and paralegal labor as substitutes
All factors must be substitutes
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
items.feedback: The scenario identifies software and paralegal labor as substitutes. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: A new machine replaces manual cutting but makes finishing workers more productive. How does this affect demand for manual cutters and finishing workers?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
Demand can fall for cutting labor and rise for complementary finishing labor
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
items.feedback: Demand can fall for cutting labor and rise for complementary finishing labor. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: The roofing crew still produces more after hiring, but the added output falls from 8 to 6 roof sections. Which conclusion follows?
options: Total product must be falling
The latest worker has negative marginal product
Average product must equal marginal product
Marginal product is diminishing even though total product may still rise
items.feedback: The added worker still contributes 6 roof sections, so total product can rise. The smaller increment relative to 8 is diminishing marginal product.

items.stem: At a packing plant, the marginal worker produces value from 10 extra cases sold for $6 apiece. How does a $65 wage affect the hiring decision?
options: Hire whenever marginal product is positive
Compare total output with the wage instead
Hire because any positive VMP raises profit
Do not hire the worker because VMP is below the wage
items.feedback: The worker's VMP is $60 per hour (10 × $6). Because $60 is below $65, the worker costs more than the added output value.

items.stem: Homeowners cut spending on landscaping services. How should the firm's labor-demand response be represented?
options: Movement along the original labor-demand curve
A shift of labor supply
No change in the firm's labor choice
A leftward shift of landscaper labor demand
items.feedback: The product demand changes the value of labor at a given wage, so the labor-demand curve shifts.

items.stem: Engineers become more effective when supported by skilled technicians. What relationship among productive inputs does the scenario imply?
options: All factors must be substitutes
The two labor types are complements in this production setting
All factors must be complements
Only the wage can affect factor demand
items.feedback: The two labor types are complements in this production setting. Factor relationships depend on the production process described; they are not universally substitutes or complements.

items.stem: The wage for technicians rises with all demand determinants fixed. What is the labor-demand effect?
options: The labor-demand curve shifts
Labor supply must shift in the same direction
Labor demand cannot respond to product markets
Quantity of technicians demanded falls along the existing curve
items.feedback: The wage changes quantity of labor demanded along the curve.

items.stem: An engineering shortage delays every major building project. How does this affect demand for complementary construction inputs?
options: Demand for every factor moves in the same direction
Only factor supply can change
No cross-factor effect is possible in competitive markets
Demand for complementary construction labor and equipment can decline
items.feedback: Demand for complementary construction labor and equipment can decline. The direction follows the stated technological relationship between inputs, not a blanket rule about all factors.

items.stem: If fiscal expansion raises interest rates and reduces investment, the final AD shift is likely:
options: Larger because crowding out amplifies it
Smaller because crowding out offsets it
Zero because fiscal policy cannot affect AD
Negative because taxes always rise
items.feedback: Crowding out weakens the final effect of fiscal expansion on AD.

items.stem: The multiplier effect exists because one person's spending becomes
options: another person's income
a lower reserve requirement
a decrease in government spending
a fall in money demand every time
items.feedback: The multiplier works because spending becomes income, and some of that income gets spent again.

items.stem: The movement from the first AD shift to the larger final AD shift represents
options: the multiplier effect
monetary neutrality
the Fisher effect
a reserve requirement
items.feedback: The multiplier effect is the extra AD shift caused by income leading to additional consumption spending.

items.stem: Crowding out weakens fiscal expansion because higher government spending can raise interest rates and reduce
options: private investment
tax collections automatically to zero
the price level immediately
the money multiplier to infinity
items.feedback: Crowding out offsets fiscal expansion by reducing private investment when interest rates rise.

items.stem: Which situation would make the multiplier effect larger?
options: A higher MPC
A lower MPC
More crowding out
A higher reserve requirement
items.feedback: A higher MPC means more extra income is spent, which makes the multiplier larger.

items.stem: Which situation would make fiscal stimulus less powerful?
options: Strong crowding out
A high MPC with no interest-rate effect
A large initial increase in government spending
A high willingness to consume extra income
items.feedback: Crowding out weakens fiscal stimulus by reducing private investment.

items.stem: Government purchases and induced spending move demand from AD1 to AD3. If crowding out leaves demand at AD2, how much of the original expansion has been offset?
options: Part of it: final demand remains above AD1 but below AD3.
More than all of it: final demand lies below the original AD1.
None of it: the distance from AD2 to AD3 is additional induced spending.
All of it: reaching AD2 means spending has returned to its initial curve.
items.feedback: At a common price AD2 lies between AD1 and AD3. Crowding out reduces the gross expansion but does not reverse it. Identifying the offset requires distinguishing the original, gross and final demand positions.

items.stem: A fiscal package produces a gross $200 billion rightward AD shift in a simplified expenditure model. Crowding out produces a total $60 billion leftward AD offset, including all induced spending effects of the displaced investment. What net AD increase should policy analysis use?
options: $140 billion
$260 billion
$200 billion
$60 billion
items.feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 200 − 60 = $140 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

items.stem: If MPC rises from 0.5 to 0.8, the government purchases multiplier changes from:
options: 2 to 5
5 to 2
items.feedback: The multiplier is 1/(1-MPC), so it rises from 2 to 5.

items.stem: If the government raises spending by $50 billion and the multiplier is 3, the total increase in aggregate demand before crowding out is:
options: $50 billion
$100 billion
$150 billion
$200 billion
items.feedback: The total demand increase before crowding out is $50 billion × 3 = $150 billion.

items.stem: If MPC = 0.6 and income rises by $1,000, consumption rises by
items.feedback: Consumption rises by MPC times the change in income: 0.6 x $1,000 = $600.

items.stem: If MPC = 0.6, the simple spending multiplier is
items.feedback: The multiplier is 1 / (1 - 0.6) = 1 / 0.4 = 2.5.

items.stem: If MPC = 0.8 and government spending increases by $50 billion, the simple multiplier predicts a total AD increase of
options: $250 billion
$40 billion
$62.5 billion
$50 billion
items.feedback: With MPC = 0.8, the multiplier is 5. Total increase is 5 x $50 billion = $250 billion.

items.stem: A fiscal package produces a gross $300 billion rightward AD shift in a simplified expenditure model. Crowding out produces a total $80 billion leftward AD offset, including all induced spending effects of the displaced investment. What net AD increase should policy analysis use?
options: $220 billion
$380 billion
$80 billion
$300 billion
items.feedback: The two magnitudes are both total AD changes: 300 − 80 = $220 billion. Do not multiply the stated total offset again. This is an AD shift, not a guaranteed equal increase in equilibrium GDP.

items.stem: The desired net AD increase is $330. MPC is 0.5, and a total AD crowding-out offset of $110 is expected after induced effects. What purchases increase reaches the target?
options: $660; multiply the target by two, omitting the offset.
$110; subtract the offset before reversing the multiplier.
$220; divide target plus total offset by the multiplier.
$440; add the offset without reversing the multiplier.
items.feedback: 2ΔG−110=330, so ΔG=(330+110)/2=220. Reverse the net-effect equation; the offset is not an autonomous component to multiply again.

items.stem: An increase in government purchases of $120 raises AD by $480 before crowding out in the simple model. What MPC does this imply, and does it determine how much aggregate demand will rise after crowding out?
options: MPC: 0.25; the saving share equals the marginal consumption share.
MPC: 0.75; the increase before crowding out does not establish the final increase.
MPC: 4; the gross spending ratio equals the marginal consumption share.
MPC: 0.75; the increase before crowding out establishes the same final increase.
items.feedback: The spending multiplier is 4 = 1/(1 − MPC), so MPC = 0.75. This gives the demand increase before crowding out. Later crowding out can reduce the final increase.

items.stem: Two governments each increase purchases by $130. Economy A has an MPC of 0.8, and crowding out reduces its total increase in aggregate demand by $390. Economy B has an MPC of 0.5 and no crowding out. How do the final increases in aggregate demand compare?
options: Both net effects are $260; A's larger gross multiplier is offset by greater crowding out
A has the larger net effect $650; a larger MPC always wins
B has zero effect because a lower MPC eliminates every induced round
A has a negative net effect because the total crowding-out amount must be multiplied by five again
items.feedback: A: 5×130−390=260. B: 2×130=260. A larger increase before crowding out need not mean a larger increase afterward.

items.stem: Fiscal expansion would add $100 to AD before crowding out. Higher rates reduce AD by a total $30 after induced investment effects. What net increase remains?
items.feedback: Subtract the already-total offset once: 100−30=70.

items.stem: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Moving from AD1 to AD2 changes output from:
options: Y1 to Y2
Y2 to Y1
Y2 to Y3
Y3 to Y1
items.feedback: At the same price level, output rises from Y1 to Y2 when AD shifts from AD1 to AD2.

items.stem: Refer to the AD graph with constant price level P. Which curve shows the largest aggregate demand level?
options: AD1
AD2
AD3
P
items.feedback: AD3 is farthest to the right, so it shows the largest AD at price level P.

items.stem: Which policy is expansionary fiscal policy?
options: Increasing government spending
Selling government bonds by the Fed
Raising reserve requirements
Increasing the discount rate
items.feedback: Expansionary fiscal policy uses higher government spending or lower taxes to raise aggregate demand.

items.stem: Which policy is contractionary fiscal policy?
options: Increasing taxes
Buying government bonds by the Fed
Lowering reserve requirements
Cutting the discount rate
items.feedback: Higher taxes are contractionary fiscal policy because they reduce disposable income and aggregate demand.

items.stem: A tax cut shifts aggregate demand right mainly because it
options: raises disposable income and consumption
raises reserve requirements
lowers the money multiplier directly
forces banks to hold more reserves
items.feedback: A tax cut raises disposable income, which can increase consumption and shift AD right.

items.stem: A cut in government purchases shifts aggregate demand left because
options: government spending is a component of aggregate demand
money demand automatically rises
banks stop creating money
MPC becomes zero
items.feedback: Government purchases are part of AD, so reducing G shifts AD left.

items.stem: If Congress increases infrastructure spending during a recession, the direct effect is to
options: shift aggregate demand right
shift aggregate demand left
reduce the money supply
raise reserve requirements
items.feedback: Higher infrastructure spending raises G and shifts AD right.

items.stem: If the government raises taxes during an expansion, the likely AD effect is
options: AD shifts left
AD shifts right
AD becomes vertical
money supply increases automatically
items.feedback: Higher taxes reduce disposable income and consumption, shifting AD left.

items.stem: Congress increases government purchases by $80 billion while households cut consumption by $50 billion for unrelated reasons. Before multiplier effects, the net direct change in aggregate demand is:
options: A $30 billion decrease.
No change.
A $30 billion increase.
A $130 billion increase.
items.feedback: Government purchases add $80 billion while consumption subtracts $50 billion.

items.stem: A $120 billion tax rebate is issued and households spend 65 percent of the added disposable income initially. What is the first-round consumption increase?
options: $42 billion.
$184.6 billion.
$78 billion.
$120 billion.
items.feedback: First-round consumption is 0.65 × $120 billion = $78 billion.

items.stem: A temporary tax cut is mostly saved because households expect it to be reversed next year. Compared with a tax cut that is mostly spent, the AD shift is:
options: Smaller.
Necessarily leftward.
Identical.
Larger.
items.feedback: A smaller consumption response weakens the tax cut’s effect on aggregate demand.

items.stem: A tax increase of $60 billion reduces consumption by $42 billion in the first round. The implied MPC is:
items.feedback: MPC = $42 billion / $60 billion = 0.70.

items.stem: An economy faces a positive AD shock of $240 billion. If policymakers use a tax increase that reduces disposable income by $100 billion and MPC is 0.8, what is the first-round consumption reduction?
options: $80 billion
$100 billion
$20 billion
$500 billion
items.feedback: The first-round consumption reduction is MPC times the disposable income change: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

items.stem: A recessionary economy receives a temporary tax rebate. Households use half to repay debt, save one quarter, and spend one quarter. How much of the rebate immediately increases consumption?
options: 50 percent of the rebate.
100 percent of the rebate.
75 percent of the rebate.
25 percent of the rebate.
items.feedback: Only the portion spent on current consumption directly raises the consumption component of AD.

items.stem: A tax cut raises disposable income by $100 billion. If MPC = 0.8, what is the first-round increase in consumption?
options: $80 billion
$20 billion
$100 billion
$125 billion
items.feedback: The first-round consumption increase is MPC times disposable income: 0.8 x $100 billion = $80 billion.

items.stem: Government sends $80 in transfers rather than buying output. With MPC 0.6, how do government purchases and consumption initially change, and what is the total effect on aggregate demand in a simple fixed-price model with no other changes?
options: G: +$80; initial C: $0; total AD: +$200.
G: $0; initial C: −$48; total AD: −$120.
G: $0; initial C: +$48; total AD: +$120.
G: $0; initial C: $0; total AD: $0.
items.feedback: Transfers are not government purchases, but recipients can spend part of them. Initial C=.6×transfer; multiplying by 1/(1−.6)=2.5 gives total 1.5×transfer.

items.stem: A tax increase of $90 is announced, but households expect it to be temporary and reduce consumption by less than the estimate based on the marginal propensity to consume. How should the smaller initial consumption response affect the use of the spending multiplier?
options: The budget identity proves consumption falls exactly by the full tax increase
Use the consumption response supported by the evidence before calculating the additional spending it induces
The tax increase must expand consumption because temporary taxes always reverse signs
The spending multiplier must be negative because the initial response is smaller
items.feedback: The multiplier calculation depends on how consumption initially responds. If expectations change that response, use the response supported by the evidence. A budget identity does not determine how much households change their spending.

items.stem: In a fixed-price economy with idle resources and MPC 0.75, a tax cut of $100 and a purchases increase of $100 are considered separately. Which comparison distinguishes the initial and multiplied effects?
options: The purchases plan initially adds $100 and ultimately $400; the tax cut initially adds $75 and ultimately $300
Both plans initially add $100 and ultimately $400; households spend the entire tax cut
The purchases plan adds only $100; the tax cut adds $400 because taxes have the larger multiplier
Both plans contract AD by $100; taxes and purchases have the same sign
items.feedback: Purchases directly enter demand; only the MPC share of a tax cut initially becomes consumption. With multiplier 1/(1−.75)=4, the respective total effects are 4 G and 3×tax cut.

items.stem: The government reduces purchases $20 during a recession. With spending multiplier 2 and no offsets, how does this affect the existing demand shortfall?
options: It widens the shortfall by $10
It has no effect because purchases are transfers
It widens the shortfall by $40
It narrows the shortfall by $40
items.feedback: The negative purchases impulse is multiplied:−20×2=−40. It reinforces a demand recession.

items.stem: A $100 tax cut with MPC=.8 generates $80 of first-round consumption. An alternative is $90 of additional government purchases. At fixed prices, ignoring offsets and later induced spending rounds, which policy adds more to initial aggregate demand, and by how much?
options: The tax cut adds $10 more
Government purchases add $10 more
Government purchases add $90 more
The policies add the same amount
items.feedback: The repaired consumption result is $80. Direct government purchases add $90 to initial spending, so the purchase policy adds 90−80=$10 more. This compares initial effects, not full multipliers.

items.stem: If expected inflation rises while the real interest rate is unchanged, lenders will require
options: a higher nominal interest rate
a lower nominal interest rate
no repayment
a lower price level
items.feedback: Lenders care about purchasing power, so higher expected inflation is built into higher nominal interest rates.

items.stem: Two otherwise similar economies have the same long-run real interest rate, but expected inflation is 2 percent in one and 7 percent in the other. What should differ under the Fisher effect?
options: The second economy should tend to have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher.
The first economy should have a nominal interest rate about 5 percentage points higher instead because lower expected inflation raises nominal rates.
Both nominal rates must be identical because real rates match.
The second economy must have a real rate 5 points higher.
items.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

items.stem: Expected inflation falls from 6 percent to 2 percent while the long-run real interest rate remains 3 percent. What nominal-rate change is predicted?
options: The nominal rate rises from about 5 percent to about 9 percent.
The real rate falls from 3 percent to negative 1 percent automatically.
The nominal rate stays at 9 percent because only actual inflation matters.
The nominal rate falls from about 9 percent to about 5 percent.
items.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

items.stem: A one-year loan is priced when inflation is expected to be 3 percent. Actual inflation later turns out to be 8 percent. Which statement separates the Fisher effect from the realized return?
options: The Fisher effect uses actual inflation only and ignores expectations.
Unexpected inflation raises both parties’ realized real returns by the same amount.
Expected inflation influenced the nominal rate; actual inflation determines the realized real return.
The nominal rate must be rewritten after actual inflation is observed so the original expected rate no longer matters.
items.feedback: The nominal rate written into a contract reflects expected inflation at the time the contract is set; realized inflation determines the ex post real return.

items.stem: Expected inflation rises 6 percentage points while the equilibrium real interest rate falls 2 percentage points. What happens to the nominal interest rate approximately?
options: It rises about 4 percentage points because both expected inflation and the real rate matter.
It rises exactly 6 percentage points because the Fisher effect requires the real rate to remain fixed in every comparison.
It falls about 8 percentage points because expected inflation lowers nominal rates.
It is unchanged because the two components must always offset completely.
items.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

items.stem: Expected inflation falls sharply after a credible long-run policy change, but productive opportunities and saving behavior leave the real rate roughly unchanged. What does the Fisher effect predict?
options: Real interest rates must fall by exactly the same amount as expected inflation.
Nominal rates should stay fixed because only realized inflation affects contracts.
Nominal interest rates should fall as the inflation premium falls.
Nominal interest rates should rise because lower expected inflation raises the inflation premium.
items.feedback: The Fisher effect links expected inflation to the nominal interest rate, holding the underlying real interest rate constant in the long-run comparison.

items.stem: A lender expected 4 percent inflation and charged 9 percent nominal interest. Actual inflation was 8 percent. What happened to the realized real return?
options: It was lower than expected
It was higher than expected
It was unchanged
It became nominal GDP
items.feedback: Higher-than-expected inflation lowers the realized real return to lenders.

items.stem: Two long-run episodes have identical expected inflation, but the equilibrium real interest rate is higher in the second because investment demand is stronger. What should happen to the nominal rate?
options: It must be unchanged because identical expected inflation always forces identical nominal interest rates even when real saving and investment conditions differ.
It must be lower because stronger investment demand reduces nominal rates.
It must equal expected inflation because real rates disappear in the long run.
It should rise because the equilibrium real interest rate rose.
items.feedback: The one-for-one Fisher prediction requires holding the real interest rate fixed; if the real rate changes too, combine both changes.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. If the real interest rate is 3 percent and expected inflation rises from 4 percent to 9 percent, the Fisher effect predicts the nominal rate rises by:
options: 3 points
4 points
5 points
9 points
items.feedback: Expected inflation rises by 5 percentage points, so the nominal rate rises by 5 points.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. Expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 6 percent while the real interest rate stays at 2 percent. The nominal rate becomes:
options: 3 percent
5 percent
6 percent
8 percent
items.feedback: Nominal interest rate equals real interest rate plus expected inflation, so 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

items.stem: If the nominal interest rate is 9 percent and expected inflation is 4 percent, the real interest rate is approximately
options: 5 percent
13 percent
4 percent
36 percent
items.feedback: Real interest rate is approximately nominal rate minus expected inflation: 9 - 4 = 5 percent.

items.stem: If the real interest rate is 2 percent and expected inflation is 6 percent, the nominal interest rate is approximately
options: 8 percent
4 percent
3 percent
12 percent
items.feedback: Nominal interest rate is approximately real interest rate plus expected inflation: 2 + 6 = 8 percent.

items.stem: Use the Fisher approximation. If expected inflation rises from 3 percent to 8 percent and the real interest rate remains 2 percent, what happens to the nominal interest rate?
options: It rises from 5 percent to 10 percent.
It falls from 5 percent to 2 percent.
It rises from 3 percent to 8 percent.
It stays at 2 percent.
items.feedback: Nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation. It rises from 2 + 3 = 5 to 2 + 8 = 10.

items.stem: For a $100 loan, expected inflation rises from 2% to 5% while the required expected real return falls from 4% to 3%. Under the Fisher approximation, which nominal-rate comparison is correct?
options: The nominal rate remains 6%; opposite movements in components must cancel exactly
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 8%; the real-rate decline partly offsets the inflation-expectation increase
The nominal rate rises from 6% to 9%; the real rate must be held fixed despite the supplied change
The nominal rate falls from 6% to 5%; subtract expected inflation from the required real return
items.feedback: Initially i≈r+πe=4+2=6. Later i≈3+5=8. A one-for-one response to expected inflation requires a fixed real rate, which is not the case here.

items.stem: A $120 fixed-rate loan has nominal interest 7% when expected inflation is 3%. Actual inflation later turns out to be 6%. Which pair separates the rate-setting prediction from the realized outcome?
options: The expected real return was about 4%; the realized real return is about 1%, without changing the contractual nominal rate
The expected real return was about 1%; the nominal contract automatically resets to 10% after inflation is observed
Both expected and realized real returns are 4% because the lender chose a fixed nominal rate
The nominal rate becomes 6% because actual inflation replaces the contractual rate
items.feedback: Fisher rate setting uses expected inflation at agreement; ex post purchasing power uses actual inflation. Thus 7−3=4% expected and 7−6=1% realized; the nominal contract remains 7%.

items.stem: In a loan market financing $140 of projects, nominal rates fall 2 percentage points while the expected real rate is unchanged. Within the Fisher approximation, what inference follows and what remains unproved?
options: Expected inflation rose 2 points; actual future inflation must rise equally
Actual inflation already fell 2 points; no expectation assumption is needed
The real rate fell 2 points despite the stated fixed-real-rate condition
Expected inflation fell 2 points; actual future inflation need not equal that forecast
items.feedback: With Δr=0, Δi≈Δπe. A two-point nominal decline implies a two-point expectation decline in this model, but forecasts are not necessarily realized.

items.stem: Using the Fisher approximation, expected inflation rises from 6% to 8% while the expected real rate remains 2%. What new nominal rate is consistent with both conditions?
items.feedback: Nominal≈real+expected inflation=2+8=10%, up from 8%.

items.stem: A contract quotes 8% nominal interest and expected inflation 6%. If a new contract has expected inflation 3% with the same expected real return, what nominal rate should it quote?
items.feedback: Original expected real return≈8−6=2%; new nominal≈2+3=5%.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. How does the demand shift change equilibrium?
options: The rate rises from 1.0 to 1.2 and quantity rises from 100 to 150
The rate falls from 1.2 to 1.0 and quantity falls from 150 to 100
The rate rises from 1.0 to 1.2 while quantity stays at 100
The rate remains 1.0 while quantity rises from 100 to 150
items.feedback: The equilibrium moves along S0 from A to B, raising both the foreign-currency price of a dollar and the quantity exchanged.

items.stem: The market begins at A on D0 and S0. Demand shifts to D1 while S0 stays fixed. By how much does equilibrium quantity change?
options: It decreases by 50
It increases by 100
It does not change
It increases by 50
items.feedback: Equilibrium quantity rises from 100 at A to 150 at B, an increase of 50.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What happens when supply moves from S0 to S1?
options: Quantity rises from 100 to 150 and the rate rises from 0.8 to 1.0
Quantity stays at 100 and the rate falls to 0.8
Quantity rises from 100 to 150 and the rate falls from 1.0 to 0.8
Quantity falls from 150 to 100 and the rate rises from 0.8 to 1.0
items.feedback: The equilibrium changes from A on S0 to B on S1 along unchanged D0.

items.stem: A rise in foreign demand for domestic goods shifts which side of the currency market?
options: Supply of domestic currency shifts left
Demand for domestic currency shifts right
Supply of domestic currency shifts right
Demand for domestic currency shifts left
items.feedback: Foreign buyers require more domestic currency at each exchange rate to purchase the additional exports.

items.stem: An increase in NCO changes the foreign-exchange market by shifting:
options: Domestic-currency supply right
Domestic-currency demand right
Domestic-currency supply left
Domestic-currency demand left
items.feedback: More net foreign-asset purchases cause residents to supply more domestic currency at every exchange rate.

items.stem: What condition defines equilibrium in the market for U.S. dollars?
options: The exchange rate equals the value at which demand for dollars would fall to zero.
Everyone buying dollars has the same reason for doing so as everyone selling dollars.
The quantity of dollars supplied stays fixed regardless of the quantity demanded.
The quantity of dollars demanded equals the quantity supplied at the prevailing exchange rate.
items.feedback: At the equilibrium exchange rate, the quantity of dollars people want to buy equals the quantity they want to sell. Equality of quantities at that rate, rather than identical motives or curve intercepts, clears the market.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What appreciation is associated with the demand increase?
options: An increase of 0.5 foreign-currency unit per dollar, or 50 percent
An increase of 0.2 foreign-currency unit per dollar, or 20 percent
A decrease of 0.2 foreign-currency unit per dollar, or 16.7 percent
An increase of 0.2 foreign-currency unit per dollar, or 25 percent
items.feedback: The rate rises from 1.0 to 1.2; 0.2 divided by the initial 1.0 equals 20 percent.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Which calculation correctly describes the move from A to B after supply shifts?
options: Quantity rises 50 percent and the dollar depreciates 20 percent
Quantity rises 20 percent and the dollar depreciates 50 percent
Quantity rises 50 percent and the dollar appreciates 20 percent
Quantity falls 33.3 percent and the dollar depreciates 25 percent
items.feedback: Quantity rises from 100 to 150, or 50 percent. The rate falls from 1.0 to 0.8 foreign-currency unit per dollar, a 20 percent depreciation.

items.stem: The market begins at A on D0 and S0. Demand shifts to D1 while S0 stays fixed. What is the change in equilibrium quantity?
options: An increase of 150 units
An increase of 50 units
Zero
A decrease of 50 units
items.feedback: Quantity rises from 100 at A to 150 at B.

items.stem: Foreign consumers shift spending toward domestic goods. What happens in the currency market?
options: Currency demand rises and the domestic currency appreciates
Currency supply rises and the domestic currency depreciates
Currency demand falls and the domestic currency depreciates
Currency supply falls while the exchange rate is unchanged
items.feedback: The export-demand increase raises demand for domestic currency, increasing its equilibrium value with supply fixed.

items.stem: Domestic residents reduce foreign-asset purchases. What happens to currency supply?
options: It shifts right
Demand shifts left
There is movement down along supply
It shifts left
items.feedback: Lower NCO means fewer domestic-currency units are offered in exchange for foreign currency.

items.stem: In the standard open-economy model, net capital outflow is fixed. A student says a higher exchange rate must increase the quantity supplied. Which correction distinguishes a movement along vertical supply from a shift?
options: Moving up the vertical supply curve raises both NCO and supplied quantity
A higher exchange rate shifts vertical supply right even with NCO fixed
Moving along vertical supply requires an increase in foreign demand at every rate
Moving up the vertical supply curve leaves quantity fixed; changing NCO shifts that curve
items.feedback: A vertical supply curve contains multiple exchange rates at one quantity. Moving along it does not change NCO; a change in NCO moves the whole curve horizontally. A separate demand shift can produce a new equilibrium rate at the same supplied quantity.

items.stem: A household buys a newly built home. In GDP accounting, this is counted as:
options: Consumption
Investment
Government purchases
Net exports
items.feedback: New residential construction is counted as investment, not consumption.

items.stem: A state government pays workers to repair highways. Which GDP component rises?
options: Consumption
Investment
Government purchases
Net exports
items.feedback: Government spending on goods and services is counted as government purchases.

items.stem: Which transaction increases investment in GDP accounting?
options: A household buys groceries
A firm buys new delivery trucks
The government sends unemployment benefits
A consumer buys imported shoes
items.feedback: Business purchases of new capital goods are investment.

items.stem: The federal government sends pension benefits and separately buys new rescue vehicles. Which transaction enters G directly?
options: Only the purchase of rescue vehicles
Only the payment of pension benefits
Both government transactions enter G directly
Neither transaction enters current government purchases
items.feedback: Transfers redistribute income and are excluded from G; a later purchase can enter the appropriate spending component.

items.stem: A developer completes a new apartment building that will be rented to households. How is the construction classified?
options: Household consumption
Government purchases
A financial transfer
Residential investment
items.feedback: New residential construction is counted as residential investment, even when the completed units will be rented to households.

items.stem: Why are imports subtracted in C + I + G + X − M?
options: Because every import directly reduces household consumption spending
To force exports and imports to carry opposite accounting signs
To remove foreign production already embedded in domestic spending
Because imported goods provide no value to domestic buyers
items.feedback: Imports are subtracted because imported final spending may already appear in C, I, or G and foreign production must not enter domestic GDP.

items.stem: A firm produces $500M in goods, sells $450M, and unintentionally accumulates $50M in inventories. Which GDP component includes the unsold goods?
options: Investment
Consumption
Government purchases
Net exports
items.feedback: Inventory accumulation is counted as investment, even when unplanned.

items.stem: A firm produces $10M of goods in December but sells $7M in December and $3M in January. How should the $3M be treated for December GDP?
options: It counts as inventory investment in December
It is excluded until January
It counts as consumption in December
It is subtracted from December GDP
items.feedback: Goods produced but not sold are counted as inventory investment in the period produced.

items.stem: A firm buys a new domestically produced machine for $1M and a share of stock in another company for $1M. What is the direct effect on GDP?
options: GDP rises $1M; the stock purchase is financial
GDP rises by $2M because both are investments
GDP does not change because firms made both purchases
GDP rises only from the stock purchase
items.feedback: Economic investment in GDP means new capital goods, not financial asset purchases.

items.stem: A retailer sells $4 million of goods produced last year and produces $6 million of new goods this year. What production enters this year’s GDP?
options: $4 million of current sales
$10 million of sales plus production
$2 million of net new production
$6 million of current production
items.feedback: GDP records the $6 million of goods produced this year. Selling $4 million of goods produced last year changes inventories but does not add new current production.

items.stem: Suppose C = $14T, I = $4T, G = $5T, exports = $3T, and imports = $4.5T. What is GDP?
A U.S. firm builds $100 million of equipment domestically and sells $70 million of it this year, keeping $30 million in inventory. What is counted in GDP?
options: $100 million because unsold output is inventory investment
$70 million because only sold goods count
$30 million because only inventory counts
$0 because business equipment is excluded
items.feedback: Current production counts whether sold or added to inventories, so all $100 million counts.

items.stem: If consumption is $12 trillion, investment is $4 trillion, government purchases are $5 trillion, exports are $3 trillion, and imports are $4 trillion, what is GDP?
options: $20 trillion
$21 trillion
$24 trillion
$28 trillion

items.stem: A U.S. firm produces $10 million in goods but sells only $7 million this year. The remaining $3 million is added to inventories. How much is counted in GDP?
options: $7 million
$3 million
$10 million
items.feedback: Unsold output is counted as inventory investment, so all $10 million is counted.

items.stem: Imported machinery costing $95 is purchased by a domestic firm; installation supplied domestically costs $23. Assume both enter gross investment. Which accounting adjustment avoids counting foreign production in domestic GDP?
options: G rises $95 and I rises $23; domestic GDP rises $118
I rises $118 and M rises $95; domestic GDP rises $23
I rises $23 and M rises $95; domestic GDP falls $72
I rises $118 and M is unchanged; domestic GDP rises $118
items.feedback: Gross investment includes the installed purchase, 95+23; subtracting imported machinery once through M leaves the $23 domestic installation service.

items.stem: A domestic firm sells $100 of last year's inventory to households and produces $24 of new goods that remain unsold. No other production occurs. How do the sales and inventory change enter consumption, investment and GDP?
options: C = $100, inventory I = $-76, GDP = $24
C = $100, inventory I = $24, GDP = $124
C = $0, inventory I = $-76, GDP = $-76
C = $100, inventory I = $76, GDP = $176
items.feedback: Consumption records the sale, but inventory investment is new accumulation 24 minus withdrawal 100. C+I = 100+(24−100) = $24, this year's production.

items.stem: Which pair is classified as investment in GDP accounting?
options: A pension payment plus a household appliance purchase
An imported restaurant meal plus a tax refund
A new home plus added business inventories
A used home plus a corporate bond purchase
items.feedback: GDP investment includes business fixed investment, residential construction, and changes in inventories.

items.stem: A household buys a newly produced domestic car for $30,000; a firm buys a newly produced domestic machine for $20,000. Which pair enters the expenditure accounts?
items.feedback: Household final purchases enter consumption; productive equipment purchased by a firm enters investment.

items.stem: A household buys an imported appliance for $500 and pays a domestic installer $100. Both payments enter consumption. How much does this transaction add to domestic GDP after the import offset?
items.feedback: Consumption rises 600, but imports subtract 500 through NX. The domestic installation 100 remains in GDP.

items.stem: A factory makes $100 of new domestic output and sells $80 this period. The unsold $20 stays in inventory. What current production total is recorded?
options: $80: only sold goods count
$120: production 100 plus inventory 20
$20: only inventory is new production
$100: sales 80 plus inventory investment 20
items.feedback: Unsold current production is inventory investment. Final sales 80 plus inventory accumulation 20 record the same 100 produced.

items.stem: A student says GDP can be measured by adding up either total income or total expenditure. Why is that true?
options: Each buyer’s spending becomes a seller’s income
GDP only counts income earned by households, not spending
The government adjusts income until it equals spending
Exports and imports must always be equal
items.feedback: The income and expenditure approaches match because each dollar spent becomes income to someone else.

items.stem: Which example best shows the income-expenditure identity in action?
options: $40 of meal spending becomes $40 of restaurant revenue.
A used car is resold and counted twice in GDP
A government transfer payment raises GDP directly
A household saves money under a mattress
items.feedback: The restaurant sale shows spending by the buyer becoming income to the seller.

items.stem: Which transaction is counted in U.S. GDP?
options: A U.S. company buys shares of another company
A U.S. household buys a used refrigerator
A German tourist pays for a hotel room in Florida
A U.S. citizen buys a used car from a neighbor
items.feedback: The hotel service is produced in the United States, so it counts in U.S. GDP.

items.stem: A laptop produced last year is sold used this year for $700. How does this affect this year's GDP?
options: GDP rises by $700
GDP rises only if the laptop was imported
GDP does not rise from the used-good sale
GDP rises by the original price
items.feedback: Used goods are not counted in current GDP because they were counted when first produced.

items.stem: A homeowner pays a contractor $12,000 to renovate a kitchen. Why is this counted in GDP?
options: It is a market service produced during the current period
It is a transfer payment
It is a used good
It is counted only if paid in cash
items.feedback: Paid renovation work is current market production and is counted in GDP.

items.stem: Which item would be excluded from GDP because it is non-market production?
options: A paid haircut
A restaurant meal
A person mowing their own lawn
A new home purchase
items.feedback: Unpaid work performed for yourself is generally not counted in GDP.

items.stem: A U.S. firm earns profits from a factory located in Vietnam. Why is this not part of U.S. GDP?
options: GDP counts production within U.S. borders, not income earned abroad by U.S. residents
Profits are excluded from GDP because GDP measures wage income rather than business income earned by firms
Foreign production enters U.S. GDP when the resulting goods or services are eventually sold to U.S. consumers
GDP assigns production to the owner's home country rather than to the country where the production occurs
items.feedback: GDP is domestic production. Income earned abroad relates more to national income measures, not U.S. GDP.

items.stem: A firm produces $600,000 of final output. It pays $350,000 in wages, $100,000 in rent, $50,000 in interest, and keeps $100,000 in profit. What does this example show about GDP measurement?
options: Expenditure on output and income earned from production both equal $600,000
Only wages count in GDP, so GDP is $350,000
Profit is excluded from GDP, so GDP is $500,000
GDP cannot be measured from income
items.feedback: The value of final output equals the income generated in producing it: wages, rent, interest, and profit all add to $600,000.

items.stem: Suppose expenditure GDP is $22 trillion. Income data show $13 trillion in wages, $3 trillion in rent and interest, $4 trillion in profit, and $2 trillion in other production income. What do these figures show?
options: The income and expenditure approaches both measure GDP at $22 trillion.
The income approach measures $20 trillion because other production income is excluded.
The expenditure approach measures $24 trillion because other production income is added again.
The figures cannot be compared because wages are excluded from the income approach.
items.feedback: The income categories sum to $22 trillion, matching expenditure GDP. The two approaches measure the same current domestic production from different sides.

items.stem: A U.S. company produces $2 million of software in Ireland and sells it to customers in Europe. How does this affect U.S. GDP?
options: It does not count in U.S. GDP
It counts in U.S. GDP because the firm is U.S.-owned
It counts as U.S. government purchases
It counts only if the software is downloaded in the U.S.
items.feedback: GDP is based on production within a country's borders, not ownership of the firm.

items.stem: A Canadian company produces cars in Tennessee and sells them to U.S. households. How are those cars treated in U.S. GDP?
options: They count because they were produced inside the United States
They do not count because the company is foreign-owned
They count only as imports
They count only as transfer payments
items.feedback: GDP counts production within national borders, regardless of whether the producer is domestically or foreign owned.

items.stem: A household pays $2,000 for illegal services and $2,000 for legal market services. Which statement best explains the GDP issue?
options: Legal services count; hidden or illegal production is often missed
Both are always fully counted because all services are visible
Neither counts because services are excluded from GDP
Only illegal activity counts because it is current production
items.feedback: GDP aims to count market production, but illegal or hidden activity is often excluded or poorly measured.

items.stem: Which transaction is most likely counted in current GDP?
options: A homeowner pays a licensed contractor to build a new deck
A homeowner builds a deck alone using leftover materials already owned
A household buys shares in a construction company
A collector resells an antique table
items.feedback: Paid current market production counts. Financial transactions, used-good sales, and unpaid household production generally do not.

items.stem: A household pays $30 for a restaurant meal, including $5 of sales tax. How should this be interpreted for GDP?
options: Count the final service; the tax is not government purchases
Only the pre-tax $25 counts because taxes are never linked to GDP
Only the $5 tax counts as government purchases
Nothing counts because meals are services
items.feedback: GDP counts the market value of final goods and services; taxes do not turn the meal into government purchases.

items.stem: A firm buys steel for $80, adds labor and capital services, and sells a machine for $230 to another firm. If the machine is newly produced and used in production, how much does GDP increase?
items.feedback: The newly produced machine is a final capital good, so its full market value of $230 is counted.

items.stem: Suppose firms sell $900 billion of final goods and households, firms, government, and foreigners buy all of it. What should total income from producing those goods equal?
options: $450 billion
$900 billion
It depends only on taxes
items.feedback: Total expenditure on final output becomes total income earned from producing that output.

items.stem: If total income generated by current production is $18 trillion, what is total expenditure on that production?
options: $9 trillion
$18 trillion
$36 trillion
Impossible to compare
items.feedback: In GDP accounting, total income and total expenditure are two ways of measuring the same economic activity.

items.stem: A farmer sells wheat to a miller for $100. The miller sells flour to a baker for $160. The baker sells bread to consumers for $250. How much is added to GDP?
items.feedback: GDP counts the final bread sale of $250, not each intermediate transaction separately.

items.stem: A domestic factory produces $92 of final goods, sells $67, and holds the remainder as new inventory. How much is counted in current GDP, and what happens to GDP when the remaining inventory is sold next year without new production?
options: Current GDP includes $92; next year's inventory sale is offset by inventory disinvestment
Current GDP includes $67; next year's sale adds the remaining output again
Current GDP includes $159; next year's sale contributes nothing
Current GDP includes $25; only unsold goods are counted this year
items.feedback: Production, not only sales, is counted: sales 67 plus inventory investment 25 equals 92. A later sale of that inventory is offset by a fall in inventories, avoiding a second count.

items.stem: A current domestic final sale is $96. Wages are $56, other production income is $15, and profit is the residual. A reviewer claims expenditure exceeds income because profit is omitted from the income account. Which calculation corrects the reviewer’s claim?
options: Profit is $71; adding it doubles total income
Profit is zero; the expenditure-income gap is genuine output
Profit is $25; adding it makes income equal the $96 expenditure
Profit is $40; only wages count as costs in the income account
items.feedback: The listed non-profit income totals $71. Residual profit is 96−71 = $25, bringing income to $96. Income and expenditure are two views of this same current production.

items.stem: Final domestic output sells for $210. Production income records show wages of $140 and rent and interest of $30. With no taxes, depreciation or discrepancy, what profit completes the income account?
items.feedback: All income from producing the output sums to 210. The missing profit is 210−140−30=40.

items.stem: A mill sells flour for $50 and a bakery sells the bread made from it to households for $120. The bakery’s value added is $70. Which GDP total agrees under both final-sales and value-added accounting?
items.feedback: Final bread sales 120 equal mill value added 50 plus bakery value added 70. Counting flour again with final sales double-counts it.

items.stem: A neighborhood app awards a visible badge for weekly recycling. Participation rises among users who value recognition but barely changes for others. What is the best interpretation?
options: A nonmonetary incentive can produce different responses across people
The badge guarantees recycling because everyone can see it
Recognition is not an incentive because no cash changes hands
Different responses prove the badge did not change any payoff
items.feedback: Recognition can change expected benefits, while its importance varies across users.

items.stem: A new toll reduces traffic on a busy road. What does this show?
options: People respond to the higher cost of using the road
Scarcity has been eliminated
The road is now a public good
Demand for driving must have increased
items.feedback: The toll raises the cost of using the road, which gives drivers an incentive to change behavior.

items.stem: A school rewards perfect attendance, and some sick students attend class. This is:
options: Proof that incentives never work.
A positive externality by definition.
An elimination of scarcity.
An unintended response to the incentive.
items.feedback: The reward increased attendance but also encouraged undesirable attendance while ill.

items.stem: A performance bonus is based only on the number of calls handled, and service quality falls. What design problem occurred?
options: The metric rewarded quantity while omitting quality.
Workers ignored all incentives.
The bonus created a public good.
Higher output necessarily means higher quality.
items.feedback: People may optimize the rewarded metric at the expense of unmeasured goals.

items.stem: A warehouse pays a bonus for packages shipped per hour but charges workers for verified damage. What response is most plausible?
options: Workers balance speed against the expected cost of damage
Workers maximize speed because only rewards affect behavior
Damage must fall to zero for the incentives to exist
Every worker chooses the same speed regardless of risk
items.feedback: The speed bonus and damage consequence change different parts of the worker’s payoff.

items.stem: A parking fine doubles, but patrols become rare. Why might violations change little?
options: The expected penalty may remain small because enforcement is unlikely
A larger statutory fine can never affect behavior when drivers know it exists
Drivers respond only to rewards, not penalties
Low enforcement guarantees more violations by every driver
items.feedback: Behavior responds to the expected consequence, which depends on both size and enforcement.

items.stem: Two employees receive the same attendance bonus. One changes her schedule; the other has caregiving duties and cannot. What does this show?
options: The same incentive can produce different responses under different constraints
The bonus was not an incentive for either employee because their outcomes differed
A valid incentive must change everyone’s behavior
Constraints matter only when incentives are nonmonetary
items.feedback: The bonus changes payoffs, but constraints and alternatives shape each response.

items.stem: A delivery app rewards drivers for accepting a high share of requests. Some drivers accept deliveries they are unlikely to complete and cancel later. What problem does this reveal?
options: The reward encourages drivers to improve their acceptance rating by taking requests they later cancel
The reward cannot be an incentive because cancellations rose after accepted jobs
Acceptance rate measures service quality perfectly
The response proves drivers ignored the metric
items.feedback: Drivers improve acceptance statistics while shifting the problem into later cancellations.

items.stem: A company offers either a $40 bonus or public recognition for completing training. Some workers value one more than the other. What follows?
options: Monetary and nonmonetary incentives can differ in strength across people
Only the cash option can change expected benefits
Recognition guarantees completion among all workers
Different preferences mean neither option is an incentive
items.feedback: Both rewards can alter benefits, but their value depends on the decision-maker.

items.stem: A gym charges a missed-appointment fee but waives it when members cancel a day ahead. Which decision does the rule most directly influence?
options: Whether members cancel early instead of simply not appearing
Whether every member continues the gym membership
Whether exercise produces health benefits
Whether members morally approve of cancellation rules
items.feedback: The avoidable fee makes advance cancellation more attractive relative to a no-show.

items.stem: A city gives bus riders a $2 subsidy per ride. Ridership rises, but crowding increases and wait times get longer. What is the best interpretation?
options: The subsidy changed incentives and produced an unintended consequence
The subsidy eliminated scarcity
The subsidy created a price floor
The subsidy proves marginal analysis is irrelevant
items.feedback: The subsidy encouraged more bus use, but the higher ridership created crowding and longer waits.

items.stem: A farm subsidy pays per acre planted with one crop. Farmers expand acreage onto less suitable land. Which part is the incentive and which is the response?
options: Per-acre payment is the incentive; expansion onto marginal land is a response
Expanded acreage is the incentive; payment is the outcome
Crop suitability is the incentive; planting is moral approval
The subsidy is neither because planting was already possible
items.feedback: The payment changes the benefit of each planted acre; land expansion is a resulting choice.

items.stem: A nonprofit grant rewards the number of people enrolled, not services completed. Enrollment rises and completion falls. Which measure is being optimized?
options: The funded enrollment count rather than the broader service objective
Completion because it is the organization’s stated mission
Both measures equally because they concern the same clients
Neither measure because nonprofits do not respond to funding
items.feedback: The grant rewards entry into the program, so effort shifts toward enrollment rather than completion.

items.stem: A bonus tied only to sales volume causes excessive discounting. What happened?
options: Workers ignored the bonus and changed discounting for unrelated market reasons
Workers optimized the rewarded metric rather than total profit
The bonus eliminated every tradeoff involved in making sales
Sales volume became a public good shared equally by all firms
items.feedback: The bonus raises the payoff to volume even when discounts make some sales unprofitable.

items.stem: A fee changes behavior for some people but not others. What is the best explanation?
options: The fee is not an incentive.
All people have identical marginal benefits.
People face different constraints, preferences, and alternatives.
Only laws create incentives.
items.feedback: The same fee can change the relative attractiveness of an action by different amounts for different people. Someone with a close substitute may switch, while someone with few alternatives or a high benefit from the action may continue. An unchanged choice does not mean the fee created no incentive.

items.stem: A policy subsidizes an action many people already planned to take. What limits additional impact?
options: Every payment creates an equal new action.
Subsidies cannot affect behavior.
The action has no opportunity cost.
Much of the money pays for actions already planned.
items.feedback: People who would take the action without the subsidy can receive a payment without changing their behavior. Those payments are inframarginal: they support actions already planned rather than inducing additional ones. The policy’s additional impact depends on how many people change their choice because of the subsidy.

items.stem: A call center rewards short calls and separately penalizes repeat complaints. How should agents respond?
options: Balance speed against the risk that poor service triggers repeat complaints
Make every call as short as possible because rewards dominate penalties
Ignore both rules unless all agents respond identically
Guarantee perfect service because two incentives are present
items.feedback: Agents face a reward for speed and an expected cost for unresolved problems.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Approximately what share does the bottom quintile receive under A?

About 20 percent
About 10 percent
About 90 percent
items.feedback: At the 20-percent population mark, curve A indicates an income share of about 10 percent.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Approximately what before-policy share goes to the bottom quintile?

items.stem: For hypothetical Economy B, the bottom 30 percent receive 10 percent of income. Which point belongs on its Lorenz curve?
items.feedback: Lorenz coordinates pair cumulative population from poorest upward with that group's cumulative income share.

items.stem: Workers with scarce training earn more after demand for their skill rises. Which source of income differences is illustrated?

Human capital interacting with market demand
Identical productivity across workers
items.feedback: Training can raise productivity, and stronger demand for that skill raises its market return.

items.stem: Two otherwise identical jobs pay $24 and $28 per hour. The higher-paying job alone exposes workers to danger. What hourly premium is consistent with compensation for that danger?
items.feedback: The difference, $28 − $24 = $4 per hour, is the compensating premium, not the entire risky-job wage.

items.stem: Workers with scarce training earn more after demand for their skill rises. Which source of income differences is illustrated?
