items.feedback: Training can raise productivity, and stronger demand for that skill raises its market return.

items.stem: Two jobs have equal risk and amenities, but one requires scarce technical training. Why is a higher wage in that job not evidence of a compensating differential for danger?
options: Every wage difference is compensation for danger.
Training changes wealth but cannot affect earnings.
Equal danger implies equal productivity in both jobs.
The stated difference is skill scarcity, while risk is held equal.
items.feedback: A risk premium requires a difference in risk. Here skill requirements provide a distinct explanation of the wage gap.

items.stem: In hypothetical Economy A, the official threshold for a household is $24,000 and measured money income is $21,500. Under that rule, how is the household classified?
options: Below the poverty threshold
Above the threshold because benefits are always counted
Exactly at the poverty threshold
Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
items.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $21,500, with the $24,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

items.stem: In hypothetical Economy E, the official threshold for a household is $28,000 and measured money income is $25,500. Under that rule, how is the household classified?
options: Below the poverty threshold
Above the threshold because benefits are always counted
Exactly at the poverty threshold
Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
items.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $25,500, with the $28,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

items.stem: A hypothetical poverty rule classifies households as poor only when measured money income is strictly below $31,000. A household has $31,000 of measured money income. How is it classified?
options: Poor because its income is below the threshold.
Poor because equality counts as below.
The rule cannot classify a household with measured money income.
Exactly at the threshold and not poor under this rule.
items.feedback: Compare 31000 with 31000. The rule uses a strict inequality; equality does not count as below.

items.stem: For hypothetical Economy J, the official threshold for a household is $25,000 and measured money income is $22,500. Under that rule, how is the household classified?
options: Above the threshold because benefits are always counted
Below the poverty threshold
Exactly at the poverty threshold
Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
items.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $22,500, with the $25,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

items.stem: In hypothetical Economy M, the official threshold for a household is $28,000 and measured money income is $25,500. Under that rule, how is the household classified?
options: Below the poverty threshold
Above the threshold because benefits are always counted
Exactly at the poverty threshold
Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
items.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $25,500, with the $28,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

items.stem: Why might a libertarian object to redistribution even if it narrows measured inequality?
options: A lower Gini always reduces freedom
It may violate rights to legitimately acquired property.
All transfers are in kind
Markets never generate income differences
items.feedback: Libertarian evaluation emphasizes the process by which holdings are acquired rather than equality of outcomes alone.

items.stem: Policies A and B produce incomes (10, 80) and (15, 60) for two groups. Which does a maximin rule prefer?
options: A, because its total income is 90 rather than 75.
A, because its highest income is 80 rather than 60.
Neither, because maximin requires equal incomes.
B, because its lowest income is 15 rather than 10.
items.feedback: Maximin ranks the worst-off outcome: 15 exceeds 10 even though B has a smaller total.

items.stem: A transfer raises low incomes but requires a tax that may reduce work incentives. What is the central policy evaluation?
options: Treat incentives as the only social value
Ignore behavioral responses entirely
Compare the equity gain with efficiency and incentive costs
Assume redistribution has no tradeoff
items.feedback: Redistribution is commonly evaluated by balancing equity and insurance against administrative and incentive costs.

items.stem: A transfer raises low incomes but requires a tax that may reduce work incentives. What is the central policy evaluation?
options: Treat incentives as the only social value
Ignore behavioral responses entirely
Compare the equity gain with efficiency and incentive costs
Assume redistribution has no tradeoff
items.feedback: Redistribution is commonly evaluated by balancing equity and insurance against administrative and incentive costs.

items.stem: An evaluator accepts unequal holdings when they result from legitimate acquisition and voluntary exchange. Which additional fact would most directly challenge that evaluator’s acceptance?
options: The highest income is twice the lowest.
Part of the holdings resulted from theft.
A voluntary gift raises one person’s wealth.
The final distribution has a positive Gini coefficient.
items.feedback: Theft contradicts legitimate acquisition; inequality alone does not establish that contradiction under the stated criterion.

items.stem: A hypothetical poverty rule classifies households as poor only when measured money income is strictly below $30,000. A household has $28,400 of measured money income. How is it classified?
options: Above the threshold and not poor.
Exactly at the threshold.
Poor under this rule.
The rule cannot classify a household with measured money income.
items.feedback: Compare 28400 with 30000. The rule uses a strict inequality; equality does not count as below.

items.stem: A hypothetical poverty rule classifies households as poor only when measured money income is strictly below $26,000. A household has $25,000 of measured money income. How is it classified?
options: Above the threshold and not poor.
Exactly at the threshold.
Poor under this rule.
The rule cannot classify a household with measured money income.
items.feedback: Compare 25000 with 26000. The rule uses a strict inequality; equality does not count as below.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Approximately what before-policy share goes to households from the 60th through 80th percentiles?
options: About 15 percent
About 25 percent
About 30 percent
About 55 percent
items.feedback: Subtract the approximate readings: about 55 percent at 80 minus about 30 percent at 60 is about 25 percent.

About 20 percent
About 98 percent
About 2 percent

About 20 percent
About 10 percent
About 90 percent

items.stem: Two otherwise similar jobs pay differently because one exposes workers to substantial danger. What can explain the pay gap?
options: A poverty threshold
A Lorenz-curve crossing
An in-kind transfer
A compensating wage differential
items.feedback: A riskier or less pleasant job may need to pay more to attract workers.

items.stem: Workers with scarce training earn more after demand for their skill rises. Which source of income differences is illustrated?
options: Only random measurement error
A universal fall in labor demand
Human capital interacting with market demand
Identical productivity across workers

items.stem: A safety improvement eliminates a job hazard without changing productivity, worker skills or other job amenities. In a competitive labor market, what happens to the compensating part of its wage?
options: It tends to rise because the job is safer.
It stays fixed because compensating differentials depend only on productivity.
It becomes an inheritance payment rather than labor income.
It tends to fall because the undesirable attribute has been removed.
items.feedback: Workers require less compensation for risk when the risk falls, holding other determinants of pay fixed.

items.stem: Workers with scarce training earn more after demand for their skill rises. Which source of income differences is illustrated?
options: Only random measurement error
A universal fall in labor demand
Human capital interacting with market demand
Identical productivity across workers
items.feedback: Training can raise productivity, and stronger demand for that skill raises its market return.

items.stem: A household receives a one-time $60,000 inheritance and saves it. Its annual wage remains $30,000. Which statement correctly separates stocks and flows?
options: The inheritance raises its wage to $90,000 every year.
The inheritance raises its asset stock; it does not by itself raise its annual wage flow.
Saving the inheritance prevents it from affecting wealth.
The inheritance is a debt because it is not earned through labor.
items.feedback: Accumulated assets are wealth measured at a point in time. Wages are a flow over a period, and the inherited asset need not change that flow.

items.stem: For hypothetical Economy F, the official threshold for a household is $29,000 and measured money income is $26,500. Under that rule, how is the household classified?
options: Above the threshold because benefits are always counted
Below the poverty threshold
Exactly at the poverty threshold
Classification cannot use an explicit threshold

Exactly at the poverty threshold
Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
items.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $21,500, with the $24,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

items.stem: A household has $25,800 in measured income against a $27,000 poverty threshold. A cash grant counts dollar for dollar and changes no other income. What is the smallest grant that reaches the threshold?
items.feedback: The shortfall is $27,000 − $25,800 = $1,200. Reaching the threshold requires closing that gap.

options: Treat incentives as the only social value
Ignore behavioral responses entirely
Compare the equity gain with efficiency and incentive costs
Assume redistribution has no tradeoff
items.feedback: Redistribution is commonly evaluated by balancing equity and insurance against administrative and incentive costs.

items.stem: A voluntary gift reduces wealth inequality, while a compulsory transfer would produce the same final distribution. Why might an entitlement-based evaluator distinguish them?
options: Identical final distributions necessarily imply identical acquisition processes.
Consent and legitimate acquisition affect the assessment even when final distributions match.
Voluntary gifts cannot change a wealth distribution.
An entitlement rule ranks arrangements solely by their Gini coefficients.
items.feedback: An entitlement view evaluates how holdings are obtained and transferred, so consent can matter independently of the final distribution.

options: 10 percent
30 percent
45 percent
15 percent

options: Above the threshold because benefits are always counted

Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
items.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $26,500, with the $29,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Approximately what share goes to the bottom 20 percent?
options: About 15 percent
About 5 percent
About 20 percent
About 95 percent
items.feedback: The first plotted quintile point is about (20,5), so the cumulative income share is approximately 5 percent.

items.stem: Total income is $200 million. Using the Lorenz curve, how much goes to the bottom 60%, and why is applying their population percentage directly to income incorrect?
options: $80 million; population share differs from the plotted income share.
$60 million; a population share is always the same as an income share.
$60 million; population share differs from the plotted income share.
$80 million; a population share is always the same as an income share.
items.feedback: At population 60%, the curve gives income share 30%. Thus the group receives 0.30 × 200 = $60 million. $120 million would use the equality benchmark instead of the observed distribution.

items.stem: Refer to the graph above. Approximately what share goes to the top 20 percent?
options: About 20 percent
About 55 percent
About 80 percent
About 45 percent
items.feedback: The bottom 80 percent receive about 55 percent, leaving approximately 45 percent for the top quintile.

items.stem: Use the vertical guide drawn to the Lorenz curve. What income share would the equality line assign to that same group of households, and why?
options: 40%; under equality the group’s income share equals its population share.
60%; under equality the group’s income share equals its population share.
40%; under equality the group’s income share equals the observed Lorenz share even if the shares differ.
60%; under equality the group’s income share equals the observed Lorenz share even if the shares differ.
items.feedback: The guide is at the bottom 40% of households, whose observed income share is 15%. Perfect equality would give them 40% of income. The equality line is a benchmark, not the observed distribution.

items.feedback: Lorenz coordinates pair cumulative population from poorest upward with that group's cumulative income share.

Below the poverty threshold

Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
items.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $22,500, with the $25,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

items.feedback: Lorenz coordinates pair cumulative population from poorest upward with that group's cumulative income share.

options: Only random measurement error
A universal fall in labor demand

items.feedback: Training can raise productivity, and stronger demand for that skill raises its market return.

options: Below the poverty threshold
Above the threshold because benefits are always counted
Exactly at the poverty threshold
Classification cannot use an explicit threshold
items.feedback: Compare the specified money-income measure, $21,500, with the $24,000 threshold; the rule is mechanical even though the measure has limitations.

items.stem: Why is it misleading to compare a $5 wage in 1970 directly to a $15 wage today?
options: The purchasing power of money changes over time
Wages are not prices
Inflation only affects GDP, not wages
Nominal values are always real values
items.feedback: Dollar amounts from different years need to be adjusted for changes in the price level.

items.stem: A pension has a full cost-of-living adjustment tied to the CPI. If measured inflation is 4 percent, what is the intended effect?
options: Raise the nominal payment about 4% to protect purchasing power.
Reduce the nominal payment about 4% to offset inflation.
Hold the nominal payment fixed so its real value automatically rises.
Convert the pension payment into a market interest rate.
items.feedback: A CPI-linked adjustment raises the nominal amount to offset measured price growth.

items.stem: A salary rises 6% while the relevant price index rises 4%. What happens to real purchasing power?
options: It rises modestly
It falls by 10%
It is exactly unchanged
It rises by the full 6%
items.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

items.stem: A rent payment is indexed upward 3% when the relevant price index rises 3%. What is the intended real effect?
options: Raise the real rent by 6%
Cut the nominal rent by 3%
Convert rent into a real interest rate
Keep the payment’s purchasing power roughly constant
items.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

items.stem: A nominal salary is unchanged while the consumer price level falls. What happens to its purchasing power?
options: It becomes an indexed tax threshold
It rises
It falls by definition
It remains unchanged in real terms
items.feedback: Put nominal amounts in common purchasing-power units before making the real comparison.

items.stem: A nominal wage rises 8% while CPI rises 5%. Using the exact ratio and rounding to one decimal place, how much does the real wage rise?
options: About 2.9%
Exactly 3.0%
About 13.4%
About 1.6%
items.feedback: Real wage growth=(1.08/1.05−1)×100≈2.8571%, or 2.9%. Subtracting rates gives only the 3% approximation.

items.stem: A tax threshold is adjusted by only half of CPI inflation. What happens to its real value?
options: It rises faster than prices
It remains exactly constant
It becomes a nominal interest rate
It falls
items.feedback: Indexation adjusts a nominal amount using a specified index; lags or an imperfectly matched index can still change real value.

items.stem: A contract raises its nominal payment 3% each year while inflation is 6%. What happens to the real payment?
options: It declines
It rises about 9%
It remains constant because the payment increased
It equals the nominal interest rate
items.feedback: Compare the nominal change with the relevant price-index change to determine purchasing-power change.

items.stem: A car cost $8,000 in the past when the CPI was 80. The equivalent current-dollar price is $28,000. What is the current CPI?
items.feedback: 28000 = 8000 x current CPI/80, so current CPI = 280.

items.stem: A current salary of $96,000 is equivalent to $60,000 in year-T dollars. If the current CPI is 240, what was the CPI in year T?
A current income of $84,000 equals $60,000 in year-T dollars. If CPI today is 210, what was CPI in year T?
A scholarship rises 15% while CPI rises 10%. Using the exact ratio and rounding to one decimal place, what is its real increase?
options: About 4.5%
Exactly 5.0%
About 25.0% because the two nominal changes are added together
About 1.5%
items.feedback: Real scholarship growth=(1.15/1.10−1)×100≈4.5455%, or 4.5%. The nominal 15% gain is partly offset by the 10% price increase.

items.stem: A wage was $18,000 when the CPI was 90. The CPI is now 270. What is the wage in today's dollars?
items.feedback: Today's dollars = 18000 x 270/90 = 54000.

items.stem: A tuition bill was $4,000 when the CPI was 125. In today's dollars, it equals $6,400. What is today's CPI?
items.feedback: 6400 = 4000 x today's CPI/125, so today's CPI = 200.

items.stem: A salary is $72,000 today when the CPI is 240. What was its equivalent value in year-T dollars when the CPI was 160?
A salary was $30,000 when the CPI was 150. The CPI is now 225. What is that salary in today's dollars?
items.feedback: Today's dollars = 30000 x 225/150 = 45000.

items.stem: A movie ticket cost $4 when the CPI was 80. The CPI is now 240. What is the ticket price in today's dollars?
items.feedback: Today's dollars = 4 x 240/80 = 12.

items.stem: A $190 monthly benefit is fully indexed to a 5% CPI rise, but its recipient's actual fixed basket rises 8%. Which conclusion distinguishes index protection from household purchasing power?
options: CPI-adjusted value falls 3%; household purchasing power is preserved
Both measures rise 13% because the index and basket changes add
CPI-adjusted value is preserved; purchasing power over this household basket falls about 2.8%
Both CPI-adjusted and household purchasing power are preserved because the contract is indexed
items.feedback: The contract preserves value relative to CPI, not every household basket. For this basket the real factor is 1.05/1.08, or about a 2.78% decline.

items.stem: A past monthly payment was $200 when CPI was 100. A current payment is $260 when CPI is 125. Which comparison uses common purchasing-power units?
options: The payments have equal purchasing power; both CPI and the payment increased
The current payment is $10 higher in current dollars; the past payment converts to $250
The current payment is $60 higher in real terms; compare unadjusted dollar amounts
The past payment is $10 higher in current dollars; deflate the past payment again
items.feedback: The past payment in current dollars is 200×125/100 = 250. The current payment exceeds it by 10.

items.stem: A $210 indexed benefit resets once annually. Immediately after a reset, prices rise while the next reset is six months away. Which proposal addresses the specific loss without promising complete protection against a mismatched household basket?
options: Reset more frequently to reduce the lag; index mismatch can still leave real-value differences
Reset less frequently to reduce the lag; a CPI rule eliminates all household mismatch
Replace the index with the original nominal amount; fixed payments follow current prices
Use the GDP deflator regardless of consumption; domestic output prices always equal each household basket
items.feedback: More frequent adjustment can shorten the timing gap. Even prompt CPI indexation cannot guarantee unchanged purchasing power for a different household consumption basket.

items.stem: Why can heavy reliance on printing money become dangerous?
options: It can create rapid inflation and reduce money's value
It guarantees higher real GDP forever
It eliminates all tax burdens
It makes nominal variables real
items.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but it reduces the value of money and can create high inflation.

items.stem: A government repeatedly prints money to pay its bills. Which risk is most directly connected to this policy?
options: Inflation tax and possible hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real output
Permanent monetary neutrality failure
A lower price level forever
items.feedback: Printing money can finance spending, but repeated reliance on it can create inflation or hyperinflation.

items.stem: Why is the inflation tax called a tax even though Congress may not pass a tax law?
options: It reduces the purchasing power of money people already hold.
It raises real GDP automatically.
It only applies to people who owe income taxes.
It directly increases the real wage.
items.feedback: Inflation acts like a tax on money holders by reducing the purchasing power of their cash balances.

items.stem: If prices are falling across the economy, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises.
It falls.
It becomes zero.
It becomes the nominal interest rate.
items.feedback: Deflation means falling prices, so each dollar buys more. The value of money rises.

items.stem: Inflation falls from 7 percent to 2 percent, but the overall price level is still rising. Which description is correct?
options: The economy is experiencing disinflation, not deflation.
The economy is experiencing deflation because inflation is lower.
The economy is experiencing hyperinflation because prices are still rising.
The price level must be falling by 5 percent.
items.feedback: Disinflation means the inflation rate falls while remaining positive; deflation means the overall price level is falling.

items.stem: A country prints money to cover deficits, prices rise rapidly, and people rush to spend cash before it loses value. Which idea is most central?
options: Inflation tax and falling money value
Crowding out and rising investment
LRAS growth and lower inflation
Commodity money and stable prices
items.feedback: Printing money can finance spending through an inflation tax, reducing the value of money.

items.stem: A country has no ability to borrow and keeps financing deficits by creating money. What is the likely risk if this continues?
options: High inflation or hyperinflation
A guaranteed increase in real GDP without inflation
Permanent deflation
A lower money supply
items.feedback: Persistent money creation to finance deficits can trigger high inflation or hyperinflation.

items.stem: An economy enters unexpected deflation while households carry fixed nominal mortgage debt. What happens to the real debt burden, other things equal?
options: It rises because each repayment dollar has greater purchasing power.
It falls because lower prices make nominal debts shrink automatically.
It is unchanged because the price level cannot affect fixed nominal contracts.
It disappears because deflation forces lenders to cancel nominal debt.
items.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

items.stem: If a government prints money to cover spending and the public starts expecting higher future inflation, what happens to nominal interest rates under the Fisher effect?
options: They rise as expected inflation rises.
They fall because money supply rose.
They stay fixed because real rates cannot change.
They become equal to the reserve ratio.
items.feedback: If money finance raises expected inflation, nominal interest rates tend to rise through the Fisher effect.

items.stem: A heavily indebted economy experiences an unexpected 6 percent fall in the overall price level while nominal debts are fixed. Which balance-sheet effect is most likely?
options: Debtors receive an automatic reduction in the nominal face value of their debts.
Creditors lose because every repayment dollar is worth less in real terms.
The fall in the price level is disinflation and therefore cannot affect real debt burdens.
Debtors face a higher real repayment burden, which can weaken spending and financial positions.
items.feedback: Deflation raises the purchasing power of each dollar, increasing the real burden of fixed nominal debt and favoring creditors relative to debtors.

items.stem: If the price level falls from 125 to 120, what happens to the value of money?
options: It rises because 1/P is larger.
It falls because 1/P is smaller.
It stays constant because P changed by less than 10.
It becomes equal to velocity.
items.feedback: When the price level falls, each dollar buys more, so the value of money rises.

items.stem: A household holds $100 in currency while the price level rises 25%. No interest is paid. Which loss and interpretation fit the inflation-tax mechanism?
options: Real purchasing power falls 20%; nominal cash is unchanged without a tax bill.
Real purchasing power falls 25%; the price rise is the purchasing-power loss.
Nominal cash falls 25%; inflation removes currency through an implicit tax bill.
Real purchasing power is unchanged; holding the same nominal cash preserves its value.
items.feedback: Real balances are M/P. With nominal currency fixed and prices multiplied by 1.25, purchasing power becomes 1/1.25=.8 of its original level, a 20% loss.

items.stem: Inflation falls from 8% to 3%. A report calls this a fall in the price level and predicts a lower real burden of fixed nominal debt. Which correction is needed?
options: Deflation: prices fall 5%; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
Zero inflation: prices are unchanged; fixed nominal debt keeps its real value.
Accelerating inflation: prices rise faster; fixed nominal debt gains real value.
Disinflation: prices still rise; fixed nominal debt continues losing real value.
items.feedback: A positive inflation rate still raises the price level. A slower rise is disinflation, whereas deflation is a falling price level; fixed-debt effects also depend on the relevant price comparison.

items.stem: A household owes a fixed nominal $140. Prices fall 10% while its nominal debt is unchanged. Which debt-burden comparison is correct?
options: The real burden rises exactly 10%; reciprocal percentage changes are equal
The real burden is unchanged because a fixed nominal debt is also fixed in real terms
The real burden rises about 11.1%; the same nominal repayment buys more goods
The real burden falls 10%; cheaper goods make every nominal debt smaller in real terms
items.feedback: The real-debt factor is 1/.90≈1.1111. Falling prices increase, rather than decrease, the purchasing power needed to repay a fixed nominal amount.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A bank expects a guaranteed bailout and therefore chooses a riskier portfolio. What causes the distortion?
options: The bank's hidden type before borrowing
Perfect screening
A lower opportunity cost of voting
Protection shifts part of the downside to others
items.feedback: When decision makers do not bear the full marginal loss, post-protection risk taking can rise.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Drivers privately know their preexisting accident risk, which the insurer cannot observe. High-risk drivers are more likely to buy insurance, but no driver changes behavior after buying it. Which conclusion follows?
options: Every accident after purchase establishes moral hazard.
Insurance has necessarily reduced every driver’s care.
The pattern is adverse selection, not evidence of moral hazard.
The insurer has eliminated private information.
items.feedback: Selection into coverage depends on privately known risk. Moral hazard would require a change in behavior caused by the contract.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Insured drivers have more accidents than uninsured drivers. What additional comparison helps test whether insurance caused moral hazard?
options: Compare only the total number of drivers in each group.
Assume all drivers had identical risk before insurance.
Compare how otherwise similar drivers change care when coverage changes.
Treat each accident as direct evidence of less care.
items.feedback: A raw difference may reflect preexisting risk. A credible comparison of behavior under different coverage helps identify the incentive effect.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An insurer reimburses all losses. It then adds a deductible that makes the insured bear part of each loss, holding information and all other terms fixed. Which incentive changes most directly?
options: The insured bears a smaller loss and therefore has less reason for care.
The insured has a stronger financial reason to prevent a loss.
The insurer learns every hidden characteristic before contracting.
The deductible guarantees no accident can occur.
items.feedback: A deductible leaves some loss with the insured and can strengthen care incentives, without guaranteeing perfect care or revealing all types.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An insured driver maintains exactly the same level of care before and after coverage. An accident then occurs. Does that accident alone establish moral hazard?
options: Yes; every insured loss proves reduced care.
Yes; the insurer’s payment establishes hidden precontract risk.
No; moral hazard is impossible in insurance.
No; the accident alone does not demonstrate a coverage-induced change in behavior.
items.feedback: A bad outcome can occur without a change in incentives or behavior. The stated unchanged care does not demonstrate moral hazard.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A driver conceals careless behavior after buying insurance. The insurer raises premiums for every customer. Why might that response fail to target the source of moral hazard?
options: Any higher premium makes all future actions observable.
A uniform premium necessarily eliminates hidden action.
The premium increase need not reward the individual driver for greater care.
Carelessness must have occurred before the insurance contract.
items.feedback: An incentive contract must connect an individual’s action or outcome to a consequence. A uniform price rise alone may leave the relevant marginal incentive unchanged.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An insurer offers a high-deductible and a low-deductible plan so customers reveal risk through their choice. What mechanism is this?
options: Signaling by applicants only
A Condorcet vote
Anchoring
Screening by the less-informed insurer
items.feedback: The uninformed side designs a menu that induces different hidden types to self-select.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A lender requires collateral before approving a loan. What informational role can collateral play?
options: It insures the borrower against every loss
It screens or separates borrowers by willingness and ability to bear default consequences
It creates moral hazard intentionally
It proves all borrowers have identical risk
items.feedback: Contract terms can elicit private information when different risk types choose differently or face different costs.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A credential costs both worker types $2,000 and gives each a $5,000 wage premium. Can these payoffs alone separate the types?
options: No; both types gain by obtaining it.
Yes; only high-productivity workers gain.
Yes; neither worker type gains.
No; the credential must reduce wages.
items.feedback: Each type gains $3,000. Equal incentives to obtain the credential do not separate the types.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A credential has no effect on productive skill but is harder for low-productivity workers to earn. Could it still convey information?
options: Yes, if the different costs induce different choices by type.
No, because only training can affect employers’ beliefs.
Yes, because every worker must obtain it.
No, because signaling requires identical costs for both types.
items.feedback: A signal can reveal an existing characteristic without causing that characteristic; credibility depends on incentives to imitate.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A job applicant independently obtains a credible certificate before approaching employers. Employers did not require or design a menu of choices. Which information mechanism is described?
options: Screening by the employer
Moral hazard after employment
A benefits cliff
Signaling by the informed applicant
items.feedback: The informed side takes an observable action to communicate its type.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An informed seller voluntarily posts a warranty that is much more expensive for low-quality sellers to honor. Why can it convey quality?
options: All sellers face identical warranty costs and incentives.
Low-quality sellers may find imitation less profitable because expected warranty costs are higher.
Posting a warranty mechanically improves the physical product.
A warranty prevents buyers from learning about defects.
items.feedback: Different expected costs can make the observable warranty a credible signal rather than cheap talk.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: High-productivity workers gain $8,000 from a credential and pay $2,000 to earn it. Low-productivity workers gain $3,000 and pay $5,000. Which outcome is supported?
options: Only high-productivity workers choose the credential.
Both types choose the credential.
Only low-productivity workers choose the credential.
Neither type chooses the credential.
items.feedback: The high type has a positive net benefit of $6,000; the low type has a net cost of $2,000. These payoffs support separation.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A driver takes less care after obtaining broad insurance coverage. Which information problem does this illustrate?
options: Adverse selection before coverage
A credible quality signal
Moral hazard
Perfectly observed contracting
items.feedback: Coverage changes the incentive for an action taken after the contract; this is moral hazard.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Behavior is perfectly monitored and a contract can condition payment on every action. What happens to hidden-action moral hazard?
options: It becomes adverse selection automatically
It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives
It must increase
It makes insurance unnecessary in every case
items.feedback: Observable, contractible action allows terms to reward care or penalize risk, though monitoring itself may be costly.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Two banks hold identical assets initially. Only one receives a credible promise that taxpayers will absorb large future losses. With other incentives fixed, which response is consistent with moral hazard?
options: The protected bank selects less risk because it bears all taxpayers’ losses.
Both banks must select identical risk because their initial assets match.
The unprotected bank becomes insured merely because another bank is protected.
The protected bank selects more risk because it bears less downside.
items.feedback: The guarantee changes the protected bank’s marginal exposure to losses even though initial assets are equal.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A driver’s coverage expands while accident risk and driving conditions remain unchanged. Which response would be inconsistent with the claim that broader coverage reduced care in this case?
options: The driver stops paying for a useful safety precaution.
The driver begins leaving the vehicle unlocked.
The driver maintains exactly the same safety behavior.
The driver increases risky driving because losses are covered.
items.feedback: Unchanged care does not support the specified behavioral mechanism. Coverage creates an incentive possibility, not proof that every person responds.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Monitoring costs $8 per policy and is expected to reduce real accident losses by $5, with no other benefits or costs. Is monitoring justified by net resource savings in this example?
options: Yes; every reduction in moral hazard exceeds its cost.
No; it costs $3 more than the expected loss reduction.
Yes; the net saving is $13.
No; the reduction in losses is a transfer rather than a resource benefit.
items.feedback: The resource gain is $5 and the cost is $8, giving net savings of −$3.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Why can a credential reveal productivity when it is more costly for low-productivity workers to obtain?
options: Different net benefits can lead the two types to choose differently.
The credential must physically raise every worker’s productivity.
All workers must find it equally attractive to obtain.
Employers must observe productivity before seeing the credential.
items.feedback: A cost difference can support separation if high-productivity workers want the credential and low-productivity workers do not.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An employer offers two contract packages that induce applicants with different private productivity to choose differently. Who designs the information-revealing action, and what is it called?
options: The informed applicant designs screening.
The uninformed employer sends a signal of applicant quality.
The applicants disclose all types through a compulsory public test.
The uninformed employer designs screening.
items.feedback: Screening is initiated by the less-informed side through offers that reveal private information via choices.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A bank offers borrowers a choice between a low-interest loan with collateral and a high-interest loan without collateral. Borrowers privately know their repayment risk. Which action constitutes screening?
options: A borrower’s unsolicited public reputation campaign
The bank’s design of the contract menu
The bank’s payment after a default
A borrower’s change in effort after the loan
items.feedback: The uninformed bank designs alternatives intended to reveal risk through borrowers’ choices.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A credential raises productive skill equally for all workers. Does that benefit alone establish that the credential separates workers by their prior productivity?
options: No; skill formation alone does not establish separation by prior type.
Yes; all training is necessarily a separating signal.
Yes; equal skill gains imply different credential costs.
No; credentials can never both teach and signal.
items.feedback: Human-capital formation and signaling are distinct mechanisms. Evidence of one does not, by itself, demonstrate the other.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An insurer offers a high-deductible and a low-deductible plan so customers reveal risk through their choice. What mechanism is this?
options: Signaling by applicants only
A Condorcet vote
Anchoring
Screening by the less-informed insurer
items.feedback: The uninformed side designs a menu that induces different hidden types to self-select.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A bank expects a guaranteed bailout and therefore chooses a riskier portfolio. What causes the distortion?
options: The bank's hidden type before borrowing
Perfect screening
A lower opportunity cost of voting
Protection shifts part of the downside to others
items.feedback: When decision makers do not bear the full marginal loss, post-protection risk taking can rise.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A deductible reduces claims, but some customers also stop buying insurance. Which observation directly supports a reduction in moral hazard?
options: Customers who remain insured take more care.
Only low-risk customers leave the insurance pool.
The insurer collects fewer premiums.
The number of insured customers falls.
items.feedback: Moral hazard concerns behavior after coverage. Changes in who purchases coverage concern selection and do not by themselves establish greater care.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An insurer adds a deductible, but a separate employer plan reimburses that deductible in full. What happens to its incentive for the customer to prevent losses?
options: Reimbursement weakens the incentive created by the deductible.
Reimbursement makes the customer bear more of each loss.
Reimbursement reveals the customer’s inherited risk.
Reimbursement necessarily eliminates all accidents.
items.feedback: If another party fully repays the deductible, the customer does not bear that marginal loss and the intended incentive is weakened.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A customer can avoid a $100 loss by spending $10 on care. Full insurance repays the loss. If the policy instead leaves the first $20 of the loss uninsured, how does the private incentive change?
options: Avoiding the deductible can make the $10 precaution worthwhile.
The customer still bears none of the preventable loss.
Care becomes worthwhile only if it costs more than $20.
The deductible changes the physical loss to $20.
items.feedback: Without care the customer now bears $20; spending $10 to avoid it is privately worthwhile. The physical loss remains $100.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: Why can a deductible reduce moral hazard?
options: It reveals every customer's risk type
The insured person bears part of the marginal cost of a loss
It guarantees that no accident occurs
It makes coverage a public good
items.feedback: Cost sharing preserves some incentive to take care after coverage begins.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: An insurer offers plans with different deductibles so applicants reveal risk through their choices. What mechanism is this?
options: Signaling by the insurer
Screening by the less-informed insurer
A default nudge
A Condorcet vote
items.feedback: The uninformed side designs a menu that induces hidden types to self-select.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: If an insurer can observe every safety action and enforce contract terms that reward or penalize those actions, what happens to hidden-action moral hazard?
options: It can be greatly reduced through enforceable incentives
It automatically becomes adverse selection
It must increase
It makes every insurance contract unnecessary
items.feedback: When enforceable contract terms reward or penalize observed safety actions, they can reduce the hidden-action problem.

items.topic: Information Asymmetry, Behavioral Economics, and Political Economy
items.stem: A job applicant chooses to obtain an unsolicited certificate before applying; an employer separately offers a menu of trial contracts to reveal applicants’ types. Which action is signaling?
options: The applicant’s certificate
The employer’s contract menu
Both actions are signaling by the informed side.
Neither action can convey information.
items.feedback: The informed applicant initiates the certificate signal. The uninformed employer initiates the screening menu.

items.stem: An economist shows a PPF shifting outward after years of investment in capital and technology. What is the best interpretation?
options: The economy's productive capacity has increased
The economy moved inside the PPF because resources are idle
The CPI basket became fixed
A tax wedge disappeared
items.feedback: An outward PPF shift means the economy can produce more because resources, technology, or productivity improved.

items.stem: A minimum wage is raised above the equilibrium wage for low-skill labor. What is the expected market result?
options: A shortage of labor, meaning firms cannot find enough workers
No change because price floors never bind
An automatic increase in productivity
A surplus of labor, meaning more workers want jobs than firms want to hire
items.feedback: A binding minimum wage is a price floor. It raises the wage above equilibrium and can create a surplus of labor.

items.stem: At $10 per hour, firms hire 1,000 workers and 1,000 workers want jobs. At a $15 minimum wage, firms want 800 workers and 1,200 workers want jobs. What is the labor surplus?
options: 400 workers
200 workers
800 workers
1,200 workers
items.feedback: The surplus is workers wanting jobs minus workers firms want to hire: 1,200 - 800 = 400.

items.stem: A tax is imposed on sellers. Buyers pay a higher price, sellers receive a lower price, and fewer units are sold. What concept ties these effects together?
options: A price floor that creates a labor surplus
A tax wedge that shrinks the market
Substitution bias in the CPI
Discouraged-worker measurement
items.feedback: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and sellers receive, reducing the quantity sold.

items.stem: A tax is legally imposed on buyers instead of sellers. What does tax-incidence analysis imply?
options: Buyers always bear 100% of the burden
Legal assignment alone does not determine the burden
Sellers always bear 100% of the burden
The tax disappears from the market
items.feedback: Tax incidence depends on market responses, not simply on whether the law says buyers or sellers pay the tax.

items.stem: Demand is less elastic than supply. Which side bears more of a per-unit tax?
options: Sellers bear more because buyers can easily leave
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because taxes do not affect prices
Buyers bear more because they respond less to the price change
items.feedback: The less elastic side of the market bears more of the tax burden because it has fewer good alternatives.

items.stem: Gasoline prices rise after a supply disruption. A city responds with a binding price ceiling. What is the most likely result?
options: A surplus because suppliers produce more at the lower price
No effect because ceilings above equilibrium are always binding
A shortage because the legal price is held below the market-clearing price
Higher productivity because gasoline is cheaper
items.feedback: A binding price ceiling below equilibrium creates a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.

items.stem: A storm reduces supply while demand stays the same. Before any price control, what happens in the market?
options: Equilibrium price falls and equilibrium quantity rises
Both price and quantity rise
Equilibrium price rises and equilibrium quantity falls
Both price and quantity fall
items.feedback: A decrease in supply shifts supply left, raising equilibrium price and lowering equilibrium quantity.

items.stem: A binding price ceiling holds the posted price below equilibrium. What happens to the underlying scarcity?
options: Scarcity disappears when prices are legally capped
All consumers get more of the good
Shortages cause waiting, side markets, favoritism, or lower quality
The CPI cannot measure any price change
items.feedback: A ceiling can hold down the legal money price, but scarcity still appears through shortages and nonprice rationing.

items.stem: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Demer becomes a net importer of tablets. Relative to its no-trade equilibrium price, where must the world price lie?
options: Below the no-trade price.
Above the no-trade price.
Exactly at the no-trade price.
Its position cannot be inferred from net imports.
items.feedback: Net imports mean domestic demand exceeds domestic supply at the world price. With ordinary demand and supply, that gap occurs below the autarky equilibrium price.

items.stem: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Estara’s no-trade wool-blanket price is $53, and the world price is $30. Relative to autarky, what happens to domestic production and consumption?
options: Production rises; consumption falls.
Production falls; consumption rises.
Both production and consumption rise.
Both production and consumption fall.
items.feedback: Opening to the lower world price moves domestic producers down supply and consumers down demand: domestic production falls, consumption rises, and imports fill the gap.

items.stem: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. At the world price, Faron’s firms produce 90 batches of tiles and its residents consume 60. What is the trade position?
options: Imports of 30 batches.
Exports of 60 batches.
Imports of 150 batches.
Exports of 30 batches.
items.feedback: Domestic production exceeds domestic consumption by 90 - 60 = 30 batches. Those excess batches are exported.

items.stem: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Galena exports medical gloves at a world price of $58. What does this imply about its no-trade equilibrium price?
options: It must have been above $58.
It must have equaled $58.
It must have been below $58.
It could have been either above or below $58.
items.feedback: Exports occur when the world price is above autarky: domestic supply exceeds domestic demand. Therefore the no-trade price was below $58.

items.stem: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Haven’s no-trade garden-tool price is $60 and Ilyria’s is $35. Both face a world price of $44. Which prediction follows?
options: Haven imports and Ilyria exports.
Both countries import.
Haven exports and Ilyria imports.
Both countries export.
items.feedback: Compare each domestic no-trade price with the same world price: $44 $35 makes Ilyria an exporter. Comparing the two countries’ prices only to one another is insufficient.

items.stem: Assume a small competitive country, unchanged domestic curves, free trade and no transport costs. Juno’s no-trade olive-oil price is $62. The world price first is $38, then rises to $70. Which change in trade position follows?
options: Exporter at both world prices.
Importer at $38, exporter at $70.
Exporter at $38, importer at $70.
Importer at both world prices.
items.feedback: At $38 below autarky, domestic demand exceeds supply and Juno imports. At $70 above autarky, domestic supply exceeds demand and Juno exports. The position must be reassessed when the world price crosses $62.

items.stem: Under a voluntary export restraint, foreign firms receive free rights to supply 45 units. Buyers pay $27 while the unchanged world price is $23. Who receives the $180 scarcity rent?
options: The importing government as tariff revenue
Domestic producers in addition to their producer surplus
Domestic consumers as a price rebate
The foreign firms holding the export rights
items.feedback: The price wedge is $4 and 45 units cross the border: $180. The foreign holders of the free rights receive the rents; the importing treasury collects no tariff.

items.stem: Compared with free trade at Pw = $4, the tariff in the displayed trade graph reduces imports by:
options: 50 thousand
100 thousand
150 thousand
200 thousand
items.feedback: Free-trade imports are 250 − 50 = 200 thousand; after the tariff they are 100 thousand.

items.stem: At the quota-induced domestic price of $6 in the displayed trade graph, domestic producers supply:
options: 75 thousand
175 thousand
150 thousand
200 thousand
items.feedback: The $6 line intersects supply at Q = 150 thousand.

items.stem: A policy analyst says “trade is beneficial, so nobody can be harmed by opening the market.” What is wrong with the statement?
options: Only exporters can gain from trade
Consumer and producer surplus never change with trade
Net gains do not imply every group gains
Trade can never raise total surplus
items.feedback: The standard result is aggregate: winners can gain more than losers lose.

items.stem: In an importing market, which pair is most consistent with opening to free trade at a lower world price?
options: Both consumer and producer surplus must rise by the same amount
Consumer surplus rises; producer surplus falls
Consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises
Both consumer and producer surplus must fall
items.feedback: Lower prices benefit domestic buyers and hurt domestic sellers in an importing market.

items.stem: In an exporting market, which pair is most consistent with opening to free trade at a higher world price?
options: Consumer surplus falls; producer surplus rises
Consumer surplus rises; producer surplus falls
Both sides lose equally
Consumer surplus and producer surplus cannot change
items.feedback: Higher domestic prices hurt buyers but benefit sellers in an exporting market.

items.stem: Why does a small-country tariff reduce total surplus even though it creates government revenue?
options: Producer surplus always falls under a tariff
The world price rises by the full tariff
Some lost consumer surplus becomes deadweight loss rather than a transfer
Government revenue is never part of national surplus
items.feedback: Part of the consumer loss is transferred to producers and government; the production and consumption distortions are net losses.

items.stem: A quota allows 30 imported units. The domestic price is $18 and the world price is $14. What is total quota rent?
A tariff and quota produce the same domestic price and import quantity. What determines whether their national welfare effects are identical?
options: Whether producers earn any surplus
Who receives the quota rents
Whether domestic consumers exist
Whether the world price is positive
items.feedback: A tariff creates government revenue; a quota can create equivalent rents that may go to domestic or foreign license holders.

items.stem: A binding quota is tightened. In the standard import model, which combination is most likely?
options: Domestic price rises and imports fall
Domestic price falls and imports rise
Domestic price and imports both remain fixed
Domestic price falls and exports rise
items.feedback: A tighter quantity limit restricts import supply further and pushes the domestic price upward.

items.stem: Refer to the quota-rent graph. What is the value of rectangle R?
items.feedback: The domestic-world price gap is $10 across 20 imported units.

items.stem: Consumer surplus rises by $780 and producer surplus falls by $460. Total surplus changes by:
items.feedback: Total surplus rises by $780 − $460 = $320.

items.stem: Producer surplus rises by $900 and consumer surplus falls by $540. Total surplus changes by:
items.feedback: Total surplus rises by $900 − $540 = $360.

items.stem: At Pw=$30 in the import graph, consumer surplus equals:
items.feedback: At Pw = $30, consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 50 × 50 = $1,250.

items.stem: At Pw=$30 in the import graph, producer surplus equals:
items.feedback: At Pw = $30, producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: ½ × 10 × 10 = $50.

items.stem: At Pw=$70 in the export graph, consumer surplus equals:
items.feedback: At Pw = $70, consumer surplus is the triangle below demand and above price: ½ × 10 × 10 = $50.

items.stem: At Pw=$70 in the export graph, producer surplus equals:
items.feedback: At Pw = $70, producer surplus is the triangle above supply and below price: ½ × 50 × 50 = $1,250.

items.stem: No-trade total surplus is $900 and open-trade total surplus is $1,300. Gains from trade are:
items.feedback: Gains from trade equal the increase in total surplus: $1,300 − $900 = $400.

items.stem: Which is a transfer rather than a net loss?
options: A mutually beneficial trade prevented by policy
High-cost production replacing imports
Consumption valued above world cost that no longer occurs
A shift of surplus from consumers to producers
items.feedback: A shift of surplus from consumers to producers is a transfer between domestic groups. Prevented mutually beneficial trades and inefficient production are net social losses.

items.stem: Why do import gains exceed producer losses in the standard model?
options: Lower-cost sourcing and added consumption create extra surplus
Producer losses are excluded
Imports raise domestic price
Domestic production expands
items.feedback: With imports, lower-cost foreign supply replaces some higher-cost domestic production and the lower price creates additional consumption gains. Together those gains exceed the producer-surplus loss.

items.stem: Why do export gains exceed consumer losses in the standard model?
options: Consumer losses are excluded
Higher-value foreign sales and added production create extra surplus
Exports lower domestic price
Domestic production contracts
items.feedback: With exports, additional domestic production is sold where the world price exceeds marginal cost, and those production gains exceed the consumer-surplus loss from the higher domestic price.

items.stem: Trade raises total surplus but lowers income in one region. This illustrates:
options: Trade has no efficiency gain
Equity is identical to total surplus
Efficiency and equity can point to different concerns
Imports must be banned
items.feedback: Trade can increase total surplus while imposing concentrated losses on particular regions or groups, so efficiency and equity are separate questions.

items.stem: Potential compensation means:
options: Losers are automatically paid
No one loses
The government must impose a quota
Winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible
items.feedback: If total surplus rises, the winners gain enough in aggregate that compensation could be possible, but compensation occurs only if an actual transfer or policy is implemented.

items.stem: In an import market, domestic price falls from $50 to $30. Which group loses?
options: Domestic producers
Domestic consumers
Foreign consumers only
The government automatically
items.feedback: A lower import price reduces the price domestic producers receive and the quantity they sell, so domestic producers lose surplus.

items.stem: In an export market, domestic price rises from $50 to $70. Which group loses?
options: Domestic producers
Domestic consumers
Foreign producers only
The government automatically
items.feedback: A higher export price raises the price domestic consumers pay and reduces the quantity they buy, so domestic consumers lose surplus.

items.stem: Which measure is needed for national gains from trade?
options: Change in import quantity alone
Change in producer revenue alone
Change in total domestic consumer plus producer surplus
Change in the physical trade balance alone
items.feedback: National gains from trade are measured by the change in total domestic surplus: consumer surplus plus producer surplus.

items.stem: Why is every-person-gains not required for aggregate gains?
options: Individual losses are ignored
Prices do not matter
Only firms count
Total surplus sums gains and losses across groups
items.feedback: Aggregate gains require total gains to exceed total losses; they do not require every person or group to gain.

items.stem: If domestic quantity demanded is 50 and domestic quantity supplied is 10 at the world price, the 40-unit trade gap represents:
options: Imports
Exports
Tariff revenue
Producer surplus
items.feedback: At the world price, domestic quantity demanded exceeds domestic quantity supplied by 40 units. That excess demand is filled by imports.

items.stem: If domestic quantity supplied is 50 and domestic quantity demanded is 10 at the world price, the 40-unit trade gap represents:
options: Imports
Exports
Quota rent
Consumer surplus
items.feedback: At the world price, domestic quantity supplied exceeds domestic quantity demanded by 40 units. That excess supply is exported.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Which quantity combination is correct after the tariff?
options: Qs = 50 thousand; Qd = 250 thousand; imports = 200 thousand
Qs = 200 thousand; Qd = 100 thousand; exports = 100 thousand
Qs = Qd = 150 thousand; imports = 0
Qs = 100 thousand; Qd = 200 thousand; imports = 100 thousand
items.feedback: At the tariff-inclusive price of $6, supply is 100 thousand and demand is 200 thousand, leaving 100 thousand imports.

items.stem: An economy has national saving of $640 billion and domestic investment of $500 billion. What is NCO?
options: $1.14 trillion
$140 billion
−$140 billion
$500 billion
items.feedback: From S = I + NCO, NCO = $640 billion − $500 billion = $140 billion.

items.stem: A country records NCO of −$60 billion. What must its net exports equal?
options: −$60 billion
$60 billion
An amount that cannot be inferred
items.feedback: NX and NCO are equal in the accounts, so negative NCO implies an equal trade deficit.

items.stem: Domestic residents buy $240 billion of foreign assets while foreigners buy $310 billion of domestic assets. What is NCO?
options: $70 billion
$240 billion
$550 billion
−$70 billion
items.feedback: NCO = $240 billion − $310 billion = −$70 billion, indicating net capital inflow.

items.stem: A household buys a $2,000 imported computer with no other economic change. What does GDP accounting do?
options: Investment rises by $2,000 and GDP rises by $2,000
Net exports rise by $2,000 while consumption is unchanged
Consumption rises by $2,000 and imports rise by $2,000, leaving GDP unchanged
GDP falls by $2,000 because imports are subtracted
items.feedback: The purchase enters consumption, while the import subtraction removes the foreign-produced computer from domestic GDP.

items.stem: If national saving is less than domestic investment, which combination is consistent with the identities?
options: Zero NCO and a trade deficit
Negative NCO and a trade deficit
Positive NCO and a trade surplus
Positive NCO and balanced trade
items.feedback: S − I equals NCO, so S below I makes NCO negative; NX = NCO makes net exports negative as well.

items.stem: A country has a $90 billion trade surplus and domestic investment of $260 billion. What national saving is consistent with the accounts?
options: $170 billion
$260 billion
$440 billion
$350 billion
items.feedback: NX = NCO = $90 billion, and S = I + NCO = $260 billion + $90 billion = $350 billion.

items.stem: National saving is $300 billion and investment is $360 billion. Which external balance follows?
options: NCO and NX are $60 billion
NCO is −$60 billion and NX is $60 billion
Both balances are $660 billion
NCO and NX are −$60 billion
items.feedback: S − I = −$60 billion, and the identity makes both NCO and NX equal to that amount.

items.stem: A domestic airline buys a newly produced aircraft from France. How does the purchase enter domestic GDP accounting?
options: It enters consumption but not imports
It directly reduces domestic output
It raises investment and imports by the same amount
It lowers investment and raises exports
items.feedback: The aircraft is business investment, but its foreign production is removed through the import term.

items.stem: If the trade account is balanced, what must be true of NCO in the same consistent accounts?
options: NCO equals domestic investment
NCO equals zero
NCO is positive
NCO is negative
items.feedback: Balanced trade means NX = 0, and NX = NCO requires NCO = 0.

items.stem: A student computes net exports as imports minus exports. Which correction fixes the sign?
options: Use saving plus investment
Subtract imports from exports
Add imports to exports
Subtract exports from imports
items.feedback: Net exports are X − M, so a larger import value makes NX smaller, not larger.

items.stem: A binding minimum wage above equilibrium creates unemployment because:
options: Quantity of labor supplied exceeds quantity of labor demanded
Quantity of labor demanded exceeds quantity supplied
All workers leave the labor force
Firms hire more low-skill workers
items.feedback: A wage floor above equilibrium creates a surplus of labor.

items.stem: How can unemployment insurance improve worker outcomes even if it lengthens unemployment spells?
options: It supports income while workers seek better matches
It eliminates structural mismatch immediately
It forces all firms to hire
It lowers the labor force to zero
items.feedback: Unemployment insurance can support job seekers, but may also reduce urgency to accept a job quickly.

items.stem: A union negotiates wages above the competitive equilibrium. What is the likely effect in that labor market?
options: More workers want jobs than firms want to hire
Firms hire every worker who wants a job
Labor demand shifts to infinity
The unemployment rate is impossible to calculate
items.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can create a surplus of labor in that market.

items.stem: Efficiency wage theory says firms may pay above-equilibrium wages because higher wages can:
options: Improve effort, retention, or worker quality
Guarantee zero unemployment
Eliminate all inflation
Make GDP equal CPI
items.feedback: Efficiency wages can make workers more productive or reduce costly turnover.

items.stem: How do a union wage and an efficiency wage differ most directly?
options: A union wage is bargained collectively; an efficiency wage is voluntarily chosen by the firm
A union wage is always below equilibrium; an efficiency wage is always legally mandated
A union wage affects only prices; an efficiency wage affects only GDP accounting
They are identical policies imposed by government in every labor market
items.feedback: Unions bargain over wages, while firms may voluntarily pay efficiency wages; both can keep wages above market-clearing levels under some conditions.

items.stem: A state improves job-search assistance while leaving unemployment benefits unchanged. Which outcome is most directly targeted?
options: Higher cyclical unemployment through weaker aggregate demand
A larger labor surplus from a binding minimum wage
A permanent increase in structural mismatch
Shorter frictional unemployment spells through faster matching
items.feedback: Job-search assistance improves worker-firm matching, so it can shorten normal search spells and reduce frictional unemployment.

items.stem: A union contract raises wages above the competitive equilibrium. Which workers are most likely hurt?
options: Workers no longer hired at the higher union wage
All union workers who keep their jobs
Only retired workers
Only consumers of imported goods
items.feedback: Above-equilibrium wages can reduce labor demanded, hurting workers who cannot get hired.

items.stem: A union wage raises pay for employed members but reduces hiring by firms. Which statement best captures the tradeoff?
options: Insiders gain while some outsiders lose job opportunities
All workers must benefit equally
The unemployment rate must fall to zero
The policy only affects CPI
items.feedback: Union wage gains can help employed members but reduce opportunities for workers not hired.

items.stem: Above-market wages improve effort among 290 retained employees. A proposal predicts that productivity gains must exactly offset reduced hiring. Which missing comparison is essential?
options: Whether retained employees are classified as unemployed when the wage is above equilibrium
Whether the statutory unemployment denominator should exclude workers receiving higher wages
Whether every firm uses identical technology, which alone guarantees an exact offset
The size of the productivity/turnover benefit relative to the higher labor cost and hiring response
items.feedback: The efficiency mechanism can benefit the employer, but it does not algebraically guarantee a particular employment or cost offset. Relative magnitudes determine the net result.

items.stem: A competitive labor market initially clears at $15 with a legal minimum of $12. Labor demand then falls so that the new market-clearing wage would be $10. The minimum stays $12; at that wage firms demand 90 workers and 120 offer labor. What changes under the competitive wage-floor model?
options: The minimum stays nonbinding; employment is 120 and there is no labor surplus
The minimum changes from binding to nonbinding; employment is 90 and the labor surplus is 30
The minimum changes from nonbinding to binding; employment is 90 and the labor surplus is 30
The minimum changes from nonbinding to binding; employment is 120 and the labor surplus is 90
items.feedback: Initially $12 is below equilibrium and does not bind. After equilibrium falls to $10, the unchanged $12 floor binds. Firms hire the 90 workers demanded at that wage; 120−90=30 workers are the excess supply of labor.

items.stem: A firm claims higher pay is profitable because it cuts turnover costs. What comparison tests that claim rather than assuming any wage premium pays for itself?
options: Compare posted wages across firms alone; a higher wage establishes higher profit.
Compare added wage expense with reduced turnover costs and any productivity gain.
Compare the wage with the legal minimum alone; retention costs cannot affect profit.
Compare headcounts alone; wage expense and worker productivity do not affect profit.
items.feedback: The efficiency-wage claim is behavioral, not an accounting identity. The firm must weigh the extra wage bill against lower hiring/training costs from quits and any productivity benefit; a premium alone does not prove profitability.

items.stem: A labor market would clear at $18. Firms instead maintain a $22 efficiency wage to reduce costly quits. At $22, 120 workers offer labor and firms want to hire 90. In this simple model, what employment and labor surplus result while firms maintain that wage?
options: 120 employed; no workers in excess supply
90 employed; no workers in excess supply
90 employed; 30 workers in excess supply
120 employed; 30 workers in excess supply
items.feedback: At the maintained wage, firms hire the 90 workers demanded. Labor supplied exceeds labor demanded by 120−90=30. The turnover incentive can explain maintaining the high wage without eliminating the associated excess supply.

items.stem: Why can GDP rise while well-being does not clearly improve?
options: GDP fails to record any final goods sold in legal markets
Every production increase automatically reduces leisure and environmental quality
Higher GDP guarantees equal gains for households across the income distribution
GDP may ignore pollution, leisure loss, and unequal distribution
items.feedback: GDP is useful, but it misses important quality-of-life factors.

items.stem: Which statement is the strongest evaluation of GDP as a welfare measure?
options: GDP is complete whenever nominal prices remain unchanged
GDP measures only leisure, safety, and environmental quality
GDP is useful but misses nonmarket quality-of-life factors
GDP is useless because it excludes all current market production
items.feedback: GDP is useful but incomplete as a measure of well-being.

items.stem: A software update greatly improves usefulness while its market price is unchanged. What difficulty can arise?
options: GDP may not fully capture the quality improvement
Real GDP must fall because price is unchanged
The update counts only as a transfer
GDP already measures every consumer benefit exactly
items.feedback: GDP per person does not show distribution and may incompletely capture product-quality change.

items.stem: A factory expands output while causing more pollution. What is the careful conclusion?
options: GDP and welfare must rise by the same percentage
Welfare must fall because production increased
Pollution is subtracted automatically from nominal GDP
GDP rises, while the net welfare effect remains uncertain
items.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

items.stem: A family replaces unpaid home cooking with otherwise similar restaurant meals. What can happen?
options: GDP is unchanged because meals are identical
Real output must double
GDP rises because more activity is purchased in markets
GDP falls because restaurant work is intermediate
items.feedback: Moving activity into or out of markets can change GDP even when useful services or consumer benefit move differently.

items.stem: Production is unchanged, but workplace injuries fall after a safety improvement. What does GDP alone miss?
options: A transfer counted in government purchases
A welfare gain from greater safety
A decline in all final output
A required increase in imports
items.feedback: Leisure, environmental quality, and health or safety can change independently of measured output.

items.stem: A country cuts pollution regulations, output rises, but air quality worsens and illness increases. What does this show about GDP?
options: GDP must fall whenever pollution or illness increases after production
GDP automatically subtracts every environmental and health cost from output
Higher measured production proves that every resident became better off
GDP may rise even when broader well-being does not clearly improve
items.feedback: GDP counts production but does not fully capture environmental damage or health costs.

items.stem: Two countries have equal GDP per person, but one has more leisure, cleaner air, and lower crime. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: GDP per person misses some important parts of well-being
The cleaner country must have lower real GDP
GDP perfectly ranks living standards
Crime and leisure are already fully included in GDP
items.feedback: GDP per person is useful but incomplete because it misses non-market quality-of-life factors.

items.stem: Two countries have the same real GDP per person, but one has longer life expectancy, safer streets, and cleaner water. What follows?
options: Equal measured output does not imply equal well-being
Both countries must have equal welfare
The safer country must have lower real GDP
Health and safety are fully included in the GDP average
items.feedback: GDP is a strong measure of market production for its purpose, but it omits some dimensions of welfare.

items.stem: Country A has higher GDP per person than Country B, but Country B has cleaner air, more leisure, and longer life expectancy. What should an economist conclude?
options: GDP per person is useful but incomplete for comparing well-being
Country A must have higher well-being in every respect
Country B must have higher GDP once adjusted correctly
GDP ignores all market output
items.feedback: GDP per person helps compare material output but misses some important well-being measures.

items.stem: A hurricane destroys homes, and rebuilding activity raises GDP. Why is this not necessarily an improvement in well-being?
options: GDP excludes all construction completed after a natural disaster
Destroyed homes are recorded as current business investment spending
Rebuilding makes the original household losses irrelevant to welfare
GDP counts rebuilding, not the destruction’s welfare loss
items.feedback: GDP can rise from rebuilding even though society is replacing destroyed assets.

items.stem: A country increases GDP by requiring longer work hours and reducing vacation time. What GDP limitation does this expose?
options: GDP omits lost leisure
GDP excludes wages
GDP cannot count final goods
GDP only counts imports
items.feedback: GDP measures production but does not fully value leisure.

items.stem: A country has GDP of $2T and population of 20M. Another has GDP of $4T and population of 80M. Which has higher GDP per person?
options: The first country, with $100,000 per person versus $50,000
The second country, because total GDP is larger
They are equal because both are measured in trillions
It cannot be determined without imports
items.feedback: GDP per person is $2T/20M = $100,000 and $4T/80M = $50,000.

items.stem: Real GDP per person rises 21% while leisure falls and air quality deteriorates. What can be concluded about output per person and well-being?
options: Output per person increased, but the net welfare change requires valuing the omitted losses
Output per person increased, so welfare must have increased by exactly the same percentage
Output per person decreased because environmental damage is automatically deducted from GDP
Output per person is unknown because GDP cannot be measured when leisure changes
items.feedback: Real GDP per person measures average production, not a complete welfare index. Leisure and environmental quality can offset some or all benefits; their values are not supplied.

items.stem: Two countries have the same real GDP per person of $21200. One has greater inequality and poorer health outcomes. Which conclusion respects both the production data and their limits?
options: Every resident has equal income; different health outcomes therefore cannot change the ranking
The less equal country has lower real GDP per person once inequality is read into the given measure
The data establish neither output nor welfare because all averages exclude distribution
Average measured output is equal; distribution and health can still support different welfare rankings
items.feedback: Equal GDP per person establishes equality of average measured production, not individual incomes or a complete welfare ranking. Distribution and health are separate evidence.

items.stem: A storm destroys existing homes. Rebuilding produces $23 million of current construction, while families lose housing services during repairs. Which GDP-versus-welfare comparison is correct?
