Reserves rose; credit and spending responses remain limited.
Reserves rose; the natural unemployment rate therefore falls permanently.
items.feedback: Reserve implementation, lending behavior and expenditure are distinct stages. Weak later links can limit aggregate-demand effects without undoing the initial reserve operation.

items.stem: A contractionary monetary shock raises rates and reduces investment by $90, but export demand rises independently. What can be concluded about total AD without knowing export and induced effects?
options: Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; monetary policy establishes a net decline.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; relative contributions determine the net result.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; trade demand establishes a net increase.
Investment lowers AD; exports raise it; opposing directions establish an exact offset.
items.feedback: A correct sign for one transmission chain is not a complete net forecast under a second shock. Compare the final contributions before assigning the total AD direction.

items.stem: In the standard short-run model, monetary easing lowers interest rates, making $100 in investment more attractive. However, weaker expected sales offset that incentive. Why might aggregate demand respond only weakly to the monetary easing?
options: Weaker expected sales can reduce investment despite lower interest rates.
Monetary easing failed to lower interest rates, despite the observed decline.
Investment cannot affect aggregate demand because capital spending is excluded from it.
An unreported increase in reserve requirements restricted lending despite the monetary easing.
items.feedback: Lower interest rates affect aggregate demand only if spending responds. Weaker expected sales can make firms reluctant to invest even when borrowing becomes cheaper.

items.stem: In the scarce-reserves model, monetary expansion lowers interest but firms do not increase investment. Which next part of the usual transmission chain is weakened?
options: The investment-driven rise in aggregate demand
The already-observed fall in interest
The definition of required reserves
The classification of currency in money
items.feedback: The chain from rates to investment fails to deliver the usual spending increase, so the investment contribution to AD is weaker.

items.stem: In a scarce-reserves model, monetary expansion lowers rates and investment rises $10. With spending multiplier 2 and no other spending change, what AD effect follows?
options: A $20 decrease
A $20 increase
A $10 decrease
A $5 increase
items.feedback: The autonomous investment increase 10 is multiplied by 2, raising AD20.

items.stem: In a scarce-reserves model, monetary contraction raises rates and reduces investment $15. With spending multiplier 2 and no other spending change, what AD effect follows?
options: A $30 increase
A $30 decrease
A $15 increase
A $7.5 decrease
items.feedback: The autonomous investment reduction 15 produces a total demand reduction 30.

items.stem: A student says credit card balances should be counted in M1 because people use cards to buy goods. What is the best correction?
options: Credit cards are borrowing, not money balances
Credit cards are currency held by the public
Credit cards are checkable deposits
Credit cards are savings deposits
items.feedback: Credit cards allow borrowing. They are not money balances like currency or checkable deposits.

items.stem: A household keeps cash because it wants to make purchases quickly, compare prices, and save some value for later. Which answer matches all three functions?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, reserve ratio, fiat money
Unit of account, leverage, discount rate
Medium of exchange, multiplier, bank capital
items.feedback: Money buys goods, measures prices, and can transfer purchasing power into the future.

items.stem: A student says, 'Money is valuable because the dollar bill itself has valuable paper.' What is the best correction?
options: Fiat money has value because people accept it and the government supports its use.
Fiat money has value because its paper is worth more than its face value.
Commodity money and fiat money are the same thing.
Money only has value if it can be exchanged for gold.
items.feedback: Fiat money does not need intrinsic value. Its value comes from general acceptance and government backing.

items.stem: A grocery store lists apples at $2 per pound. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Unit of account
Store of value
Medium of exchange
Fractional reserve
items.feedback: The price tag uses money to measure value, so money is acting as a unit of account.

items.stem: A person keeps $500 in cash for emergencies. Which function of money is most directly involved?
options: Store of value
Unit of account
Medium of exchange
Money multiplier
items.feedback: The cash is preserving purchasing power for later, so it is serving as a store of value.

items.stem: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Which item would be counted in M2 but not in M1?
options: A savings deposit
Currency in your wallet
A checking account deposit
A traveler's check
items.feedback: Savings deposits are near monies. They belong in M2, not M1.

items.stem: Why does money make specialization easier?
options: It removes the need for a double coincidence of wants.
It makes all goods cost the same amount.
It prevents prices from changing.
It eliminates scarcity.
items.feedback: Money reduces transaction costs because people no longer need to find someone who wants exactly what they offer.

items.stem: Which statement best explains why currency held by a bank does not count the same way as currency held by the public?
options: Bank-held currency is reserves; public-held currency is circulating money.
Currency held by banks is automatically counted twice in M1.
Currency held by banks is commodity money.
Currency held by banks is never money.
items.feedback: Currency held by banks is treated as reserves. Currency in the money supply refers to currency held by the public.

items.stem: A household moves $4,000 from a checking account into a retail money-market mutual fund. What happens?
options: M1 falls while M2 is unchanged.
M1 and M2 both fall by $4,000.
M1 is unchanged while M2 rises.
M1 and M2 both rise by $4,000.
items.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2, while retail money-market mutual funds are in M2 but not M1. The transfer lowers M1 without changing M2.

items.stem: A payment app transfers balances instantly from users’ checking accounts but holds no separate monetary balance. How should the app affect measured money?
options: Every transfer through the app permanently increases the measured M1 stock.
The app balance enters M2 even though no separate monetary balance exists.
It changes payment convenience without creating a new money balance.
Using the app removes the linked checking deposits from measured money.
items.feedback: A payment platform that merely accesses checking deposits changes how money is used, not how much money exists.

items.stem: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $3,000, savings deposits are $2,500, small time deposits are $1,200, retail money market funds are $800, and large time deposits are $900. If large time deposits are not counted in M2, what is M2?
items.feedback: M2 = M1 + savings deposits + small time deposits + retail money market funds = $3,000 + $2,500 + $1,200 + $800 = $7,500.

items.stem: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. A household moves $10,000 from a checking account to a savings account. What happens to M1 and M2, using standard course definitions?
options: M1 falls, while M2 is unchanged.
Both M1 and M2 fall.
M1 is unchanged, while M2 rises.
Both M1 and M2 rise.
items.feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2; savings deposits are in M2 but not M1. Moving funds to savings lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.

items.stem: The Fed buys bonds, banks lend more, and the public redeposits most loan proceeds. Which money measures are most likely affected first?
options: Bank deposits and M1 rise, with broader effects on M2 depending on where funds are held.
Commodity-money holdings rise because bond purchases convert financial assets into physical commodity money
Real GDP rises immediately while the quantity of bank deposits is unaffected by the lending and redeposit process
M1 falls because additional bank lending reduces the checkable deposits held by households and businesses
items.feedback: Bank lending creates deposits, and checkable deposits are part of M1. M2 can also be affected depending on where funds are held.

items.stem: A farmer accepts dollars for corn, uses dollars to compare seed prices, and saves some dollars for next month. Which answer correctly matches the three functions of money?
options: Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value
Store of value, medium of exchange, unit of account
Unit of account, store of value, medium of exchange
Money multiplier, reserve requirement, federal funds rate
items.feedback: Buying uses money as a medium of exchange, comparing prices uses it as a unit of account, and saving it uses it as a store of value.

items.stem: Currency held by the public is $800 billion and checkable deposits are $1,200 billion. Assume these are the only M1 components with nonzero balances. What is M1?
options: $2,000 billion
$1,200 billion
$800 billion
$400 billion
items.feedback: M1 includes currency plus checkable deposits: $800 billion + $1,200 billion = $2,000 billion.

items.stem: Use U.S. monetary-aggregate definitions in effect before May 2020. Suppose M1 is $2,000 billion, savings deposits are $900 billion, small time deposits are $300 billion, and retail money market mutual funds are $200 billion. M2 is
options: $3,400 billion
$2,000 billion
$1,400 billion
$2,300 billion
items.feedback: M2 equals M1 plus near monies: $2,000 + $900 + $300 + $200 = $3,400 billion.

items.stem: A store quotes a $140 price in dollars but accepts a card that transfers dollars from a deposit account. A student calls the card a fourth function of money. Which correction connects the instrument and functions?
options: Quote: unit of account; deposit: payment medium; card: transfer instrument.
Quote: store of value; deposit: transfer instrument; card: unit of account.
Quote: payment medium; deposit: unit of account; card: money-creation instrument.
Quote: unit of account; deposit: outside money; card: commodity payment medium.
items.feedback: Distinguish the monetary unit and balances from the technology used to access them. Quoting prices uses a unit of account; paying transfers money through the card system.

items.stem: An economy has currency $160, checking $320, savings $480, and small time deposits $160. Using current U.S. definitions, what are M1 and M2?
items.feedback: M1 = 160+320+480 = 960. M2 adds the time deposit once: 960+160 = 1120. Savings already inside M1 must not be added again.

items.stem: A customer deposits $180 of currency into checking. A bank later makes a separate loan by crediting a borrower's checking account. Which comparison correctly separates the two events?
options: Neither event can change M1 because every bank deposit merely replaces currency
The currency deposit creates new M1; lending changes only the ownership of existing currency
The currency deposit changes M1 composition; the later loan can create a new deposit and raise M1
Both events create new M1 equal to the amounts credited because checking balances rise
items.feedback: In the first event, public currency falls as checking rises; in the second, a loan asset and deposit liability are created together. The initial transfer and subsequent credit creation must not be conflated.

items.stem: A new cluster of coffee shops opens near an established café. Which immediate effect is most likely for the café?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic
Its demand shifts right and becomes less elastic
Its MC curve shifts down automatically
Its ATC becomes zero
items.feedback: Entry creates more close substitutes.

items.stem: Several boutique gyms close after sustained losses. Which effect is most likely for a surviving gym?
options: Its demand shifts left and becomes more elastic because fewer alternatives remain available
Its demand shifts right and may become less elastic
Its MR becomes horizontal at zero
Its fixed cost disappears
items.feedback: Exit removes substitutes and can strengthen surviving demand.

items.stem: A firm’s price is $42, MC is $31, and ATC is $42 at the chosen output. Which statement is correct?
options: The firm earns an $11 profit per unit because price exceeds marginal cost by $11
The firm is allocatively efficient
The firm earns zero economic profit but has an $11 markup
The firm must exit
items.feedback: Price equals ATC, so profit is zero; price minus MC is the markup.

items.stem: A firm produces 24 units in long-run equilibrium, while ATC is minimized at 36 units. What is its excess capacity?
options: 24 units
36 units
60 units
12 units
items.feedback: Excess capacity is minimum-ATC output minus equilibrium output.

items.stem: An advertising campaign merely raises fixed selling cost and leaves demand unchanged. What happens to the short-run MR=MC output?
options: It remains unchanged
It rises because ATC rises
It falls because fixed cost raises MC
It becomes the minimum-ATC output
items.feedback: A pure fixed cost changes ATC and profit, not MR or MC.

items.stem: A per-unit promotional fee is imposed on every unit sold. Which curves are directly raised?
options: Only ATC
MC, AVC, and ATC
Only fixed cost and AFC
Demand and MR only
items.feedback: A per-unit selling cost is a variable cost.

items.stem: A brand campaign makes customers less willing to switch to rivals. What is the most direct demand effect?
options: Demand becomes perfectly elastic
Demand shifts only because the campaign lowers marginal cost and average variable cost
The firm’s demand becomes less elastic
MR equals price at every quantity
items.feedback: Greater loyalty reduces responsiveness to price.

items.stem: A comparison website makes prices and features easier to compare across brands. What is the likely effect?
options: Firm demand becomes vertical
Every seller becomes a monopoly because buyers can now compare all products directly
Entry becomes impossible
Firm demand becomes more elastic
items.feedback: Lower search costs make switching easier.

items.stem: After Lumen Bistro chooses Q=22.09, what price follows from P=92−1.5Q?
items.feedback: Price comes from demand at the chosen output.

items.stem: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm produces Q1=20 while ATC is minimized at Q2=36.67. What is excess capacity?
options: 20 units
36.67 units
16.67 units
items.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

items.stem: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $70 and MC is $50. What is the markup?
items.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

items.stem: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm produces Q1=24 while ATC is minimized at Q2=39.71. What is excess capacity?
options: 15.71 units
24 units
39.71 units
items.feedback: Subtract equilibrium output from the minimum-ATC output.

items.stem: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $76 and MC is $49.60. What is the markup?
items.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

items.stem: At a long-run equilibrium, price is $64 and MC is $47.80. What is the markup?
items.feedback: Markup equals price minus marginal cost.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s economic profit per unit at Q = 50?
items.feedback: Profit per unit is price minus ATC: $37 − $33 = $4.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit at the profit-maximizing output?
items.feedback: Total profit is ($37 − $33) × 50 = $200.

items.stem: A comparison website makes it easier for buyers to compare nearly identical local services. What effect is most likely on each firm’s demand?
options: Demand becomes more elastic
Demand becomes less elastic
Demand becomes vertical
Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
items.feedback: Better comparison makes substitution easier, increasing buyers’ responsiveness to one firm’s price.

items.stem: A firm pays a $3 promotional fee for every unit sold, and demand is unchanged. What is the most direct short-run effect?
options: Only fixed cost rises, so output cannot change
Demand shifts right by $3 at every quantity
ATC falls because advertising spreads fixed cost
MC rises, so the MR=MC output tends to fall
items.feedback: A per-unit selling cost raises marginal cost and tends to reduce the profit-maximizing output when demand is unchanged.

items.stem: A restaurant improves food quality. Customers are willing to pay more, but marginal production cost also rises. What determines the new profit-maximizing output?
options: The cost increase alone
The old output because quality is nonprice competition
The new MR and MC curves together
The demand shift alone
items.feedback: Quality improvement can affect both willingness to pay and cost, so the new optimum still requires comparing MR and MC.

items.stem: A policy causes several niche brands to exit. Average production cost falls, but consumers lose valued variety. What is the correct welfare conclusion?
options: Welfare must rise because average cost fell
Welfare must fall because the number of brands fell
The change is irrelevant because firms earn zero economic profit
The net effect is ambiguous without comparing cost savings with lost variety benefits
items.feedback: Efficiency analysis must weigh resource savings against the consumer value of differentiation and variety.

items.stem: An industry is classified as monopolistically competitive because it has many differentiated sellers. In one rural town, however, only two sellers actually serve customers. What is the best caution?
options: Two local sellers guarantee a natural monopoly
Differentiation becomes irrelevant whenever geography matters
The local market may display strategic interdependence that the broad model misses
The market must still be perfectly competitive locally
items.feedback: Market boundaries matter. A broad national description can hide a much more concentrated local competitive environment.

items.stem: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm earns zero economic profit but charges P>$MC$. What does this show?
options: The firm is producing at minimum ATC
Zero economic profit does not imply allocative efficiency
The firm must be earning an accounting loss
Entry has failed to eliminate all market power
items.feedback: Entry can eliminate economic profit while differentiation leaves a markup and P above MC.

items.stem: Atlas Coffee publishes verified wait times and prices. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Informational advertising
Perfectly competitive price taking
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Strategic oligopoly collusion
items.feedback: Verified prices and wait times provide product information buyers can use before purchasing. This is informational advertising rather than a claim that the firm is a price taker.

items.stem: Bloom Cosmetics links the brand to prestige without measurable performance claims. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Strategic oligopoly collusion
Persuasive differentiation
items.feedback: Associating the brand with prestige seeks to change preferences or perceived differentiation without documenting a physical performance improvement.

items.stem: Crown Dental offers a costly long warranty tied to its reputation. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
A natural-monopoly cost condition
A quality signal
Strategic oligopoly collusion
items.feedback: A costly warranty commits the seller to consequences if quality disappoints. That commitment can convey information about quality, rather than simply describe the market’s cost structure.

items.stem: Dahlia Delivery buys an annual sponsorship unrelated to order volume. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
A fixed selling cost
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Strategic oligopoly collusion
items.feedback: The annual sponsorship payment does not vary with orders, making it a fixed selling cost rather than a per-unit cost.

items.stem: Flint Apparel uses more durable fabric and better construction. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Strategic oligopoly collusion
Genuine quality differentiation
items.feedback: More durable fabric and better construction change the product’s delivered attributes. That is a real quality improvement rather than a purely prestige-based claim.

items.stem: Glade Fitness offers benefits that members keep by staying with the gym and lose if they switch, making them less responsive to its price. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Brand-based reduction in demand elasticity
Strategic oligopoly collusion
items.feedback: Benefits tied to remaining with the brand reduce switching and make quantity less responsive to its price. This lowers the absolute value of demand elasticity.

items.stem: Haven Hotels offers accommodation for guests who prefer less noise, light, and other sensory stimulation. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
Value-creating product variety
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Strategic oligopoly collusion
items.feedback: The specialized lodging format serves a distinct preference or need. Variety can create value without requiring identical products or monopoly scale economies.

items.stem: Ivory Retail supports a tool that makes rival prices easy to compare. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Information that can increase demand elasticity
Perfectly competitive price taking
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Strategic oligopoly collusion
items.feedback: Easier comparison of rival prices reduces search costs and makes switching to a cheaper alternative easier, which can increase price responsiveness.

items.stem: Jasper Learning develops a genuinely improved tutoring format. Which economic classification best fits?
options: Perfectly competitive price taking
A natural-monopoly cost condition
Strategic oligopoly collusion
Product innovation with possible temporary profit
items.feedback: An improved tutoring format changes the service itself. Buyers may value the improvement enough to support profit temporarily, while entry and imitation can erode it.

items.stem: If instead a successful quality improvement raises Summit Coffee’s demand intercept by $14 and raises MC by $6, what must be done to determine the new output?
options: Set the new MR curve equal to the new MC curve
Use the old output because both curves changed
Set the new demand curve equal to ATC
Choose minimum ATC regardless of demand
items.feedback: Both demand and marginal cost must be updated in the marginal decision.

items.stem: If instead a successful quality improvement raises Terra Salon’s demand intercept by $14 and raises MC by $6, what must be done to determine the new output?
options: Use the old output because both curves changed
Set the new demand curve equal to ATC
Choose minimum ATC regardless of demand
Set the new MR curve equal to the new MC curve
items.feedback: Both demand and marginal cost must be updated in the marginal decision.

items.stem: If instead a successful quality improvement raises Urban Fitness’s demand intercept by $14 and raises MC by $6, what must be done to determine the new output?
options: Use the old output because both curves changed
Set the new demand curve equal to ATC
Set the new MR curve equal to the new MC curve
Choose minimum ATC regardless of demand
items.feedback: Both demand and marginal cost must be updated in the marginal decision.

items.stem: If instead a successful quality improvement raises Velvet Apparel’s demand intercept by $14 and raises MC by $6, what must be done to determine the new output?
options: Use the old output because both curves changed
Set the new MR curve equal to the new MC curve
Set the new demand curve equal to ATC
Choose minimum ATC regardless of demand
items.feedback: Both demand and marginal cost must be updated in the marginal decision.

items.stem: If instead a successful quality improvement raises Willow Dental’s demand intercept by $14 and raises MC by $6, what must be done to determine the new output?
options: Set the new MR curve equal to the new MC curve
Use the old output because both curves changed
Set the new demand curve equal to ATC
Choose minimum ATC regardless of demand
items.feedback: Both demand and marginal cost must be updated in the marginal decision.

items.stem: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm has profit-maximizing output Q1=22, minimum-ATC output Q2=35.47, price $68.00 and MC=$50.40. Using the displayed values, what are its markup and excess capacity?
options: Markup $50.40; excess capacity 22 units.
Markup $17.60; excess capacity 13.47 units.
Markup $17.60; excess capacity 35.47 units.
Markup $68.00; excess capacity 13.47 units.
items.feedback: Markup is P−MC=68.00−50.40=$17.60. Excess capacity is Q2−Q1=35.47−22=13.47 units, using the displayed minimum-ATC output.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm produces 20 units in long-run equilibrium at price $70 with MC = $50. Which statement is correct?
options: Positive economic profit equal to markup times output
Zero economic profit with price equal to marginal cost
Zero economic profit with a positive markup
Positive economic profit at minimum average total cost
items.feedback: Tangency gives P=ATC while P remains above MC.

items.stem: A long-run monopolistically competitive firm charges $70, has a $20 markup over marginal cost, and produces 14.64 units less than its minimum-ATC output of 34.64. What are its marginal cost and actual output?
options: MC = $90; output = 20 units.
MC = $50; output = 49.28 units.
MC = $20; output = 14.64 units.
MC = $50; output = 20 units.
items.feedback: MC equals price minus markup: 70 − 20 = $50. Actual output is minimum-ATC output minus excess capacity: 34.64 − 14.64 = 20.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm produces 24 units in long-run equilibrium at price $76 with MC = $49.60. Which statement is correct?
options: Positive economic profit equal to markup times output
Zero economic profit with a positive markup
Zero economic profit with price equal to marginal cost
Positive economic profit at minimum average total cost
items.feedback: Tangency gives P=ATC while P remains above MC.

items.stem: At its long-run equilibrium, a monopolistically competitive firm produces 24 units, charges $76, and has marginal cost $49.60. It minimizes ATC at 42.93 units. Free entry has eliminated economic profit. Which conclusion follows?
options: ATC at 24 units is $49.60 because zero profit requires price to equal MC.
The firm must produce 42.93 units because zero profit requires minimum ATC.
ATC at 24 units is $76, even though price exceeds MC and output is below the minimum-ATC quantity.
Economic profit is $633.60 because the markup applies to all 24 units.
items.feedback: Zero economic profit means P = ATC at the chosen output, not P = MC or minimum ATC. The markup and excess capacity can persist in long-run monopolistic competition.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm maximizes profit at 18 units and would minimize ATC at 30.12 units. It produces and sells all 18 units. A student calls the 12.12-unit gap “unsold inventory.” What is the best correction?
options: The gap proves the firm produced 30.12 units and sold only 18.
The gap is excess capacity relative to the cost-minimizing scale, not goods already produced and left unsold.
The gap measures the difference between price and marginal cost.
Selling all 18 units means the firm must be producing at minimum ATC.
items.feedback: Excess capacity compares actual output with the output minimizing ATC. It does not count unsold production.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm produces 28 units in long-run equilibrium at price $82 with MC = $48.40. Which statement is correct?
options: Positive economic profit equal to markup times output
Zero economic profit with price equal to marginal cost
Positive economic profit at minimum average total cost
Zero economic profit with a positive markup
items.feedback: Tangency gives P=ATC while P remains above MC.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm charges $82 at its chosen output, where MC = $48.40 and ATC = $82. Suppose a regulator requires a price equal to MC at that same output, holding the displayed costs fixed. Would the firm cover total cost?
options: No. It would lose $33.60 per unit because the required price would be below ATC.
Yes. Price equal to MC always covers average total cost.
Yes. Zero profit at the original price guarantees zero profit after the price cut.
No. It would lose $82 per unit because all sales revenue disappears.
items.feedback: At the specified output, price would fall to $48.40 while ATC remains $82. The per-unit loss is 82 − 48.40 = $33.60. This fixed-output comparison does not predict a new regulated equilibrium.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm produces 22 units in long-run equilibrium at price $68 with MC = $50.40. Which statement is correct?
options: Positive economic profit equal to markup times output
Zero economic profit with price equal to marginal cost
Zero economic profit with a positive markup
Positive economic profit at minimum average total cost
items.feedback: Tangency gives P=ATC while P remains above MC.

items.stem: Two long-run monopolistically competitive firms charge prices equal to ATC. Firm A has a $17.60 markup and 13.47 units of excess capacity. Firm B has a $12 markup and 20 units of excess capacity. Which comparison is supported?
options: A has both the larger markup and the larger excess capacity.
B has the larger markup because it has more excess capacity.
A must earn more economic profit because its markup is larger.
A has the larger price–MC gap, while B operates farther below its own minimum-ATC output.
items.feedback: Markup and excess capacity measure different gaps. A has 17.60 > 12 in markup; B has 20 > 13.47 in excess capacity. Both have zero economic profit because P = ATC.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm produces 26 units in long-run equilibrium at price $74 with MC = $48. Which statement is correct?
options: Positive economic profit equal to markup times output
Zero economic profit with a positive markup
Zero economic profit with price equal to marginal cost
Positive economic profit at minimum average total cost
items.feedback: Tangency gives P=ATC while P remains above MC.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium has P = $74, MC = $48, output Q = 26, and minimum-ATC output of 41.62. What are its markup and excess capacity?
options: Markup $74; excess capacity 26 units
Markup $48; excess capacity 41.62 units
Markup $26; excess capacity 15.62 units
Markup $66.19; excess capacity 26 units
items.feedback: Use P−MC and QminATC−Q.

items.stem: Which elasticity change is most consistent with the entry faced by Wren Foods?
options: Demand elasticity is fixed by ATC
More substitutes make demand more elastic
The demand curve becomes vertical
MR becomes equal to price
items.feedback: Substitute availability affects responsiveness.

items.stem: Why does the entry process for Wren Foods stop in the standard long run?
options: All products become identical
Price reaches marginal cost
Expected economic profit reaches zero
Every firm reaches minimum ATC
items.feedback: Entry or exit removes the incentive for further movement.

items.stem: Which elasticity change is most consistent with the entry faced by Xenia Spa?
options: More substitutes make demand more elastic
Demand elasticity is fixed by ATC
The demand curve becomes vertical
MR becomes equal to price
items.feedback: Substitute availability affects responsiveness.

items.stem: Why does the entry process for Xenia Spa stop in the standard long run?
options: All products become identical
Expected economic profit reaches zero
Price reaches marginal cost
Every firm reaches minimum ATC
items.feedback: Entry or exit removes the incentive for further movement.

items.stem: Which elasticity change is most consistent with the exit faced by Yarrow Retail?
options: Demand elasticity is fixed by ATC
The demand curve becomes vertical
MR becomes equal to price
Fewer substitutes make demand less elastic
items.feedback: Substitute availability affects responsiveness.

items.stem: Why does the exit process for Yarrow Retail stop in the standard long run?
options: Expected economic profit reaches zero
All products become identical
Price reaches marginal cost
Every firm reaches minimum ATC
items.feedback: Entry or exit removes the incentive for further movement.

items.stem: Which elasticity change is most consistent with the exit faced by Zenith Fitness?
options: Demand elasticity is fixed by ATC
The demand curve becomes vertical
Fewer substitutes make demand less elastic
MR becomes equal to price
items.feedback: Substitute availability affects responsiveness.

items.stem: Why does the exit process for Zenith Fitness stop in the standard long run?
options: All products become identical
Price reaches marginal cost
Every firm reaches minimum ATC
Expected economic profit reaches zero
items.feedback: Entry or exit removes the incentive for further movement.

items.stem: What price does the firm charge in the long-run position shown? Why is there no further incentive to enter?
options: $82; price equals ATC, so no positive economic profit remains to attract entry.
$72; price equals ATC, so no positive economic profit remains to attract entry.
$82; price equals MC, which by itself guarantees zero economic profit.
$72; price equals MC, which by itself guarantees zero economic profit.
items.feedback: At Q1 = 28, demand and ATC meet at $82. This eliminates economic profit and the entry incentive, while MC remains only $48.40. P = MC is not the zero-profit test.

items.stem: As entry erodes short-run profit, how do the firm’s demand and ATC curves relate in the standard long-run equilibrium?
options: Demand is horizontal at minimum ATC
Demand is tangent to ATC and economic profit is zero
Price equals MC and ATC
MR is tangent to demand
items.feedback: Entry or exit continues until P=ATC at the chosen output.

items.stem: Once entry has fully adjusted the representative firm's demand, which condition indicates long-run equilibrium?
options: Demand is tangent to ATC and economic profit is zero
Demand is horizontal at minimum ATC
Price equals MC and ATC
MR is tangent to demand
items.feedback: Entry or exit continues until P=ATC at the chosen output.

items.stem: A monopolistically competitive firm in long-run equilibrium produces 24 units while minimum ATC occurs at 39.71 units. What does the difference show?
options: Markup of $15.71
Excess capacity of 15.71 units
Economic profit of $1,824
A shutdown gap
items.feedback: Excess capacity is the output gap to minimum ATC.

items.stem: A clothing boutique is incurring a short-run economic loss and firms can leave the market. What adjustment pressure follows?
options: No entry or exit
Exit
A government price ceiling
A shift to identical products
items.feedback: Short-run loss encourages exit.

items.stem: A dental practice is earning negative economic profit in a market with relatively easy exit. What market response should occur?
options: Exit
No entry or exit
A government price ceiling
A shift to identical products
items.feedback: Short-run loss encourages exit.

items.stem: If a monopolist reduces output farther below the competitive quantity while demand and cost curves are unchanged, what generally happens to deadweight loss?

items.stem: A natural monopoly has MC=$12 and ATC=$20 at the allocatively efficient quantity. If regulation sets P=$12, which outcome is most likely without a subsidy?

The firm becomes perfectly competitive
The firm’s fixed cost becomes zero

items.stem: A regulator wants lower prices but also wants the utility to maintain infrastructure and innovate. Which concern best captures the tradeoff?

Any regulation automatically produces the competitive quantity

items.stem: Demand for a utility expands enough that the relevant output range moves beyond the region where ATC is falling. What does that suggest about the natural-monopoly argument?

Fixed cost compared with total revenue
items.feedback: The shutdown threshold is average variable cost.

items.stem: Suppose only Lakeside Network’s fixed cost increases by $200. What changes in the short run?
options: MC rises; profit falls; output falls and price rises.
ATC rises; profit falls; output and price stay unchanged.
Costs stay unchanged; profit falls; output and price fall.
AVC rises; profit falls; output falls to zero and price stays unchanged.
items.feedback: The $200 increase raises total fixed cost and ATC and lowers profit by $200. It leaves demand, MR, MC and AVC unchanged, so the profit-maximizing quantity and its demand-based price do not change.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the monopoly output shown, what total cost is implied by ATC before comparing it with revenue?
items.feedback: ATC is $45 at Q = 40, so total cost is $45 × 40 = $1,800.

items.stem: Under marginal-cost pricing a natural monopoly supplies 100 units at P=$8, while ATC=$11 at that output. What subsidy covers the total-cost shortfall?
items.feedback: The shortfall is (ATC−P)Q=(11−8)×100=$300.

items.stem: Why does the natural rate of unemployment remain positive in the long run?
options: Normal job search and structural mismatches persist
Every worker is always unemployed
Inflation forces GDP to fall
The CPI excludes discouraged workers
items.feedback: The natural rate includes frictional and structural unemployment that persist in normal times.

items.stem: A rapid shift away from coal production leaves many workers without the skills demanded by expanding industries. What is the most likely effect?
options: Cyclical unemployment must fall to zero.
The natural rate must fall because jobs changed.
Frictional unemployment disappears immediately.
Structural unemployment and the natural rate may rise.
items.feedback: Sectoral change can raise structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

items.stem: Actual unemployment is below the estimated natural rate. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The labor market is unusually tight, with possible inflation pressure.
The economy has eliminated every form of unemployment.
Structural unemployment must have fallen permanently to zero.
The economy must be operating with a recessionary output gap.
items.feedback: Unemployment below the natural rate indicates a tight labor market, not the disappearance of frictional and structural unemployment.

items.stem: A temporary collapse in aggregate demand ends, and spending returns to normal. What should happen to unemployment if the natural rate itself did not change?
options: The natural rate rises permanently by the recession increase.
Cyclical unemployment fades, moving actual unemployment toward the natural rate.
Frictional unemployment falls permanently to zero after spending recovers.
Actual unemployment remains at its recession peak even after demand returns.
items.feedback: When the demand shortfall closes, cyclical unemployment recedes and the unemployment rate moves toward its natural benchmark.

items.stem: A strong expansion lowers actual unemployment, but worker matching, skills, and labor-market institutions are unchanged. What is the most careful conclusion?
options: Cyclical unemployment may have fallen without changing the natural rate
The natural rate must have fallen by the same amount as actual unemployment
Structural unemployment must have disappeared permanently
The natural rate becomes zero whenever aggregate demand is strong
items.feedback: The natural rate is the frictional-plus-structural benchmark; actual unemployment can differ because of cyclical conditions.

items.stem: A retraining program successfully moves displaced workers into growing occupations. If other conditions are unchanged, what is the most likely effect on the natural rate?
options: It must rise because more workers have changed occupations
It changes only if cyclical unemployment rises
It cannot change because the natural rate is fixed forever
It may fall because structural unemployment is reduced
items.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

items.stem: A new nationwide matching system shortens the average time between jobs without changing aggregate demand. Which effect is most plausible?
options: Cyclical unemployment rises permanently
Structural unemployment must rise by the same amount
The natural rate cannot respond to matching efficiency
Frictional unemployment and the natural rate may decline
items.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

items.stem: A long-lasting geographic mismatch develops: job openings expand in regions that displaced workers cannot easily move to. What is the most likely natural-rate effect?
options: The natural rate falls automatically because jobs exist somewhere
The natural rate is unchanged whenever total vacancies are positive
Structural unemployment can rise, pushing the natural rate upward
Only cyclical unemployment rises because location never affects structural mismatch
items.feedback: Changes in matching, worker skills, mobility, and labor-market institutions can change frictional or structural unemployment and therefore the natural rate.

items.stem: Suppose actual unemployment is 4%, natural unemployment is 5%, and inflationary pressure is rising. What is the likely labor-market interpretation?
options: Unemployment below the natural rate signals a tight labor market
Cyclical unemployment is strongly positive
Structural unemployment must be zero
All unemployment is discouraged workers
items.feedback: Actual unemployment below the natural rate suggests tight labor markets and possible inflationary pressure.

items.stem: An economy has frictional unemployment 2%, structural 3% and actual 6%. If a demand recovery removes the cyclical component without changing matching or skills, which rate remains and why?
options: 5%; frictional and structural remain after the one percentage point of cyclical unemployment disappears.
0%; removing cyclical unemployment also removes frictional and structural components.
3%; frictional unemployment disappears with the cyclical component during recovery.
6%; changes in demand leave all three unemployment components unchanged.
items.feedback: Natural unemployment=2+3=5; the initial cyclical component is 6−5=1. Recovery alone does not remove search and structural mismatch.

items.stem: Actual unemployment and the estimated natural rate both fall after demand recovery and a matching reform. What information separates the two contributions?
options: The final actual rate alone; it identifies both reform and demand contributions.
The inflation rate alone; it directly measures each unemployment component.
The initial labor force alone; unchanged population fixes both contributions.
Changes in the natural rate and in actual minus natural unemployment.
items.feedback: The natural-rate change captures changed frictional/structural conditions. The change in actual unemployment minus the natural rate captures the cyclical component. Both are needed when reform and recovery occur together.

items.stem: A reform improves matching for 220 job seekers but rapid technology change creates new skill mismatches. What can be inferred about the natural rate before their magnitudes are known?
options: Only actual unemployment can change; the natural benchmark is fixed by definition
The natural rate must rise because structural changes always dominate frictional changes
Better matching lowers its frictional component while mismatch raises its structural component; net change is uncertain
Both changes lower the natural rate because all technology improves job matching
items.feedback: The natural rate is not immutable. It combines frictional and structural components, and opposing component changes require magnitudes to sign their sum.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: At 120 yen per dollar, how many yen can $75 purchase?
items.feedback: Multiply $75 by 120 yen per dollar to obtain 9,000 yen.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: The rate changes from 1.25 Canadian dollars per U.S. dollar to 1.20. What happened to the U.S. dollar?
options: It depreciated against the Canadian dollar
It appreciated against the Canadian dollar
It appreciated by 5 percent
It remained unchanged in reciprocal terms
items.feedback: One U.S. dollar buys fewer Canadian dollars, so it depreciated.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: A hotel costs 240 euros. At 0.80 euro per dollar, what is its dollar price?
items.feedback: Divide 240 euros by 0.80 euro per dollar: the hotel costs $300.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: The dollar appreciates against the peso. Holding product prices fixed in their own currencies, which buyer gains purchasing power?
options: A U.S. exporter paid only in dollars
Both buyers gain the same foreign purchasing power
A U.S. buyer purchasing Mexican goods
A Mexican buyer purchasing U.S. goods
items.feedback: A stronger dollar buys more pesos, making peso-priced goods cheaper in dollar terms.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: If 1 euro buys $1.25, approximately how many euros does $1 buy?
options: 2.25 euros
0.80 euro
1.25 euros
0.25 euro
items.feedback: The reciprocal of 1.25 dollars per euro is 0.80 euro per dollar.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: The exchange rate rises from 100 to 110 pesos per dollar. By what percentage does the dollar appreciate under this quotation?
options: 10 percent
9.1 percent
11 percent
110 percent
items.feedback: The dollar's value rises by 10 pesos on a base of 100, so the appreciation is 10 percent.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: The rate moves from $1.20 per euro to $1.32 per euro. Which statement is correct?
options: The euro depreciates about 9.1 percent
The number of euros one dollar buys also rises 10 percent
The euro appreciates 10 percent against the dollar
The dollar appreciates 10 percent against the euro
items.feedback: The dollar price of one euro rises by $0.12 on a $1.20 base, so the euro appreciates 10 percent.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: A student sees the quotation fall from 1.10 dollars per euro to 1.00 dollar per euro and says the dollar depreciated. What is the error?
options: The student is correct because every lower quotation is depreciation
The euro appreciated because its dollar price fell
No currency changed because the quotation reached one
Fewer dollars are needed per euro, so the dollar appreciated
items.feedback: The dollar price of the euro fell, meaning each dollar can obtain more euros than before.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: The exchange rate falls from 1.40 to 1.33 foreign-currency units per domestic unit. What is the percentage depreciation?
options: 5.3 percent
9.5 percent
5 percent
7 percent
items.feedback: The decline is 0.07 on a base of 1.40, which equals 5 percent.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: If 4 units of domestic currency can buy 5 units of foreign currency, how many units of domestic currency can one unit of foreign currency buy?
options: 5 domestic units per foreign unit
0.80 domestic unit per foreign unit
1.25 domestic units per foreign unit
4 domestic units per foreign unit
items.feedback: Divide 4 domestic currency units by 5 foreign currency units: one unit of foreign currency buys 0.80 unit of domestic currency.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: A foreign bond's value is unchanged in euros, but the euro appreciates against the dollar. What happens to its dollar value?
options: It rises
It falls
It remains fixed
It becomes equal to its euro coupon
items.feedback: Each euro converts into more dollars after the euro appreciates.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: A student says a rise in euros per dollar is a dollar depreciation. Which rule corrects the mistake?
options: If one dollar buys more euros, the dollar appreciated
A higher quoted number means both currencies depreciated
Only reciprocal rates reveal currency direction
A dollar appreciation means one dollar buys fewer euros
items.feedback: Read the units literally: more euros per dollar means greater foreign purchasing power for the dollar.

items.topic: Nominal Exchange Rates and Currency Values
items.stem: Quote e as foreign units per domestic unit and define the real exchange rate as eP/P*. The nominal exchange rate rises 10%, while domestic and foreign prices are unchanged. Does the nominal appreciation also represent real appreciation?
options: No; the real exchange rate stays unchanged whenever prices are unchanged
Yes; but the real exchange rate rises 20% because both price levels enter
Yes; the real exchange rate rises 10%
No; the real exchange rate falls 10%
items.feedback: With P/P* unchanged, the real exchange rate changes in the same proportion as e. Under this quotation the rise is appreciation.

items.stem: Four firms have market shares of 35%, 25%, 20%, and 10%, with the remaining firms holding 10%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
items.feedback: Add the shares of the four largest firms.

items.stem: Row’s payoff is higher with strategy B whether Column chooses X or Y. What does Row have?
options: A Nash equilibrium X
A jointly maximizing payoff
No best response
A dominant strategy B
items.feedback: B beats Row’s alternative under both Column actions.

items.stem: A cell is a Nash equilibrium when:
options: Neither firm can improve by changing strategy alone
The cell with the largest total payoff even though one player would deviate alone
It contains equal payoffs
Both firms chose the same letter
items.feedback: Nash equilibrium requires mutual best responses.

items.stem: A game has two outcomes in which both players are best responding. What does the game have?
options: No equilibrium
Two pure-strategy Nash equilibria
Two dominant strategies for each player
A unique prisoner’s dilemma
items.feedback: Games can have multiple equilibria.

items.stem: Several firms raise prices after a common input cost increase. Why does this not by itself prove collusion?
options: Parallel price changes are conclusive evidence of an explicit agreement.
Input costs affect only fixed cost
Independent firms may respond similarly to the same cost shock
Parallel prices always maximize total surplus
items.feedback: Common conditions can produce parallel conduct without agreement.

items.stem: An incumbent builds capacity that would be useful even if entry occurs. Why can this deter entry?
options: It eliminates every fixed cost
It turns the market into perfect competition
It guarantees a legal monopoly
The capacity can make an aggressive post-entry response credible
items.feedback: A sunk commitment can alter the incumbent’s later incentives.

items.stem: An incumbent threatens to cut price below variable cost after entry, but doing so would be very costly and temporary. The threat is likely:
options: Not credible
A dominant strategy
A concentration ratio
Automatically profitable
items.feedback: The incumbent may not rationally carry out the threat later.

items.stem: A firm maintains a lower price today to reduce expected entrant profit. What is the strategic cost?
options: It raises current monopoly profit automatically
It sacrifices some current profit
It eliminates marginal cost
It guarantees no future rivalry
items.feedback: Limit pricing trades current profit for possible entry deterrence.

items.stem: In the kinked-demand model, rivals are assumed to match:
options: Price increases but never cuts
Every advertising campaign
Price cuts more readily than price increases
All capacity expansions
items.feedback: This asymmetry creates the kink.

items.stem: If MC changes within the discontinuity in the kinked-demand MR curve, the model predicts:
options: Price must fall to zero
The demand kink disappears
The market becomes competitive
Price and output may remain unchanged
items.feedback: The same output can remain optimal while MC crosses the MR gap.

items.stem: An effective cartel raises price and reduces output. Which part of lost consumer surplus is not transferred to producers?
options: Deadweight loss
Cartel profit
Fixed cost
Accounting revenue
items.feedback: Lost mutually beneficial trades create DWL.

items.stem: A merger raises HHI but also creates verified large cost savings. What is the sound conclusion?
options: The merger must be approved
Both increased market power and efficiencies must be evaluated
The merger must be blocked
HHI becomes irrelevant
items.feedback: Concentration and efficiency evidence both matter.

items.stem: A merger lowers marginal cost, but the merged firm keeps price high because rivalry weakens. What does this show?
options: Every efficiency improves consumer surplus
Lower cost removes market power
Cost savings need not be passed fully to consumers
Merger concentration cannot matter
items.feedback: Pass-through depends on competitive pressure.

items.stem: Why can foreign competition affect a domestic concentration assessment?
options: Imports are excluded from every market definition
Foreign firms never affect price
HHI measures only domestic costs
Imports may provide substitutes that constrain domestic firms
items.feedback: Relevant competitors may include foreign suppliers.

items.stem: A firm increases product quality rather than cutting price. This is:
options: Nonprice competition
Tacit collusion automatically
A concentration-ratio calculation
A shutdown decision
items.feedback: Oligopolists can compete on quality and other dimensions.

items.stem: Heavy advertising builds brand loyalty and reduces switching. What strategic effect is most plausible?
options: Every firm becomes a price taker
Price competition may soften because firm demand becomes less elastic
Entry barriers disappear
Marginal revenue equals price
items.feedback: Loyalty can reduce substitution among brands.

items.stem: Why can game theory yield different predictions across oligopoly markets?
options: Game theory assumes identical markets
Every oligopoly has one dominant strategy
Firm costs never matter
Payoffs, information, timing, and repetition differ
items.feedback: Strategic settings differ across industries.

items.stem: Three national wireless carriers dominate a market. Before one carrier cuts price, its managers estimate how the other two are likely to respond. Which feature of oligopoly is being illustrated?
options: Perfect information with no rivalry
Automatic collusion
Zero barriers to entry
Strategic interdependence
items.feedback: The payoff from one firm’s choice depends partly on how a small number of major rivals react.

items.stem: An industry’s HHI rises after two sizable firms merge. What does the increase directly establish?
options: The merger is automatically unlawful
The merged firm must now be a monopolist because any increase in HHI implies complete control of the market
Market concentration increased under the chosen market definition
Consumer welfare necessarily fell
items.feedback: HHI measures concentration; welfare and policy conclusions require additional evidence about competition and efficiencies.

items.stem: At a proposed outcome, Firm A could gain by changing its action while Firm B kept its action fixed. What does that imply?
options: Firm A has a dominant strategy
The game has no strategic interdependence
The proposed outcome is not a Nash equilibrium
The proposed outcome must maximize joint profit
items.feedback: A unilateral profitable deviation means at least one player is not best responding, so the cell is not Nash.

items.stem: Two firms could earn $20 million each by coordinating, but the Nash equilibrium gives each $14 million. What does this illustrate?
options: Dominant strategies always produce the joint-payoff maximum
A Nash equilibrium need not maximize combined payoff
Every Nash equilibrium is efficient
Coordination eliminates strategic incentives
items.feedback: Mutual best responses can lead to a stable outcome with lower total payoff than a cooperative alternative.

items.stem: In payoff order (Row, Column), the cell for Row choosing A and Column choosing Y is (6, 15). Which comparison is relevant when finding Row’s best response to Y?
options: Compare Row’s first-number payoffs across Row’s available actions in column Y
Compare Column’s second-number payoffs across every column, regardless of which action Column has already chosen
Add both payoffs in every cell and choose the largest sum
Compare only the diagonal cells
items.feedback: A best-response calculation holds the rival action fixed and compares the player’s own payoff across its alternatives.

items.stem: Why can firms end up at an outcome they both consider worse than another available outcome?
options: Firms are required to choose the outcome with the lowest combined payoff whenever their interests conflict
A Nash equilibrium always minimizes profit
Payoff matrices ignore strategic behavior
Individual incentives to deviate can make the better joint outcome unstable
items.feedback: A jointly attractive cell need not survive if one player can gain by deviating while the rival cooperates.

items.stem: A cartel has already chosen its joint-profit-maximizing total output. Why might it assign more production to a member with lower marginal cost?
options: Shifting output toward the lower-cost producer can reduce the cartel’s total production cost
Equal quotas always maximize joint profit
Higher-cost firms must produce more to preserve competition
Output allocation cannot affect cartel profit once total output is fixed, even when members have different marginal costs
items.feedback: For a fixed cartel total, allocating more production to lower-marginal-cost members can raise combined profit.

items.stem: Three firms agree to keep prices high. One firm quietly gives large rebates while publicly posting the agreed price. Economically, the rebates are best interpreted as:
options: Proof that the cartel has eliminated all competition because no member can gain market share without openly cutting the posted price
A required form of price leadership
A concentration measure
Cheating that captures extra sales while rivals maintain the collusive price
items.feedback: Secret rebates undermine the agreement by letting one member expand sales at the others’ expense.

items.stem: Which market condition makes a cartel harder to sustain?
options: A small number of firms with similar objectives
A credible punishment system that quickly detects and penalizes members who secretly exceed their agreed output
Many opportunities for members to make secret sales that rivals cannot observe
Frequent transparent reporting of member sales
items.feedback: When cheating is hard to observe, deviations are easier and enforcement becomes weaker.

items.stem: A cartel restricts total output below the competitive level. What is the intended effect on the market price?
options: Create a perfectly elastic industry demand curve so the cartel can sell any quantity at the higher price
Raise price by moving up the market demand curve
Force price down to marginal cost
Make price independent of demand
items.feedback: Restricting industry output raises the price buyers are willing to pay along downward-sloping market demand.

items.stem: Two firms with market shares of 18% and 12% merge. Holding all other shares fixed, why does HHI rise?
items.feedback: The merged share is 18% + 12% = 30%. Its squared share is 900, compared with 324 + 144 = 468 before the merger. HHI rises by 432 = 2 × 18 × 12, with other shares unchanged.

items.stem: A proposed merger would eliminate the closest competitor but also reduce marginal cost substantially. What is the best economic approach?
options: Compare reduced competition with verified cost savings and how much they lower customer prices
Approve the merger automatically because costs fall
Block the merger automatically because concentration rises
Ignore cost effects because only the number of firms matters
items.feedback: Merger analysis requires weighing competitive harm against genuine efficiencies rather than using one fact mechanically.

items.stem: A domestic industry has a high concentration ratio, but buyers can readily switch to imported substitutes when domestic prices rise. What does this imply?
options: The market must be a monopoly
High concentration guarantees collusion
Domestic concentration alone may overstate the firms’ effective market power
Imports are irrelevant to market definition
items.feedback: Competitive constraints from close substitutes, including imports when relevant, matter to the economic market definition.

items.stem: Refer to the payoff matrix. Identify the joint-payoff-maximizing cell.
options: Row B, Column Y
Row A, Column X
Row A, Column Y
Row B, Column X
items.feedback: The cooperative benchmark maximizes the sum of payoffs.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 30%, 27%, 18%, 15%, 10%. What is the HHI?
items.feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 30² + 27² + 18² + 15² + 10² = 2278. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 35%, 25%, 17%, 12%, 11%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
items.feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 35 + 25 + 17 + 12 = 89%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 41%, 22%, 16%, 11%, 10%. What is the HHI?
items.feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 41² + 22² + 16² + 11² + 10² = 2642. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 29%, 27%, 18%, 15%, 11%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
items.feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 29 + 27 + 18 + 15 = 89%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 34%, 25%, 17%, 12%, 12%. What is the HHI?
items.feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 34² + 25² + 17² + 12² + 12² = 2358. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 40%, 22%, 16%, 11%, 11%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
items.feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 40 + 22 + 16 + 11 = 89%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 28%, 27%, 18%, 15%, 12%. What is the HHI?
items.feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 28² + 27² + 18² + 15² + 12² = 2206. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 33%, 25%, 17%, 12%, 13%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
items.feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 33 + 25 + 17 + 13 = 88%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 39%, 22%, 16%, 11%, 12%. What is the HHI?
items.feedback: HHI squares and sums all percentage shares: 39² + 22² + 16² + 11² + 12² = 2526. Adding unsquared shares would not measure HHI.

items.stem: The firms’ market shares are 27%, 27%, 18%, 15%, 13%. What is the four-firm concentration ratio?
items.feedback: Rank the shares and add the four largest: 27 + 27 + 18 + 15 = 87%. The fifth firm is excluded; shares are not squared.

items.stem: Refer to the cartel graph. Determine the joint-profit-maximizing output.
options: 40 units
10 units
20 units
30 units
items.feedback: Industry MR=100−4Q meets MC=20 at Q=20; demand then gives P=60. This marginal equality selects the cartel’s joint output; demand=MC would instead give the competitive benchmark 40.

items.stem: Refer to the cartel graph. Determine the joint-profit-maximizing output.
options: 80 units
20 units
40 units
60 units
items.feedback: Industry MR=110−2Q meets MC=30 at Q=40; demand then gives P=70. This marginal equality selects the cartel’s joint output; demand=MC would instead give the competitive benchmark 80.

items.stem: Refer to the cartel graph. Determine the joint-profit-maximizing output.
options: 48 units
12 units
24 units
36 units
items.feedback: Industry MR=90−3Q meets MC=18 at Q=24; demand then gives P=54. This marginal equality selects the cartel’s joint output; demand=MC would instead give the competitive benchmark 48.

items.stem: Shares 15% and 9% combine. What is the direct HHI increase?
items.feedback: Merging shares 15% and 9% replaces 15²+9² with (15+9)². The increase is 2×15×9=270 HHI points; other firms’ squared shares are unchanged.

items.stem: Shares 21% and 17% combine. What is the direct HHI increase?
items.feedback: Merging shares 21% and 17% replaces 21²+17² with (21+17)². The increase is 2×21×17=714 HHI points; other firms’ squared shares are unchanged.

items.stem: Shares 27% and 11% combine. What is the direct HHI increase?
items.feedback: Merging shares 27% and 11% replaces 27²+11² with (27+11)². The increase is 2×27×11=594 HHI points; other firms’ squared shares are unchanged.

items.stem: Shares 33% and 19% combine. What is the direct HHI increase?
items.feedback: Merging shares 33% and 19% replaces 33²+19² with (33+19)². The increase is 2×33×19=1254 HHI points; other firms’ squared shares are unchanged.

items.stem: Shares 19% and 13% combine. What is the direct HHI increase?
items.feedback: Merging shares 19% and 13% replaces 19²+13² with (19+13)². The increase is 2×19×13=494 HHI points; other firms’ squared shares are unchanged.

items.stem: Why can a collusive outcome be jointly profitable but unstable?
options: Each member may gain privately by cheating
Joint profit is always negative
Firms cannot observe price
Cartels are price takers
items.feedback: Private and collective incentives diverge.

items.stem: What output rule does an effective cartel use?
options: Price equals MC
Industry MR equals industry MC
Demand equals ATC
Each firm produces at minimum AVC
items.feedback: The cartel behaves like a monopolist.

items.stem: What makes monitoring useful?
options: It removes the cheating incentive entirely
It lowers HHI
It increases the chance cheating is detected
It guarantees legal enforcement
items.feedback: Detection supports punishment.

items.stem: Why does an indefinite horizon support cooperation better than a known final round?
options: Demand becomes horizontal
MC equals price
Market shares become equal
Future punishment retains value
items.feedback: A longer expected relationship increases future stakes.

items.stem: What makes a punishment threat credible?
options: Punishment is optimal after cheating occurs
Punishment was announced
Punishment hurts the cheater
The cartel has four members
items.feedback: The punisher must rationally carry it out.

items.stem: Why can price wars persist after a mistake?
options: Firms become price takers
Each response can trigger another retaliation
HHI automatically falls to zero
Demand becomes perfectly inelastic
items.feedback: Retaliation can create a destructive feedback loop.

items.stem: What distinguishes tacit coordination from explicit collusion?
options: Tacit coordination has no strategic behavior
Explicit collusion is always legal
Tacit coordination lacks an explicit agreement
Tacit coordination requires identical prices
items.feedback: Tacit coordination arises without an explicit pact.

items.stem: Why is parallel pricing ambiguous evidence?
options: Collusion never affects price
Prices cannot move together
HHI measures costs exactly
Common demand or cost shocks can produce similar independent responses
items.feedback: Parallel conduct can have competitive explanations.

items.stem: Refer to the cartel graph. What is the cartel price?
items.feedback: Set MR = MC for output, then read price from demand.

items.stem: Refer to the cartel graph. What is the cartel price?
items.feedback: Set MR = MC for output, then read price from demand.

items.stem: Assume the firms interact indefinitely. Cooperating pays 10 each period, starting now. Cheating pays 15 now, followed by 4 every period forever starting next period. Multiply each future payoff by 0.55 for every period ahead. Under these payoffs, is continuing cooperation preferable to cheating?
options: Repetition guarantees cooperation regardless of payoffs
Cooperation is sustainable under the stated payoffs
Punishment is costless
The one-shot joint maximum is automatically Nash
items.feedback: Cooperation: 10/(1−0.55) = 22.22. Cheating: 15 + 0.55×4/(1−0.55) = 19.89. Cooperate to receive the larger present value; the difference is 2.33. Current payoffs are not discounted; punishment begins next period and continues indefinitely.

items.stem: Assume the firms interact indefinitely. Cooperating pays 11 each period, starting now. Cheating pays 16 now, followed by 4 every period forever starting next period. Multiply each future payoff by 0.62 for every period ahead. Under these payoffs, is continuing cooperation preferable to cheating?
options: Repetition guarantees cooperation regardless of payoffs
Punishment is costless
Cooperation is sustainable under the stated payoffs
The one-shot joint maximum is automatically Nash
items.feedback: Cooperation: 11/(1−0.62) = 28.95. Cheating: 16 + 0.62×4/(1−0.62) = 22.53. Cooperate to receive the larger present value; the difference is 6.42. Current payoffs are not discounted; punishment begins next period and continues indefinitely.

items.stem: Assume the firms interact indefinitely. Cooperating pays 12 each period, starting now. Cheating pays 17 now, followed by 5 every period forever starting next period. Multiply each future payoff by 0.69 for every period ahead. Under these payoffs, is continuing cooperation preferable to cheating?
options: Repetition guarantees cooperation regardless of payoffs
Punishment is costless
The one-shot joint maximum is automatically Nash
Cooperation is sustainable under the stated payoffs
items.feedback: Cooperation: 12/(1−0.69) = 38.71. Cheating: 17 + 0.69×5/(1−0.69) = 28.13. Cooperate to receive the larger present value; the difference is 10.58. Current payoffs are not discounted; punishment begins next period and continues indefinitely.

items.stem: Assume the firms interact indefinitely. Cooperating pays 13 each period, starting now. Cheating pays 18 now, followed by 5 every period forever starting next period. Multiply each future payoff by 0.76 for every period ahead. Under these payoffs, is continuing cooperation preferable to cheating?
options: Cooperation is sustainable under the stated payoffs
Repetition guarantees cooperation regardless of payoffs
Punishment is costless
The one-shot joint maximum is automatically Nash
items.feedback: Cooperation: 13/(1−0.76) = 54.17. Cheating: 18 + 0.76×5/(1−0.76) = 33.83. Cooperate to receive the larger present value; the difference is 20.33. Current payoffs are not discounted; punishment begins next period and continues indefinitely.

items.stem: Assume the firms interact indefinitely. Cooperating pays 14 each period, starting now. Cheating pays 19 now, followed by 6 every period forever starting next period. Multiply each future payoff by 0.83 for every period ahead. Under these payoffs, is continuing cooperation preferable to cheating?
options: Repetition guarantees cooperation regardless of payoffs
Cooperation is sustainable under the stated payoffs
Punishment is costless
The one-shot joint maximum is automatically Nash
items.feedback: Cooperation: 14/(1−0.83) = 82.35. Cheating: 19 + 0.83×6/(1−0.83) = 48.29. Cooperate to receive the larger present value; the difference is 34.06. Current payoffs are not discounted; punishment begins next period and continues indefinitely.

items.stem: A payoff cell at row A and column Y is (7,3), with the row player listed first. What does it report?
options: Row chooses Y and earns 3; column chooses A and earns 7.
Both players earn the joint payoff 10.
Row chooses A and earns 7; column chooses Y and earns 3.
Row earns 3 and column earns 7.
items.feedback: The row/column positions identify actions, and the stated payoff order assigns 7 to the row player and 3 to the column player.

items.stem: In the standard long-run open-economy model, which change follows first from a larger budget deficit?
options: National saving rises, so the real interest rate falls
Investment demand falls, so NCO rises
Currency demand rises, so public saving rises
National saving falls, so the real interest rate rises
items.feedback: Lower public saving reduces loanable-funds supply and raises the equilibrium real rate.

items.stem: A higher domestic real interest rate caused by a deficit changes the foreign-exchange market by:
options: Reducing exports and shifting currency demand left first
Increasing saving and shifting currency demand right
Reducing NCO and shifting currency supply left
Increasing NCO and shifting currency supply right
items.feedback: The higher return attracts funds toward domestic assets, so fewer domestic-currency units are supplied to acquire foreign assets.

items.stem: As NCO-determined supply changes from S0 to S1, how does the dollar change in value?
options: It appreciates 20%, because the foreign-currency price of a dollar rises from 1.0 to 1.2.
It appreciates 50%, because the foreign-currency price of a dollar rises from 1.0 to 1.5.
It depreciates 50%, because a dollar buys 1.5 rather than 1.0 foreign-currency units.
Its value is unchanged; the smaller quantity of dollars supplied affects trading volume alone.
items.feedback: The graph moves from A at 1.0 to B at 1.5 foreign-currency units per dollar. Each dollar buys more foreign currency, so it appreciates by 50%. The lower NCO-determined quantity is consistent with that rise.

items.stem: Why does a real currency appreciation tend to reduce aggregate demand, holding its other components fixed?
options: It lowers net exports, a component of aggregate demand
It lowers the domestic money supply by identity
It raises government purchases
It shifts long-run aggregate supply left
items.feedback: Relatively expensive domestic goods reduce exports and encourage imports, lowering NX and AD.

items.stem: An import quota directly reduces import demand. In the standard long-run open-economy model with NCO fixed, what offsets this effect?
options: A fall in national saving that raises NCO
A currency depreciation that raises exports further
A fall in domestic investment equal to the quota
A real appreciation that reduces exports and encourages other imports
items.feedback: The quota raises demand for domestic currency, but appreciation brings NX back to the level fixed by NCO.

items.stem: Political instability triggers capital flight. What happens to currency supply in foreign exchange?
options: Currency demand shifts right
It stays fixed because capital flows use asset markets
It shifts right
It shifts left
items.feedback: Higher NCO means more domestic currency is offered to purchase foreign assets.

items.stem: Which fiscal-policy transmission could explain the change from S0 to S1 in this foreign-exchange diagram?
options: A larger deficit raises domestic real rates, reduces NCO and lowers the dollar supply.
A smaller deficit lowers domestic real rates, increases NCO and raises the dollar supply.
A larger deficit raises domestic real rates and increases residents' purchases of foreign assets.
A smaller deficit directly raises foreign demand for domestic exports, shifting dollar supply.
items.feedback: S1 is left of S0, indicating lower NCO-determined dollar supply. A larger deficit can reduce national saving, raise real rates and discourage net capital outflow. The currency-market effect comes through asset transactions, not a direct shift in export demand.

items.stem: In the standard long-run open-economy model, why doesn’t an import quota necessarily increase net exports?
options: Quotas increase national saving by the import reduction
Foreigners stop demanding domestic currency
The quota raises domestic investment by identity
Exchange-rate appreciation offsets the direct trade effect when NCO is fixed
items.feedback: Trade policy changes currency demand and the real exchange rate, but not the saving-investment balance that sets NCO and NX.

items.stem: In a short-run dollar market with upward-sloping supply, fixed domestic and foreign prices, and e quoted in foreign currency per dollar, a foreign recession reduces export demand. Which immediate demand and exchange-rate channel follows?
options: The supply of loanable funds rises and appreciation cushions the export-demand loss
Dollar demand rises and depreciation reinforces the export-demand loss
Dollar demand falls and depreciation cushions the initial export-demand loss
Dollar supply falls and appreciation raises net exports
items.feedback: Weaker foreign demand shifts dollar demand left. With upward-sloping supply, e falls; fixed prices make this a real depreciation that cushions the initial goods-demand loss. This conditional short-run channel does not assert a permanent NX decline in the separate fixed-NCO model.

items.stem: A student says a budget deficit raises NCO because government borrowing sends funds abroad. Which link corrects the chain?
options: Government borrowing shifts currency demand right directly
NCO rises whenever public saving falls
The higher domestic real interest rate reduces NCO
The deficit lowers domestic rates and raises NCO
items.feedback: Lower national saving raises the domestic real rate, making domestic assets relatively attractive and reducing NCO.

items.stem: A laboratory assistant works an extra Saturday shift and gives up a study group that would improve preparation for a licensing exam. Which interpretation is best?
options: The value of improved exam preparation is part of the shift’s opportunity cost
The earned wage offsets the study group’s benefit in the opportunity-cost calculation
Transportation and other out-of-pocket expenses make up the shift’s opportunity cost
The opportunity cost combines the values of several unchosen Saturday activities
items.feedback: A valuable nonmonetary alternative can be the next-best option forgone.

items.stem: A worker can take a one-day class, work an overtime shift earning $180, or attend a recreational event valued at $120. If the worker takes the class, the opportunity cost is:
options: $300, the sum of both rejected alternatives.
$180, the value of the next-best alternative.
$120, because recreation is not work.
Zero if the class has no tuition.
