items.feedback: The overtime shift is the most valuable forgone option, so it determines opportunity cost.

items.stem: A student pays $12,000 in tuition and gives up $24,000 in earnings to attend school for a year. The opportunity cost is at least:
items.feedback: The full opportunity cost includes explicit tuition and forgone earnings.

items.stem: A farmer can plant wheat worth $42,000 or soybeans worth $50,000 on the same field. If wheat is planted, the opportunity cost is:
options: $42,000, the value of the wheat that is chosen
$92,000, the combined value of wheat and soybeans
$8,000, the difference between the two crop values.
$50,000 in forgone soybean output.
items.feedback: The next-best alternative is the soybean crop worth $50,000.

items.stem: A firm uses a warehouse it owns for storage instead of renting it out for $30,000 per year. The storage decision has an implicit cost of:
options: The building’s recorded depreciation expense.
$0 because ownership avoids a rental payment.
The difference between neighborhood property values.
$30,000 per year.
items.feedback: Forgone rental income is an implicit opportunity cost.

items.stem: A photographer can accept a portrait job worth $500, an event job worth $650, or spend the day editing a personal project valued at $420. If the portrait job is chosen, what is its opportunity cost?
options: $650 from the event job
$1,070 from both rejected options
$500 from the chosen portrait job
$420 from the least valuable alternative
items.feedback: The $650 event job is the highest-valued option forgone.

items.stem: A free certification exam takes five hours. A worker would otherwise earn $25 per hour and also pays $15 for transit. Ignoring other effects, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $140 from forgone wages plus transit
$125 from forgone wages only
$15 because only cash payments count
$110 after subtracting transit from wages
items.feedback: Five hours of wages equal $125; adding $15 transit gives $140.

items.stem: A printer owned by a design firm can produce client brochures worth $9,000 or internal marketing materials worth $6,500. If it produces internal materials, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $9,000 in forgone client work
$2,500 as the difference in values
$6,500 from the chosen materials
Zero because the firm owns the printer
items.feedback: The best forgone use of the printer is the $9,000 client work.

items.stem: A student spends three hours at a free festival instead of tutoring for $22 per hour. Ignoring other costs, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $66 in forgone tutoring wages
$22 because only one hourly wage counts
$0 because festival admission is free
$88 from adding the chosen event’s value
items.feedback: Three forgone tutoring hours at $22 each equal $66.

items.stem: A club paid a nonrefundable $2,000 deposit for a banquet. Today it can hold the banquet or use the date for a fundraiser expected to net $3,500. Which amount is the opportunity cost of holding the banquet now?
options: $3,500 from the forgone fundraiser
$2,000 from the nonrefundable deposit
$5,500 from adding both amounts
$1,500 from subtracting the deposit
items.feedback: The deposit cannot be changed; the fundraiser is the current alternative forgone.

items.stem: A mechanic plans to repair personal equipment, giving up a customer job worth $300. Before work begins, a $450 emergency job becomes available. If the personal repair remains the choice, what is its opportunity cost?
options: $450 because the best available alternative changed
$300 because the original plan fixes the cost
$750 because both customer jobs are forgone
$150 because only the increase matters
items.feedback: The new $450 job replaces the $300 job as the best option forgone.

items.stem: A consultant can accept Project A for a net benefit of $18,000, Project B for $15,000, or Project C for $9,000. If Project A is chosen, its opportunity cost is:
items.feedback: Project B is the highest-valued forgone alternative.

items.stem: A worker’s hourly wage rises from $20 to $32. Holding preferences constant, how does this change the opportunity cost of taking an unpaid hour off?
options: Stays at zero because no payment is made.
Equals the combined value of every alternative activity.
Rises by $12 because the forgone hourly wage is higher.
Falls because leisure is now more valuable.
items.feedback: The forgone wage from an hour of work is now larger.

items.stem: A nonprofit receives a donated building and chooses to use it as offices rather than lease it for $90,000 annually. Which statement is correct?
options: The opportunity cost is the donor’s original purchase price
The opportunity cost is zero because the building was donated
The donation has no purchase price, but office use carries a $90,000 annual opportunity cost.
The opportunity cost is the sum of the values of all possible future uses.
items.feedback: Current opportunity cost is based on the best forgone use, here the lease income.

items.stem: Military engineers can repair a base runway, restore a civilian bridge worth $18 million, or reinforce a dam worth $23 million. The runway is selected for strategic reasons. Which economic statement follows?
options: Its opportunity cost is the $23 million dam reinforcement
Its opportunity cost is every civilian project added together
Strategic importance eliminates opportunity cost
Its opportunity cost is the lower-valued bridge project
items.feedback: Even a required choice forgoes the highest-valued feasible alternative use.

items.stem: A free municipal charging station requires a two-hour wait. One driver could earn $35 per hour during that time; another values the same two hours at $20 total. Which statement is best?
options: The first driver faces the larger time opportunity cost
Both drivers face zero cost because charging is free
Both drivers face the same cost because the wait is identical
The second driver faces the larger cost because leisure is nonmonetary
items.feedback: Opportunity cost depends on the value of each person’s best alternative use of time.

items.stem: A student can earn $120 working Saturday or attend a free exam review session. If attending the session raises her expected exam score enough to be worth $180 to her, what is the net benefit of attending the review?
items.feedback: The opportunity cost is the $120 in forgone wages. Net benefit is $180 - $120 = $60.

items.stem: A worker can produce 10 reports or 5 presentations in a day. What is the opportunity cost of one presentation?
options: 2 reports
5 reports
10 reports
50 reports
items.feedback: Giving up 10 reports to gain 5 presentations means each presentation costs 2 reports.

items.stem: A musician spends an evening rehearsing and gives up both a paid performance worth $220 and family time valued at $160. Which alternative determines the opportunity cost?
options: The $220 performance because it is the more valuable forgone option
The $160 family time because nonmonetary options always rank first
Both alternatives added together for a total of $380
Zero because rehearsal may improve future performance
items.feedback: Only the highest-valued forgone alternative determines opportunity cost.

items.stem: A firm uses owned office space that could rent for $24,000. What implicit cost belongs in the decision?
options: The average rent of all comparable office spaces.
$24,000 in forgone rent.
$0 because the space is owned.
The building’s original purchase price.
items.feedback: Forgone rent is the opportunity cost of using the space.

items.stem: Tuition is $10,000 and forgone earnings are $30,000. The minimum opportunity cost of attending school is:
items.feedback: Both tuition and forgone earnings are part of the full cost.

items.stem: A worker attends a free six-hour workshop instead of a shift paying $24 per hour and pays $12 for parking. Ignoring benefits, what is the opportunity cost?
options: $156 from forgone wages plus parking
$144 from forgone wages only
$12 because the workshop is free
$132 after subtracting parking
items.feedback: Six hours at $24 equals $144; adding $12 parking gives $156.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces price $24. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $8, $13, $17, $21, $26, $32. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
options: 4 units
3 units
5 units
0 units
items.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

items.stem: At price $24, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $21. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
Increase output
Raise the market price
Shut down regardless of AVC
items.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces price $30. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $10, $16, $22, $28, $35, $43. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
options: 3 units
5 units
4 units
0 units
items.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

items.stem: At price $30, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $28. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
Raise the market price
Shut down regardless of AVC
Increase output
items.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces price $15. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $4, $8, $11, $14, $18, $23. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
options: 4 units
3 units
5 units
0 units
items.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

items.stem: At price $15, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $14. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
Increase output
Raise the market price
Shut down regardless of AVC
items.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces price $27. Marginal costs for units 1–6 are $9, $14, $19, $25, $31, $38. Which output maximizes profit or minimizes loss?
options: 3 units
5 units
4 units
0 units
items.feedback: Produce through the last unit with MC no greater than MR.

items.stem: At price $27, a firm is producing 3 units and the next unit has MC $25. What should the firm do?
options: Do not add the next unit
Raise the market price
Shut down regardless of AVC
Increase output
items.feedback: Compare the next unit’s MC with MR, which equals price.

items.stem: A competitive firm produces 60 units at price $28. ATC at that output is $34. What is profit per unit?
items.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

items.stem: At its MR=MC output of 45 units, a competitive firm has P=$24, ATC=$24, and AVC=$17. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Zero economic profit
Economic profit of $1,080
Economic loss of $1,080
The firm must shut down
items.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

items.stem: A competitive firm produces 45 units at price $24. ATC at that output is $24. What is profit per unit?
items.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

items.stem: At its MR=MC output of 55 units, a competitive firm has P=$19, ATC=$28, and AVC=$16. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Shut down and eliminate all costs
Earn profit of $495
Produce and incur a loss of $495
Exit immediately because P<ATC
items.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

items.stem: A competitive firm produces 55 units at price $19. ATC at that output is $28. What is profit per unit?
items.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

items.stem: At its MR=MC output of 40 units, a competitive firm has P=$14, ATC=$26, and AVC=$18. What is the correct short-run conclusion?
options: Shut down in the short run
Produce 40 units despite P<AVC
Earn zero economic profit
Raise price to ATC
items.feedback: Choose output using MR and MC, then compare price with ATC and AVC.

items.stem: A competitive firm produces 40 units at price $14. ATC at that output is $26. What is profit per unit?
items.feedback: Profit per unit equals P−ATC.

items.stem: Competitive firms are earning positive economic profit. What happens as entry occurs?
options: Market supply falls and price rises
Firm demand becomes downward sloping
Market supply increases and market price falls
Fixed cost disappears
items.feedback: Entry shifts market supply right and erodes profit.

items.stem: Competitive firms are earning economic losses. What happens as firms exit?
options: Market supply increases and price falls
Firm MR falls below price
AVC becomes fixed
Market supply decreases and market price rises
items.feedback: Exit shifts market supply left and reduces remaining firms’ losses.

items.stem: In a constant-cost industry, demand rises permanently. After long-run adjustment, price typically:
options: Returns to its original level
Stays at the short-run peak
Falls to zero
Equals minimum AVC but not ATC
items.feedback: Entry expands output without changing input prices or cost curves.

items.stem: In an increasing-cost industry, demand rises permanently. Long-run price typically ends:
options: At the original price exactly
Above the original price but below the short-run price
Below the original price
At zero economic profit only if price is zero
items.feedback: Industry expansion raises input costs, so long-run price rises.

items.stem: In a decreasing-cost industry, demand rises permanently. Long-run price can end:
options: Above the short-run price
Exactly at minimum AVC only
Below the original price
At the original price by definition
items.feedback: External economies can lower firms’ costs as the industry expands.

items.stem: At long-run competitive equilibrium, which pair holds?
options: P > MC and P > ATC
P = AVC and MC = AFC
MR < P and ATC = 0
P = MC and P = minimum ATC
items.feedback: Long-run competition combines allocative and productive efficiency.

items.stem: A technology improvement lowers marginal cost. At the same market price, the firm generally chooses:
options: A smaller output
The same output because price is fixed
A larger output
Immediate exit
items.feedback: Lower MC moves the P=MC output to a larger quantity.

items.stem: A competitive outcome has P=MC but the firm is not at minimum ATC. The outcome is:
options: Productively efficient but not allocatively efficient
Both efficient by definition
Neither condition can ever occur
Allocatively efficient but not productively efficient
items.feedback: P=MC is allocative efficiency; minimum ATC is productive efficiency.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At Q = 50, what is average variable cost?
items.feedback: The AVC guide at Q = 50 is $10.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At an output of 50 units, what is the firm’s economic profit per unit?
options: $10 per unit
$20 per unit
$30 per unit
$40 per unit
items.feedback: Profit per unit is P − ATC = $30 − $20 = $10.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit at the profit-maximizing output?
items.feedback: Total profit is ($30 − $20) × 50 = $500.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What economic profit does the firm earn at the output?
items.feedback: Because P equals ATC at Q = 50, economic profit is zero.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is average total cost at an output of 30 units?
items.feedback: The ATC guide at Q = 30 is $40.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is average variable cost at an output of 30 units?
items.feedback: The AVC guide at Q = 30 is $20.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. At the firm’s chosen output in the loss graph, what is the loss per unit?
options: $20 per unit
$30 per unit
$10 per unit
$40 per unit
items.feedback: Loss per unit is ATC − P = $40 − $30 = $10.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the firm’s shutdown price?
items.feedback: Minimum AVC is $20 at point A.

items.stem: At what price does the positive-output portion of short-run supply begin in the graph, and why is lower MC excluded?
options: $30 at B; lower prices do not cover minimum AVC.
$20 at A; any positive MC guarantees that producing covers total cost.
$20 at A; lower prices do not cover minimum AVC.
$30 at B; any positive MC guarantees that producing covers total cost.
items.feedback: A is at price 20 and the minimum of AVC. The rising MC segment from there gives operating supply. Below 20, a possible MC crossing is insufficient because revenue cannot cover variable cost.

items.stem: Refer to the paired market and firm graph. At an output of 90 units, what is the firm’s economic profit per unit?
options: $20 per unit
$5 per unit
$15 per unit
$40 per unit
items.feedback: Price is $40 and ATC is $20, so profit per unit is $20.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is total economic profit for the representative firm?
Refer to the graph. What is the representative firm’s total economic loss?
At the firm’s chosen output, how much does price exceed AVC? Why can it be worthwhile to operate even with an economic loss?
options: $5 per unit; production covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost.
$3 per unit; production covers variable cost and contributes toward fixed cost.
$5 per unit; covering variable cost necessarily establishes positive economic profit.
$3 per unit; covering variable cost necessarily establishes positive economic profit.
items.feedback: The market gives P = 15 and the firm chooses Q = 50 with AVC = 10 and ATC = 18. The 5 margin over AVC contributes toward fixed cost, though P below ATC means an economic loss.

items.stem: At the long-run position shown, what are the firm’s total revenue and economic profit?
options: Revenue $1,250 and economic profit $0; price equals ATC.
Revenue $1,000 and economic profit $0; price equals ATC.
Revenue $1,250 and economic profit $1,250; revenue itself is the net return above economic cost.
Revenue $1,000 and economic profit $1,000; revenue itself is the net return above economic cost.
items.feedback: At Q = 50, P = ATC = 25, so revenue and economic cost both equal 1250. Their difference, not revenue alone, is economic profit: zero.

items.stem: In the firm panel, find the price and profit-maximizing output. Which cost relationships show that this is a long-run competitive equilibrium, with no incentive for entry or exit?
options: P = $20, Q = 40; P = MC = minimum ATC gives zero economic profit and no net entry or exit pressure.
P = $25, Q = 50; P = MC = minimum ATC gives zero economic profit and no net entry or exit pressure.
P = $25, Q = 50; normal returns to the owners are excluded from ATC, so economic profit must be positive.
P = $25, Q = 50; P above AVC measures positive economic profit even when P equals ATC.
items.feedback: The market supplies price 25 to the firm. Its rising MC crosses at Q = 50, also the ATC minimum. P = MC gives marginal efficiency; P = min ATC gives productive efficiency and zero economic profit. Covering AVC alone is only a short-run operating criterion.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces a constant market price of $15. Which total-revenue pattern is consistent with price taking?
options: Total revenue rises by a smaller amount with each additional unit
Total revenue is fixed because the firm cannot change price
Total revenue falls whenever output rises
Each additional unit raises total revenue by $15
items.feedback: With constant price, total revenue increases linearly and each unit adds the same amount.

items.stem: A competitive firm sells 40 units at $9 and then 45 units at the same price. By how much does total revenue increase?
items.feedback: Five additional units at $9 each add $45 to total revenue.

items.stem: A competitive firm faces P = $11. At the output where MR = MC, AVC = $8 and ATC = $15. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Exit immediately because fixed cost is positive
Produce in the short run and incur a loss
Shut down because price is below ATC
Earn a $3 profit per unit
items.feedback: Price covers AVC but not ATC, so the firm produces and uses revenue to cover variable cost plus part of fixed cost.

items.stem: At the best positive output, a firm faces P = $7, AVC = $9, and ATC = $13. What should it do in the short run?
options: Shut down because revenue cannot cover variable cost
Produce because price is positive
Produce because price is below ATC
Raise output until ATC falls to $7
items.feedback: When P < AVC, producing fails to cover avoidable variable cost.

items.stem: A competitive firm has already paid a nonrefundable annual license fee. The fee increases while market price, MC, and AVC are unchanged. What happens to the short-run output decision?
options: Output falls because every fixed-cost increase shifts MC upward
The firm must shut down immediately
Output rises to spread the fee across more units
The profit-maximizing positive output is unchanged, though profit is lower
items.feedback: A fixed-cost change affects profit and ATC but not MC or AVC, so it does not change the marginal output choice or shutdown threshold.

items.stem: At price $16, 30 identical firms each supply 5 units. At price $22, each supplies 8 units. What is the industry response?
options: Market quantity supplied falls from 240 to 150 units
Market quantity supplied stays at 30 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 150 to 240 units
Market quantity supplied rises from 35 to 38 units
items.feedback: Horizontal aggregation multiplies each firm’s quantity by the number of identical firms.

items.stem: A fixed insurance premium increases by $4,000 for every firm in a competitive industry. Market demand and variable costs are unchanged. In the immediate short run, what happens to each operating firm’s supply curve?
options: It becomes horizontal at minimum ATC
It does not shift because MC and AVC are unchanged
It shifts left because ATC rises
It shifts right because firms need more output
items.feedback: Fixed cost affects profit but not the short-run MC-above-AVC supply schedule.

items.stem: A per-unit fee raises MC and AVC by $2 at every positive output. Which supply effect is most consistent?
options: The firm requires a higher market price to supply a given quantity
The supply curve is unchanged because the fee is fixed
The firm supplies more at every price
Only ATC changes, so shutdown price cannot change
items.feedback: A per-unit cost raises marginal and variable cost, shifting the operating supply schedule upward.

items.stem: A firm has minimum AVC of $9. At P = $8, its quantity supplied is zero; at P = $12, it supplies where P = MC. What does this illustrate?
options: The entire MC curve is supply even below AVC
ATC alone determines the firm’s supply
Market demand is the firm’s supply curve
The supply curve includes rising MC only above the shutdown threshold
items.feedback: The shutdown threshold determines where the rising MC curve becomes the firm’s short-run supply.

items.stem: Ten firms each increase quantity supplied by 3 units when price rises. If no firms enter or exit, industry quantity supplied increases by:
options: 13 units
300 units
30 units
3 units
items.feedback: Industry supply sums the individual output responses: 10 × 3 = 30.

items.stem: Market demand increases in a competitive industry. Before entry occurs, the market price rises. How does one firm respond if its costs are unchanged?
options: It cuts price below the new market price to expand sales
Its P = MR line rises and it moves to a larger quantity on MC
Its MC shifts right automatically
Its ATC becomes the market supply curve
items.feedback: The market price change is transmitted to the firm as a change in MR, producing movement along its supply curve.

items.stem: A competitive industry earns positive economic profit. What long-run sequence is most consistent with the model?
options: Entry decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
Firms keep the profit permanently because they are price takers
Entry increases market supply, price falls, and economic profit is pushed toward zero
Exit decreases supply, price rises, and profit grows
items.feedback: Free entry expands industry supply and erodes positive economic profit.

items.stem: Firms in a competitive industry are sustaining economic losses. What long-run sequence is most likely?
options: Firms shut down for one day and long-run equilibrium is restored automatically
Exit reduces market supply, price rises, and losses are pushed toward zero
Entry raises supply, price falls, and losses deepen indefinitely
Exit raises supply and lowers price
items.feedback: Long-run exit contracts industry supply and raises the market price relative to the loss-making situation.

items.stem: A firm has positive accounting profit but zero economic profit in long-run competitive equilibrium. How can both be true?
options: Accounting profit can cover the owner’s implicit opportunity costs that economists count as costs
Economic profit ignores implicit costs
Accounting profit must always equal zero when economic profit is zero
The firm receives a subsidy equal to normal profit
items.feedback: Economic cost includes owner-supplied resources, so accounting and economic profit need not be equal.

items.stem: A firm temporarily produces zero because price is below AVC, but managers expect conditions to improve next season. This is best described as:
options: Long-run exit rather than shutdown
Entry into the industry
A break-even equilibrium
Short-run shutdown rather than long-run exit
items.feedback: A temporary zero-output choice can occur while the firm remains in the industry.

items.stem: For a representative firm in the standard constant-cost competitive benchmark, which condition is associated with long-run equilibrium?
options: P is below AVC while the firm continues forever
MR is zero at the profit-maximizing output
P = MR = MC and P equals minimum ATC
P is permanently above ATC
items.feedback: At long-run equilibrium the firm maximizes profit and entry/exit has eliminated economic profit.

items.stem: A competitive industry expands after demand rises. The larger industry raises land rents and skilled-worker wages, shifting firms’ ATC upward. Compared with the original long-run equilibrium, the new long-run price is most likely:
options: Zero
Higher
Lower
Exactly unchanged by definition
items.feedback: In an increasing-cost industry, expansion raises input costs, so a higher price is required for zero-profit long-run equilibrium.

items.stem: Demand for an industry rises permanently. As firms enter, specialized suppliers expand and input costs fall. What long-run outcome is consistent with a decreasing-cost industry?
options: Industry output rises and the long-run equilibrium price can fall below its original level
Industry output falls and price must rise
Entry stops before output changes
The long-run supply curve must be vertical
items.feedback: External cost reductions can shift firms’ costs down as the industry grows.

items.stem: Why is P = MC important for competitive allocative efficiency?
options: It means every firm earns positive economic profit
It makes all fixed costs disappear
The value buyers place on the last unit matches the opportunity cost of producing it
It guarantees equal incomes across consumers
items.feedback: At P = MC, the marginal benefit reflected by price equals marginal resource cost.

items.stem: A firm’s minimum ATC is $28 and minimum AVC is $17. What are the break-even and shutdown prices, respectively?
items.feedback: Break-even is minimum ATC; shutdown is minimum AVC.

items.stem: An industry demand increase creates short-run profit. Entry raises an input price used by every firm. What industry type is this?
options: Constant-cost industry
Increasing-cost industry
Decreasing-cost industry
Perfectly inelastic industry
items.feedback: Expansion raises firms’ cost curves.

items.stem: An industry expands and suppliers develop specialized infrastructure that lowers every firm’s cost. What industry type is this?
options: Increasing-cost industry
Constant-cost industry
Decreasing-cost industry
Shutdown industry
items.feedback: External economies lower costs as industry output expands.

items.stem: At the firm’s best output, does it cover the owner’s normal return, and is it productively efficient?
options: Yes to both; price equals minimum ATC, covering all economic costs at the lowest average cost.
It covers normal return but is not productively efficient; price exceeds ATC at an output beyond the ATC minimum.
It does not cover normal return; price is below ATC even though it covers AVC.
It is productively efficient but does not cover normal return because zero economic profit excludes implicit costs.
items.feedback: The price line is near 23 and passes through the ATC minimum and rising MC at Q1. The firm covers explicit and implicit economic costs at minimum average cost, giving normal return with zero economic profit.

items.stem: In the firm panel, estimate the final price P2. Explain why entry ends at this price.
options: $25; entry expands supply and lowers price until positive economic profit disappears.
$30; entry expands supply and lowers price until positive economic profit disappears.
$25; entry stops only when the market price is zero.
$30; entry stops only when the market price is zero.
items.feedback: The dashed final firm price P2 is near 25 at the ATC minimum. Initially P1 is above ATC at the firm’s optimum, attracting entry. Entry expands supply and lowers price until positive economic profit disappears. Zero economic profit covers normal return.

items.stem: At industry quantity 80, which approximate long-run price and cost interpretation are supported by the graph?
options: $25; industry expansion leaves firms’ minimum long-run average cost unchanged.
$30; a horizontal industry supply means each individual firm’s MC must be horizontal.
$30; industry expansion leaves firms’ minimum long-run average cost unchanged.
$25; a horizontal industry supply means each individual firm’s MC must be horizontal.
items.feedback: At Q = 80, LRS gives price near 30. Its horizontal slope means that industry expansion leaves firms’ minimum long-run average cost unchanged. Industry supply does not automatically describe one firm’s MC.

items.stem: As this industry expands along its long-run supply curve, how does the break-even price change? Which cost change is consistent with that pattern?
options: It falls; external economies can reduce firms’ costs as the industry expands.
It rises; greater industry demand for inputs can raise firms’ costs.
It stays constant; industry expansion leaves firms’ cost curves unchanged.
It falls; higher input prices raise firms’ minimum average costs.
items.feedback: The upward-sloping long-run supply curve shows a higher break-even price at larger industry output. Higher input prices or other costs associated with industry expansion can raise firms’ minimum average costs.

items.stem: As this industry expands along its long-run supply curve, how does the break-even price change? Which cost change is consistent with that pattern?
options: It falls; external economies can reduce firms’ costs as the industry expands.
It rises; greater industry demand for inputs can raise firms’ costs.
It stays constant; industry expansion leaves firms’ cost curves unchanged.
It falls; higher input prices raise firms’ minimum average costs.
items.feedback: The downward-sloping long-run supply curve shows a lower break-even price at larger industry output. External economies can lower firms’ costs as the industry expands.

items.stem: What price does the firm receive? Does it cover both explicit costs and the owner’s normal return?
options: $20; P = ATC gives zero economic profit while covering the normal return included in economic cost.
$25; P = ATC means the owner’s opportunity cost and normal return are not covered.
$20; P = ATC means the owner’s opportunity cost and normal return are not covered.
$25; P = ATC gives zero economic profit while covering the normal return included in economic cost.
items.feedback: The firm chooses Q = 50 at P = MC = 25, and ATC is also 25. Revenue covers all economic costs, including implicit opportunity costs; zero economic profit is break-even, not no return.

items.stem: At the firm’s best output, does it cover the owner’s normal return, and is it productively efficient?
options: Yes to both; price equals minimum ATC, covering all economic costs at the lowest average cost.
It covers normal return but is not productively efficient; price exceeds ATC at an output beyond the ATC minimum.
It does not cover normal return; price is below ATC even though it covers AVC.
It is productively efficient but does not cover normal return because zero economic profit excludes implicit costs.
items.feedback: The price line is near 23 and passes through the ATC minimum and rising MC at Q1. The firm covers explicit and implicit economic costs at minimum average cost, giving normal return with zero economic profit. The selected output is at minimum ATC, so it also achieves productive efficiency.

items.stem: In the firm panel, estimate the final price P2. Explain why entry ends at this price.
options: $30; entry expands supply and lowers price until positive economic profit disappears.
$25; entry stops only when the market price is zero.
$30; entry stops only when the market price is zero.
$25; entry expands supply and lowers price until positive economic profit disappears.
items.feedback: The dashed final firm price P2 is near 25 at the ATC minimum. Initially P1 is above ATC at the firm’s optimum, attracting entry. Entry expands supply and lowers price until positive economic profit disappears. Zero economic profit covers normal return.

items.stem: In the firm panel, estimate the final price P2. Explain why exit ends at this price.
options: $25; exit reduces supply and raises price until economic losses disappear.
$30; exit reduces supply and raises price until economic losses disappear.
$25; exit stops only when all firms have shut down.
$30; exit stops only when all firms have shut down.
items.feedback: The dashed final firm price P2 is near 25 at the ATC minimum. Initially P1 is below ATC at the firm’s optimum, prompting exit. Exit reduces supply and raises price until economic losses disappear. Zero economic profit covers normal return.

items.stem: In the firm panel, what price does the firm receive? Which marginal comparison establishes allocative efficiency?
options: $20; price equals MC, matching marginal willingness to pay with marginal cost.
$25; price equaling ATC is by itself the allocative-efficiency test.
$25; price equals MC, matching marginal willingness to pay with marginal cost.
$20; price equaling ATC is by itself the allocative-efficiency test.
items.feedback: The market and firm share price 25, and the firm’s MC is 25 at Q = 50. In the competitive benchmark, price reflects marginal willingness to pay. P = MC is the allocative test; P = ATC instead establishes zero profit.

items.stem: At what firm output does the graph show productive efficiency, and which cost comparison establishes it?
options: 60 units; the firm produces at minimum ATC.
50 units; any price–MC equality proves minimum ATC even without examining the average-cost curve.
60 units; any price–MC equality proves minimum ATC even without examining the average-cost curve.
50 units; the firm produces at minimum ATC.
items.feedback: The selected Q = 50 is also the ATC minimum. This establishes lowest average cost, or productive efficiency. Marginal equality alone need not place a short-run firm at minimum ATC.

items.stem: At Q1, is the firm allocatively efficient, productively efficient, both, or neither?
options: Both: price equals MC and output is at minimum ATC.
Only allocatively efficient: price equals MC but output is beyond minimum ATC.
Only productively efficient: output is at minimum ATC but price exceeds MC.
Neither: price exceeds MC and output is below minimum ATC.
items.feedback: At Q1 the price line meets MC and the ATC minimum. P = MC establishes allocative efficiency; output at minimum ATC establishes productive efficiency. The two relationships must each be checked in the graph.

items.stem: Read the firm’s initial output. As exit raises market price and the firm’s costs stay fixed, how will its output respond?
options: 50 units; the higher horizontal MR line selects more output on rising MC.
40 units; the higher horizontal MR line selects more output on rising MC.
50 units; the price increase shifts MC rather than changing the chosen point on it.
40 units; the price increase shifts MC rather than changing the chosen point on it.
items.feedback: The initial firm output is 50 at P = 15. A higher price raises MR = P and moves its intersection rightward on the unchanged rising MC curve. The firm expands output; its cost schedule does not shift.

items.stem: In the firm panel, estimate the final price P2. Explain why exit ends at this price.
options: $30; exit reduces supply and raises price until economic losses disappear.
$25; exit reduces supply and raises price until economic losses disappear.
$25; exit stops only when all firms have shut down.
$30; exit stops only when all firms have shut down.
items.feedback: The dashed final firm price P2 is near 25 at the ATC minimum. Initially P1 is below ATC at the firm’s optimum, prompting exit. Exit reduces supply and raises price until economic losses disappear. Zero economic profit covers normal return.

items.stem: At the chosen output, P=$38, ATC=$30, and Q=50. Total profit is:
At the chosen output, P=$24, ATC=$31, AVC=$18, and Q=60. What should the firm do?
options: Shut down and eliminate fixed cost
Produce and incur a $420 loss
Earn a $420 profit
Exit immediately
items.feedback: P covers AVC; loss=(31−24)×60.

items.stem: At the chosen output, P=$14 and minimum AVC=$17. What is the short-run decision?
options: Produce because P may cover AFC
Break even
Shut down
Enter the industry
items.feedback: Price is below avoidable average variable cost.

items.stem: At P=min AVC, the firm is:
options: Earning positive profit
At break-even necessarily
Required to exit
Indifferent between producing at the minimum and shutting down
items.feedback: Revenue covers variable cost exactly.

items.stem: Why can a firm produce while losing money?
options: Production can cover variable cost and part of fixed cost
Fixed cost disappears with output
ATC is irrelevant forever
The firm controls price
items.feedback: Operating can reduce the unavoidable fixed-cost loss.

items.stem: What is the approximate shutdown-price threshold in the graph, and which part of MC supplies the firm’s positive short-run output?
options: $22; rising MC at and above minimum AVC.
$18; rising MC at and above minimum AVC.
$18; the entire MC curve, including prices below minimum AVC.
$22; the entire MC curve, including prices below minimum AVC.
items.feedback: The AVC minimum is about 18, where rising MC meets it. Above this price the firm selects rising MC = P. Below it no positive output covers variable cost, so that lower MC segment is not operating supply.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Which labeled point anchors the lower end of the competitive firm’s short-run supply curve?
options: Point B
Point A
Point C
Point D
items.feedback: Supply begins where rising MC crosses minimum AVC, point A.

items.stem: Refer to the LRPC graph. Starting at point a, expected inflation adjusts upward. The long-run movement is to:
options: b
c
d
U3
items.feedback: Expectations adjust upward, SRPC shifts up, and unemployment returns to U2 at point b.

items.stem: Refer to the LRPC graph. Moving from d to c most likely reflects:
options: Expected inflation falling
Expected inflation rising
Natural unemployment rising
AD shifting right
items.feedback: As expected inflation falls, the SRPC shifts downward and unemployment returns to U2 at point c.

items.stem: Refer to the SRPC graph. Moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 at the same unemployment rate means:
options: Inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate
Inflation is lower at the same unemployment rate
Unemployment disappears
LRPC shifts right
items.feedback: SRPC2 is above SRPC1, so inflation is higher for a given unemployment rate.

items.stem: Supply conditions and the natural rate are unchanged, so only expected inflation can shift the short-run Phillips curve. What explains the change from c to f?
options: Higher expected inflation raises inflation at the same unemployment rate.
Lower expected inflation reduces inflation at the same unemployment rate.
Higher actual inflation moves the economy along the original SRPC without changing expectations.
Lower natural unemployment shifts the long-run benchmark to U3.
items.feedback: f lies above c at the same unemployment rate U3, on the higher short-run curve. With other shifters excluded, this identifies higher expected inflation.

items.stem: An adverse supply shock affects the Phillips curve by:
options: Shifting SRPC up and right
Moving down along the same SRPC
Shifting LRPC to zero unemployment
Eliminating expected inflation
items.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-unemployment tradeoff.

items.stem: If policymakers expand AD to reduce unemployment below the natural rate, what happens after expectations adjust?
options: Unemployment returns to natural and inflation stays higher
Unemployment stays permanently lower
Inflation falls below expected inflation
LRPC becomes downward sloping
items.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC up, returning unemployment to natural at higher inflation.

items.stem: At the natural unemployment rate shown, how much higher is inflation on SRPC1 than on SRPC0, and what could explain the difference with supply conditions unchanged?
options: 3 percentage points; higher expected inflation shifts the short-run curve upward.
3.6 percentage points; higher expected inflation shifts the short-run curve upward.
3.6 percentage points; a fall in the natural unemployment rate moves LRPC left.
3.6 percentage points; a change in actual inflation alone moves the economy along SRPC0.
items.feedback: At unemployment 5%, SRPC0 gives inflation 3% and SRPC1 gives 6.6%, a 3.6-point gap. With supply conditions unchanged, higher expectations can explain the curve shift. The LRPC stays fixed.

items.stem: Refer to the LRPC graph. Which movement shows expectations falling after contractionary policy?
options: d to c
c to a
a to b
b to a
items.feedback: Moving from d to c reflects lower expected inflation and return to the natural unemployment rate.

items.stem: Refer to the SRPC graph. At U3, moving from SRPC1 to SRPC2 changes inflation from:
options: I2 to I4
I4 to I2
I1 to I3
I3 to I1
items.feedback: At U3, the lower curve is at I2 and the upper curve is at I4.

items.stem: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, the move from SRPC1 to SRPC2 implies unemployment is:
options: Higher on SRPC2
Lower on SRPC2
The same on both curves
Zero on both curves
items.feedback: At a given inflation rate, the higher SRPC implies a higher unemployment rate.

items.stem: Refer to the SRPC graph. A shift from SRPC1 to SRPC2 is most consistent with:
options: Higher expected inflation or adverse supply shock
Lower expected inflation or favorable supply shock
Higher money supply with expectations fixed
Lower unemployment at every inflation rate
items.feedback: The upward SRPC shift reflects higher expected inflation or a worsened supply-side tradeoff.

items.stem: If the Fed unexpectedly increases inflation while expected inflation is fixed, unemployment moves:
options: Below the natural rate temporarily
Above the natural rate permanently
To zero permanently
Unchanged in every period
items.feedback: When actual inflation exceeds expected inflation, unemployment can temporarily fall below the natural rate.

items.stem: A student says an oil shock causes only movement along the SRPC. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC because costs and prices change directly
It shifts only AD because spending changes directly
It shifts only LRPC because inflation changes
It moves only along LRAS because output changes
items.feedback: A supply shock shifts the SRPC because it directly changes firms' costs and inflation pressure.

items.stem: A student says higher expected inflation lowers unemployment permanently. What is the correction?
options: It shifts SRPC upward and worsens the short-run tradeoff
It shifts LRPC left and improves the long-run tradeoff
It shifts AD right and lowers prices
It raises money demand and lowers rates
items.feedback: Higher expected inflation shifts the SRPC upward, giving higher inflation at each unemployment rate.

items.stem: At a given unemployment rate, how does SRPC1 compare with SRPC0?
options: SRPC1 shows a lower inflation rate
SRPC1 shows the same inflation rate
SRPC1 shows a lower natural rate
SRPC1 shows a higher inflation rate
items.feedback: Point B lies on a different short-run Phillips curve, SRPC1, so the graph is showing a curve shift rather than a movement along SRPC0.

items.stem: How should the change from c to f be interpreted in the short-run Phillips diagram?
options: Inflation rises at unchanged unemployment, indicating a shift of the short-run relationship.
Inflation falls at unchanged unemployment, indicating a shift of the short-run relationship.
Inflation rises at unchanged unemployment, indicating a demand-driven movement along SRPC1.
Unemployment rises at unchanged inflation, indicating a movement along SRPC1.
items.feedback: c and f share unemployment U3 but have inflation I2 and I4 on different curves. The change therefore involves an upward SRPC shift, not a movement along one fixed curve.

items.stem: Refer to the SRPC graph. At inflation I3, comparing SRPC1 and SRPC2 shows:
options: SRPC2 has higher unemployment
SRPC2 has lower unemployment
Both curves have U3
Both curves have U1
items.feedback: At the same inflation rate, the higher SRPC shows higher unemployment.

items.stem: Refer to the SRPC graph. Which labeled move isolates an upward SRPC shift at unemployment U3?
options: The move from point c to point f
The move from point a to point f
The move from point b to point e
The move from point c to point a
items.feedback: Points c and f share unemployment U3; moving from c on SRPC1 to f on SRPC2 isolates higher inflation at the same unemployment rate.

items.stem: Refer to the SRPC graph. The economy moves from SRPC1 to SRPC2. Which statement should be rejected?
options: The tradeoff improved because higher inflation now buys lower unemployment at every point.
The tradeoff worsened because inflation is higher at a given unemployment rate.
Expected inflation may have increased and shifted the curve upward.
An adverse supply shock may have raised both inflation pressure and unemployment risk.
items.feedback: An upward SRPC shift worsens the tradeoff because inflation is higher at the same unemployment rate.

items.stem: Use inflation = expected inflation − (unemployment − 5) + s, where s is the number of percentage points a temporary supply shock adds to inflation. Rates are in percent. Unemployment is 6%, actual inflation is 4%, and s is independently measured as +2 percentage points. What can we infer about expected inflation with this measurement, and what could we infer without it?
options: Expected inflation is 3%; without the measurement of s the data identify only expected inflation plus s
Expected inflation is 5%; without the measurement of s expectations are still separately identified
Expected inflation is 1%; subtract the unemployment gap and s from actual inflation
Expected inflation is 4%; actual inflation equals expected inflation away from natural unemployment
items.feedback: Substituting the measurements gives 4 = πe − 1 + 2, so expected inflation is 3%. Without a separate measurement of s, the data establish only πe + s = 5. Actual inflation and unemployment cannot by themselves separate expected inflation from the supply shock's effect.

items.stem: After a demand surprise moves the economy from c to a, actual inflation is held at the rate shown at a. Compare fully adjusted expectations with expectations remaining at their old level.
options: Full adjustment brings the economy to c at U2; old expectations keep it at d at U3.
Full adjustment brings the economy to b at U2 because expectations permanently raise the natural rate.
Both cases reach b immediately because holding actual inflation constant also fixes expected inflation.
Full adjustment brings the economy to b at U2; old expectations keep it at a at U1.
items.feedback: At I2, a lies on SRPC1 below natural unemployment and b lies on SRPC2 at U2. Adapting expectations moves the short-run relationship; maintaining actual inflation alone is not the same adjustment.

items.stem: In an economy, an oil-price shock raises inflation while contracts reflect old expectations. The oil shock later ends, but expected inflation has risen and remains above its original level. What can be concluded about the final SRPC?
options: At the original curve; removing the supply shock also removes expectation persistence.
Above the original curve; comparison with the shock-period curve needs magnitudes.
Below the original curve; ending a temporary shock reverses both inflationary forces.
Above the shock-period curve; the expectations effect necessarily exceeds the removed shock.
items.feedback: The final curve retains the expectation increase but loses the temporary supply offset. It is above the original; comparison with the shock period needs both magnitudes.

items.stem: A disinflation target becomes more credible, lowering expected inflation before demand is reduced further. What change in the short-run Phillips relation can ease reaching the target?
options: A downward SRPC shift allows lower inflation at a given unemployment rate
An upward SRPC shift allows lower inflation at a given unemployment rate
A rightward LRPC shift automatically removes all output cost
No relation can change until unemployment reaches zero
items.feedback: Lower expected inflation shifts SRPC down. That can reduce the needed demand contraction, without guaranteeing a completely costless transition.

items.stem: Two economies have the same natural unemployment rate but settle at different fully expected inflation rates. What does the vertical LRPC imply about their long-run unemployment rates?
options: The higher-inflation economy must have lower unemployment
The higher-inflation economy must have higher unemployment
Neither can be at its natural rate when inflation is positive
They can be equal despite different inflation rates
items.feedback: A vertical long-run curve permits different inflation rates at the same natural unemployment rate once expectations adjust.

items.stem: An economist says, 'A higher minimum wage will reduce employment among low-skill workers.' What kind of statement is this?
options: Positive
Normative
A price floor
A circular-flow claim
items.feedback: This is positive because it makes a testable claim about cause and effect.

items.stem: A commissioner says the city ought to favor safer streets even if travel takes longer. What makes this normative?
options: The ability to measure travel time
The ranking of safety against travel time
The prediction that streets can change
The reference to a city decision
items.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

items.stem: A report says a fee reduced waste and therefore is fair. What is normative?
options: The claim that the fee reduced waste
The measured amount of waste reduction
The judgment that the fee is fair
The fact that a fee was imposed.
items.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

items.stem: A weakly supported prediction later fails. What classification remains possible?
options: Normative, because the prediction turned out to be false
Normative, because the evidence supporting it was weak
Neither positive nor normative until the prediction is confirmed.
Positive, because testability does not require truth
items.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

items.stem: “Costs rose 8%, so the city should respond.” What is present?
options: A positive measurement plus a normative recommendation
A purely positive statement because it includes a measured percentage
A purely normative statement because it recommends action
Two positive claims because both parts refer to economic conditions.
items.feedback: Separate testable predictions from the value judgment used to recommend a choice.

items.stem: A program “works,” but no outcome is named. What is missing?
options: A statement that the program is desirable
A measurable claim that evidence could contradict
A recommendation about whether the program should continue
A larger sample of people who support the program.
items.feedback: Identify what observation could support or contradict the testable component.

items.stem: “Equal access matters more than maximum output.” What is this?
options: A positive claim because access and output can both be measured
A positive claim because it compares two economic outcomes
A normative ranking of competing values
Neither positive nor normative because no policy is named.
items.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

items.stem: A tax study uses the word efficient for a measurable revenue criterion. Is it necessarily normative?
options: Yes; the word efficient always expresses a value judgment
Yes; any claim about taxes is normative
Yes; a policy criterion cannot be evaluated with evidence.
No; the stated criterion can be tested with evidence
items.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

items.stem: An economist says, 'The city should accept some efficiency loss to make housing more affordable.' What makes this normative?
options: It can be tested with rental data alone
It uses a value judgment about what policy should do
It describes only current prices
It states the law of demand
items.feedback: The statement recommends what policy should do, so it is normative.

items.stem: “A bus lane reduced travel time.” What kind of claim is this?
options: Positive and empirically testable
Normative because reduced travel time is desirable
Normative because the statement concerns transportation policy
Neither, because one observed result cannot be tested.
items.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

items.stem: “The city ought to accept higher costs for cleaner air.” What kind?
options: Positive because costs and air quality can be measured
Normative because it ranks a tradeoff
Positive because the statement describes a policy tradeoff
Neither, because the statement contains no numerical estimate.
items.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

items.stem: When does a false forecast remain positive?
options: Only when the forecast describes a desirable outcome
Only when an expert made the forecast
When evidence could have tested the forecast
Never; a false claim cannot be positive.
items.feedback: A positive claim is one that evidence could in principle test, even if the claim is false.

items.stem: A drought raises the price of water-intensive crops. How does the price signal help coordinate adjustment?
options: Consumers conserve and producers seek ways to expand or redirect supply.
Consumers buy more solely because price rose.
Producers reduce output because revenue is higher.
The price prevents scarcity from existing.
items.feedback: Higher prices discourage some consumption and reward additional supply.

items.stem: The price of a product falls after a new production technology spreads. What information does the lower price convey?
options: Demand must have increased.
The product can be supplied at lower cost or has become less scarce.
Every producer should enter immediately.
The product has become a public good.
items.feedback: A supply improvement can lower price by reducing the good’s relative scarcity.

items.stem: A shortage persists because a legal ceiling prevents price from rising. Which coordinating signal is muted?
options: The signal to increase quantity demanded and reduce quantity supplied.
The signal that opportunity costs are zero.
The signal to conserve consumption and expand supply.
The signal that all buyers value the good equally.
items.feedback: A rising price would normally ration demand and attract additional supply.

items.stem: High profits in a market can function as a signal that:
options: Consumers should stop valuing the product.
Entry must be legally prohibited.
Production costs are irrelevant.
Resources may earn more by moving into that activity.
items.feedback: Profit attracts resources toward uses where buyers value output above cost.

items.stem: A firm earns losses despite producing a product consumers value. What allocation signal do losses send?
options: Consumers place no value on the product.
Resources may create more value in alternative uses.
The firm should expand regardless of cost.
Losses prove the market is competitive.
items.feedback: Losses indicate that costs exceed revenue and resources may be worth more elsewhere.

items.stem: A government caps a medicine price and separately rations access through waiting lists. What has occurred?
options: Scarcity has been eliminated.
The ceiling increased the legal market-clearing price.
Waiting time has no opportunity cost.
Nonprice rationing has replaced part of the suppressed price signal.
items.feedback: When price is constrained, queues, eligibility rules, or quality changes may allocate the scarce good.

items.stem: A carbon price raises energy prices. What information is the policy trying to add to the market signal?
options: The external climate cost associated with emissions.
A guarantee that all energy use ends.
The producer’s accounting profit only.
A fixed quantity demanded at every price.
items.feedback: The policy attempts to make private prices reflect a social cost previously omitted.

items.stem: “Prices speak when no one gives orders.” What role do prices play in a market economy?
options: They signal scarcity and help allocate resources
They eliminate scarcity completely
They prevent all shortages forever
They remove opportunity cost
items.feedback: Prices send signals to buyers and sellers about scarcity, value, and incentives.

items.stem: A resource becomes scarce, and its price rises. How do buyers and sellers usually respond?
options: Buyers buy less while sellers try to supply more
Buyers buy more while sellers supply less
Both buyers and sellers ignore the signal
Demand and supply both disappear
items.feedback: Higher prices encourage buyers to conserve and sellers to produce more.

items.stem: A student claims that a high price by itself means the market has failed. What is wrong with that claim?
options: A high price can be a scarcity signal, not automatically a market failure
High prices always prove demand disappeared
High prices always mean a price ceiling is binding
High prices eliminate the need for supply
items.feedback: A high price may simply signal scarcity and guide buyers and sellers. It is not automatically a market failure.

items.stem: An economist uses a PPF to show how producing more military goods requires producing fewer consumer goods. What is the model showing?
options: Tradeoffs and opportunity cost
Tax incidence
A binding price ceiling
A market surplus
items.feedback: The PPF shows tradeoffs because producing more of one good requires giving up some of another.

items.stem: An economy moves from a point inside its PPF to a point on the PPF. What happened?
options: It reached an unattainable point
It used idle resources more efficiently
It created a tax wedge
It shifted demand left
items.feedback: Moving from inside the PPF to the frontier means resources are being used more efficiently.

items.stem: An economy gets better technology for producing both goods. What happens to its PPF?
options: It shifts inward
It becomes a price ceiling
It shifts outward
It creates a shortage
items.feedback: Better technology increases productive capacity, shifting the PPF outward.

items.stem: A point is outside the PPF today but becomes attainable after an increase in capital and technology. What changed?
options: The market price was fixed
Demand decreased
The economy moved inside the PPF
The economy's productive capacity increased
items.feedback: More capital and better technology increase what the economy can produce.

items.stem: Which list contains all and only the efficient production points labeled in the PPF graph?
options: A, B, C, D, E
A, B, C, D, F
A, B, C, E, G
A, B, D, E, F
items.feedback: A, B, C, D, and E lie on the production possibilities frontier. F lies inside it and is inefficient; G lies outside it and is currently unattainable.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is attainable but inefficient?
options: G
F
C
E
items.feedback: Point F is inside the PPF, so it is attainable but inefficient.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Which point is currently unattainable?
options: F
A
G
D
items.feedback: Point G is outside the PPF, so it is unattainable with current resources and technology.

items.stem: Use the graph. Compare the opportunity cost of Good X over A to B and D to E. Which numerical evidence and conclusion fit the PPF?
options: The costs are 0.5 and 4 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost stays constant as more X is produced.
The costs are 0.5 and 4 Y per X; opportunity cost stays constant as more X is produced.
The costs are 0.625 and 5 Y per X; opportunity cost rises as more X is produced.
items.feedback: A to B gives up 5 Y for 8 X, so the cost is 0.625 Y per X. D to E gives up 20 Y for 4 X, so the cost is 5 Y per X. This larger sacrifice per additional X shows increasing opportunity cost along the bowed frontier.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. If the economy moves from F to C, what has happened?
options: The economy has moved from inefficient production to efficient production
The economy has moved from unattainable production to attainable production
The economy has reduced both goods
The economy has moved outside the PPF
items.feedback: Point F is inside the PPF and point C is on the PPF, so the economy moved from inefficient to efficient production.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. Moving from A to B, what is the opportunity cost per additional pizza?
options: 1 robot
2 robots
0.5 robot
40 robots
items.feedback: The move gains 40 pizzas and gives up 40 robots, so each pizza costs 1 robot.

items.stem: A storm destroys factories and equipment. What happens to the economy's PPF?
options: It shifts outward
The economy moves along the same PPF only
It shifts inward
The PPF becomes a demand curve
items.feedback: A loss of productive resources reduces what the economy can produce, shifting the PPF inward.

items.stem: A student says, 'This point is outside the PPF, so it is efficient.' What is the correction?
options: Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology
Outside the PPF is inefficient but possible
Outside the PPF means unemployment and underused resources.
Outside the PPF means a binding ceiling
items.feedback: Outside the PPF means the economy cannot reach that point with current resources and technology.

items.stem: Worker training improves human capital and shifts the PPF outward for both goods. Which economic relationship does this illustrate?
options: A price ceiling creates a shortage
Human capital raises productive capacity
A tax wedge reduces market size
A positive statement becomes normative
items.feedback: Better worker training improves human capital and can shift the PPF outward.

items.stem: A student says, “A point outside the PPF is inefficient because the economy is not producing there.” What is wrong with that statement?
options: A point outside the PPF is always efficient
A point outside the PPF shows idle resources
It is unattainable with current resources, not merely inefficient.
A point outside the PPF means opportunity cost is zero
items.feedback: Inside the PPF is inefficient. Outside the PPF is unattainable with current resources and technology.

items.stem: Use the graph. With the resources and technology represented by PPF0, which production combination would require greater productive capacity?
options: 20 pizzas and 120 robots
60 pizzas and 80 robots
80 pizzas and 60 robots
100 pizzas and 0 robots
items.feedback: At 80 pizzas, PPF0 permits fewer than 60 robots, so that combination lies outside the frontier. The other combinations are A, B, and the pizza-axis intercept, all on PPF0.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C increases production of Good X by how many units?
items.feedback: Point B has 8 units of Good X and point C has 15, so Good X increases by 7 units.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. Moving from B to C requires giving up how many units of Good Y?
items.feedback: Good Y falls from 45 at B to 35 at C, so the economy gives up 10 units of Good Y.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost of moving from C to D?
options: 6 units of Good X
15 units of Good Y
20 units of Good Y
21 units of Good X
items.feedback: Moving from C to D raises Good X from 15 to 21, but Good Y falls from 35 to 20. The opportunity cost is 15 units of Good Y.

items.stem: Refer to the PPF graph. What is the opportunity cost per additional unit of Good X when moving from C to D?
options: 6 units of Good Y
15 units of Good Y
2.5 units of Good Y
0.4 units of Good Y
items.feedback: Moving from C to D gains 6 units of Good X and gives up 15 units of Good Y, so 15 / 6 = 2.5 units of Good Y per Good X.

items.stem: A country puts unemployed workers and idle factories back to work without gaining new technology. How does this appear on its PPF?
options: Production moves to the existing frontier, showing greater efficiency but no growth.
The frontier shifts outward, showing growth in productive capacity.
Production moves outside the frontier, becoming unattainable.
The frontier shifts inward because idle resources were used.
items.feedback: Using existing resources more fully moves production to the frontier; growth requires the frontier itself to shift outward.

items.stem: A technological improvement affects only the production of medical equipment, not food. How does the PPF change?
options: The entire frontier shifts inward by the same amount.
The medical-equipment intercept moves outward; food stays fixed.
The frontier pivots outward toward the food axis only.
The economy moves along an unchanged frontier toward more food.
items.feedback: A productivity gain limited to one good expands the maximum attainable quantity of that good without changing the other intercept.

items.stem: A country wants to raise living standards. Why is raising productivity more important than simply working more hours forever?
options: Higher worker output supports higher income per person
More hours always reduce GDP
Productivity only matters for inflation
Working hours are the same as net exports
items.feedback: Sustained living-standard gains come from producing more output per worker.

items.stem: If two countries have the same number of workers but one produces twice as much output, the key difference is likely:
options: Higher productivity
Lower CPI only
Higher unemployment only
Equal physical capital
items.feedback: More output with the same labor means higher productivity.

items.stem: Using the production graph, moving from point A to point B raises output per worker by approximately how much?
items.feedback: Output per worker rises from 28.53 at A to 36.37 at B: 36.37−28.53=7.84.

items.stem: A firm produces 1,200 units in 100 hours, then 1,320 units in the same 100 hours. What is the productivity increase?
options: 20 percent
1.2 percent
No change
10 percent
items.feedback: Productivity rises from 12 units/hour (1,200/100) to 13.2 (1,320/100), a 10% increase.

items.stem: Two economies have the same output per person, but workers in Economy X work fewer hours per person. What is the strongest inference?
options: The economies must have identical technology
Economy X necessarily has more natural resources
Economy X has higher output per hour worked
Economy X must have lower output per worker
items.feedback: The same output per person produced in fewer hours means more output per hour worked.

items.stem: Output grows 12 percent while total labor hours grow 4 percent. What happens to labor productivity?
options: It cannot change unless population changes
It rises
It falls
It is unchanged
items.feedback: Productivity is output divided by labor hours; output grew faster than labor hours, so it rises.

items.stem: A country raises total output by adding more workers, but output per worker does not rise. What is the best conclusion?
options: GDP may rise without much gain in productivity or living standards
Real GDP per person must double
Productivity must rise because output rose
Inflation must fall
items.feedback: More workers can raise total output without raising output per worker.

items.stem: Output rises 30 percent while labor hours rise 20 percent. To one decimal place, what is the exact increase in output per labor hour?
options: 10.0 percent
25.0 percent
50.0 percent
8.3 percent
items.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.30/1.20)−1 = 8.3% when output rises 30% and labor hours rise 20%.

items.stem: Total output falls 2 percent while labor hours fall 5 percent. To one decimal place, what happens to labor productivity?
options: It rises 7.0 percent
It rises about 3.2 percent
It falls 7.0 percent
It falls 3.0 percent
items.feedback: Productivity changes by (0.98/0.95)−1 ≈ 3.2%, so it rises.

items.stem: A country's output per worker rises from $80,000 to $92,000. What is the percentage increase in productivity?
items.feedback: Increase = 12,000 on a base of 80,000, so productivity rises by 15%.

items.stem: Two countries have the same real GDP, but Country A has half as many workers as Country B. What must be true?
options: Country A has higher output per worker
Country B has higher productivity
Both have the same productivity
Country A has lower real GDP per worker by definition
items.feedback: Producing the same output with fewer workers means higher productivity.

items.stem: Two countries have equal real GDP per person, but one works far fewer hours per person. What can be inferred?
options: The country with fewer hours likely has higher output per hour
They must have identical productivity per hour
The country with more hours must be richer
Real GDP per person cannot be compared
items.feedback: Equal output per person with fewer hours implies greater output per hour.

items.stem: A plant automates part of production. Output rises 18 percent while labor hours fall 5 percent. To one decimal place, what happens to output per labor hour?
options: It rises 13.0 percent
It rises 23.0 percent
It falls about 13.0 percent
It rises about 24.2 percent
items.feedback: Productivity changes by (1.18/0.95)−1 ≈ 24.2%, because output rises while labor hours fall.

items.stem: A factory produces $900,000 of output using 30 workers. What is output per worker?
items.feedback: Productivity = output/workers = 900000/30 = 30000 per worker.

items.stem: If a firm produces 2,400 units with 300 labor hours, productivity is:
options: 4 units per hour
8 units per hour
300 units per hour
2,400 units per hour
items.feedback: Productivity = output/labor hours = 2400/300 = 8 units per hour.

items.stem: If productivity rises from 20 units per worker to 25 units per worker, what is the percentage increase?
items.feedback: The increase is 5 on a base of 20, so productivity rises by 25%.

items.stem: A firm produces 1100 units at 10 units per labor hour. After training, productivity is 12 units per hour and required output rises to 1320. How many labor hours are needed after both changes?
options: Hours are zero; higher productivity replaces all labor
Hours remain 110; higher output exactly matches the proportional productivity gain
Hours rise to 132; output growth alone sets required hours
Hours fall to 91.7; apply the productivity gain but ignore higher required output
items.feedback: Initial hours = 1100/10 = 110; new hours = 1320/12 = 110. Productivity gains do not necessarily reduce total hours when output demand changes too.

items.stem: Two plants produce the same 1200 units. Plant A uses 120 hours and B uses 240 hours. B then cuts hours by 40% without changing output. Which comparison is correct?
options: B's productivity rises 66.7% and remains below A's.
B's productivity rises 40% and reaches A's level.
B's productivity falls 40% and remains below A's.
B's productivity rises 100% and exceeds A's level.
items.feedback: B initially produces 5 units/hour; after hours fall to 60%, productivity is 5/0.6≈8.33, a 66.7% gain but still below A's 10.

items.stem: In an economy, Output per hour rises 5%, average hours per worker falls 5%, and employment is unchanged. Which distinction matters for total output?
options: Hourly productivity rises 5%; total output rises 5%.
Hourly productivity rises 5%; total output is unchanged.
Hourly productivity falls 5%; total output falls 5%.
Hourly productivity rises 5%; total output falls 0.25%.
items.feedback: Total output is output/hour × hours/worker × workers. The change factor is 1.05×0.95 = 0.9975, a 0.25% decline. Equal opposite percentages do not cancel multiplicatively.

items.stem: Output per worker rises in a firm with 140 employees, but average hours per worker also rises. Which additional evidence is needed to infer output-per-hour growth?
options: Observe that nominal wages rose; that establishes output per hour rose
Observe that total output rose; that establishes output per hour rose
Compare the percentage output-per-worker change with the percentage hours-per-worker change
Compare only employee head count; longer hours never affect hourly productivity
items.feedback: Output/hour equals output/worker divided by hours/worker. A higher per-worker figure can come from longer work rather than greater hourly efficiency.

items.stem: A plant initially produces 1500 units in 150 labor hours. Output later rises 20% while hours rise 25%. Which finding corrects the manager's claim that output growth proves higher labor productivity?
options: Output per hour rises 5% because hours grow faster than output
Output per hour falls 25% because the output increase is irrelevant
Total output rises, but output per hour falls 4%
Both total output and output per hour rise 20%
items.feedback: Productivity is output/hours. Its change factor is 1.20/1.25 = 0.96, a 4% decline despite more output.

items.stem: A team must produce 2,400 units. Productivity improves from 8 to 10 units per hour. How many labor hours are now needed?
options: 192 hours
240 hours
300 hours
24,000 hours
items.feedback: Required hours=output/productivity=2400/10=240, down from 300.

items.stem: If velocity is stable and real output is fixed, a one-time doubling of the money supply should eventually:
options: Double the price level
Cut the price level in half
Double real output
Eliminate inflation costs
items.feedback: With velocity and output fixed, doubling money doubles the price level.

items.stem: If the value of money falls, what must have happened to the price level?
options: The price level rose.
The price level fell.
The price level stayed fixed.
The price level became real GDP.
items.feedback: Value of money and price level move in opposite directions. If the value of money falls, the price level rises.

items.stem: Which curve is fixed by the Fed in the money supply-money demand model?
options: Money supply
Money demand
Aggregate demand
Short-run aggregate supply
items.feedback: In this model, the Fed fixes the money supply, so the money supply curve is vertical.

items.stem: The vertical axis labeled value of money is best understood as
options: 1 divided by the price level
the price level itself only
real GDP divided by money supply
the reserve ratio
items.feedback: The value of money is 1/P, which is why it moves opposite the price level.

items.stem: If money supply increases, the new equilibrium moves toward
options: a lower value of money and a higher price level
a higher value of money and a lower price level
a lower money demand curve only
a higher reserve requirement
items.feedback: An increase in money supply lowers the value of money and raises the price level.

items.stem: If velocity and output are constant, a 10 percent increase in money supply should lead to approximately
options: a 10 percent increase in the price level
a 10 percent decrease in the price level
a 10 percent increase in real output
no change in nominal variables
items.feedback: If V and Y are constant, money growth shows up as price-level growth.

items.stem: If central bank money growth continues year after year faster than real output growth, the likely long-run result is
options: ongoing inflation
permanent unemployment below zero
a permanent fall in all nominal wages
no change in prices
items.feedback: Persistent money growth faster than output growth is a recipe for inflation.

items.stem: If the Fed increases the money supply from MS1 to MS2, what happens to the equilibrium value of money and the price level?
options: The value of money falls and the price level rises.
The value of money rises and the price level falls.
Both the value of money and the price level rise.
Both the value of money and the price level fall.
items.feedback: A monetary injection lowers the value of money and raises the price level.

items.stem: At the original price level, a monetary injection creates an excess supply of money. According to the adjustment process, people try to get rid of excess money by
options: spending or lending it, raising demand and prices
holding it forever, pushing prices down
destroying it, lowering nominal GDP
turning it into real output automatically
items.feedback: People spend or lend excess money. That raises demand for goods and services, which pushes prices up.

items.stem: Money supply grows 9 percent, velocity falls 2 percent, and real output grows 3 percent. Using the growth-rate form of MV = PY, what inflation rate is implied?
options: Approximately 2 percent.
Approximately 4 percent.
Approximately 8 percent.
Approximately 14 percent.
items.feedback: Inflation is approximately money growth plus velocity growth minus real-output growth: 9 + (-2) - 3 = 4 percent.

items.stem: If the value of money falls from 1/2 to 1/4 after the money supply shift, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises from 2 to 4.
It falls from 2 to 4.
It rises from 1/2 to 1/4.
It stays unchanged because only money supply shifted.
items.feedback: Value of money is 1/P. A fall from 1/2 to 1/4 means P rises from 2 to 4.

items.stem: A student says the new equilibrium after MS rises means money is more valuable because there is more of it. What is wrong?
options: More money makes each dollar less scarce, so the value of money falls.
More money makes each dollar more scarce, so the value of money rises.
Money demand must disappear when money supply rises.
The price level must fall whenever money supply rises.
items.feedback: More money makes each dollar less scarce; with the price level higher, each dollar buys fewer goods, so the value of money falls.

items.stem: If the Fed doubles money supply while velocity and real output are stable, which quantity-theory result follows?
