items.feedback: Hold machines, methods and hours constant while comparing training status. That isolates productive worker skills. Changing the method along with training, or changing labor quantity, leaves competing explanations for the observed gain.

items.stem: A discovery increases available mineral resources for 230 workers, but extraction technology and transport remain inadequate. Which policy diagnosis best connects resources to productivity?
options: Transport limits consumption but cannot limit mineral production.
More resources remove the need for skills and sound institutions.
New resources may contribute little without adequate technology and transport.
More resources raise output per worker in the same proportion immediately.
items.feedback: Natural resources can support production, but usable technology, skills and infrastructure determine whether they can be exploited productively. More resources alone need not raise current output.

items.stem: Two otherwise identical workshops keep the same machines, worker skills and total hours. Only Workshop A adopts a new production method: its output rises from 100 to 120, while B stays at 100. Which explanation and productivity comparison are supported?
options: Extra machines are the supported source; A’s output per hour rises 20% because capital must have increased
The method is the supported source; A’s output per hour rises 20% relative to its unchanged-hours baseline
Extra hours are the supported source; A’s output per hour is unchanged because output growth is labor growth
Worker training is the supported source; A’s output per hour falls because unchanged machinery limits production
items.feedback: Machines, skills and hours are held constant, while method adoption differs. That supports technological knowledge rather than capital deepening or training. With hours fixed, output growth of (120−100)/100=20% is also productivity growth.

items.stem: A country imports identical machines while its most skilled operators emigrate. Output per remaining worker fails to rise. Which diagnosis challenges the claim that more equipment guarantees higher productivity?
options: Technology necessarily deteriorated, since capital and skills cannot affect output per worker.
Physical capital increased, but lost human capital can offset its productivity contribution.
Physical capital decreased, since imported equipment is excluded from productive capital.
Human capital increased, since a smaller workforce automatically has more skill per worker.
items.feedback: Imported machines are productive physical capital even though their purchase is offset in expenditure-account GDP. Losing skilled operators can reduce effective human capital and offset the machinery's contribution; the net outcome needs both channels.

items.stem: A workshop has 10 workers. With one machine, output is 100 units; with two machines it is 160; with three it is 200. Workers, hours, and technology stay fixed. What are the extra output from the third machine and output per worker with three machines?
options: 40 units of extra output; 20 units per worker.
100 units of extra output; 20 units per worker.
40 units of extra output; 4 units per worker.
60 units of extra output; 200 units per worker.
items.feedback: The third machine adds 200−160=40 units. With three machines, output per worker is 200/10=20. A marginal addition and the average output per worker use different denominators.

items.stem: Two economies each employ 270 workers. One has little capital per worker and the other much more, with similar technology and institutions. Which qualification should accompany a catch-up prediction?
options: The capital-poor economy must grow faster, regardless of investment or institutions.
The capital-rich economy must grow faster because its output is already higher.
Equal worker counts require equal output per worker despite differences in capital.
The capital-poor economy may catch up if investment and institutions support growth.
items.feedback: Diminishing returns can create catch-up potential when conditions are comparable. Potential is not an automatic growth guarantee without investment and productive use.

items.stem: A factory hires more workers using the same production method. Total output rises 20%, but total worker hours rise 25%. By what percentage does output per hour change?
options: Output per hour rises 20%; additional worker hours do not affect productivity measurement
Output per hour falls 4%; output growth alone does not establish a productivity gain
Output per hour rises 5%; subtract output growth from hours growth to obtain productivity growth
Output per hour is unchanged; hiring more workers always leaves productivity fixed
items.feedback: Productivity is output divided by hours. Its factor is 1.20/1.25=.96, so output per hour falls 4%. More labor can raise total production without raising productivity.

items.stem: Two plants use identical equipment and workforce sizes. One adopts a more effective workflow; its output per worker rises. Which inference is supported, and which remains unproved?
options: Organization can improve productivity; the observation does not establish additional physical capital.
Physical capital must have risen; organization cannot change output with fixed equipment.
Labor quantity must have risen; output per worker measures only employment changes.
Human capital must have fallen; higher output at fixed inputs implies less worker skill.
items.feedback: Using the same equipment and workers more effectively can raise output per worker. The comparison rules out an increase in the stated machine stock and headcount; it does not require either to have grown.

items.stem: A fixed technology gives an extra 310 units of output from the first additional machine and only 155 from the second. A proposal assumes each later machine adds the first machine's amount. What is the flaw?
options: It ignores declining total output; the second machine reduces production.
It ignores labor displacement; the second machine must halve employment.
It ignores technical progress; each machine raises future marginal gains.
It ignores diminishing marginal gains; total output can still rise.
items.feedback: With other inputs and technology fixed, added capital can increase total output at a decreasing rate. A smaller positive increment is not a fall in total output.

items.stem: A discovery increases available mineral resources for 130 workers, but extraction technology and transport remain inadequate. Which policy diagnosis best connects resources to productivity?
options: New resources may contribute little without adequate technology and transport.
More resources raise output per worker in the same proportion immediately.
Transport limits consumption but cannot limit mineral production.
More resources remove the need for skills and sound institutions.
items.feedback: Natural resources can support production, but usable technology, skills and infrastructure determine whether they can be exploited productively. More resources alone need not raise current output.

items.stem: At fixed worker hours and methods, equal successive machine investments have raised output per hour by 10 and then 6 units. Assume positive diminishing marginal returns continue. An equally costly training option would raise output per hour by 8 units. Which choice gives the larger next productivity gain?
options: Machines; their next gain must exceed 10 because the capital stock is larger
Machines; their next gain equals the accumulated gain of 16
Either; equal spending guarantees equal gains of 8
Training; its gain of 8 exceeds the next machine gain, which is below 6
items.feedback: Continued diminishing marginal returns imply that the next equal machine investment adds less than 6 units, though its gain remains positive. The stated training gain of 8 is larger. Compare marginal gains from the next choice, not total past gains.

items.stem: Two countries share technology and worker skills, but A has much less capital per worker. Both add the same small amount of capital per worker. With diminishing marginal returns, which comparison follows?
options: B gains more because its starting output is higher
Both gain the same because additions are equal
A loses output because it began with less capital
A gains more output per worker from that addition
items.feedback: Under comparable other conditions, capital is more productive at the margin where it is scarcer. This is conditional catch-up potential.

items.stem: With labor and technology fixed, successive identical machines raise output by 12, 9 and 6 units. A plan assumes a fourth adds 12. Which revision fits diminishing marginal returns?
options: Expect a gain smaller than 6 if the pattern continues
Expect a gain of 12 because the machines are identical
Expect total output to fall by 6
Expect every previous machine’s output to disappear
items.feedback: Diminishing marginal returns concern successively smaller additions to output, not a fall in total output or identical gains from identical inputs.

items.stem: A factory buys machines but cannot operate them because workers lack the necessary training. Which complementary change would make the physical-capital investment usable?
options: Count the machines as natural resources
Raise product prices without changing production
Train workers to operate the new machines
Replace worker training with more idle machines
items.feedback: Training supplies complementary human capital, allowing the new physical capital to contribute to output.

items.stem: A mineral deposit is discovered, but output cannot rise until transport links reach it. Which conclusion applies the natural-resource distinction?
options: Only human capital changed because discovery involves knowledge
The deposit is produced capital because it has economic value
Resource availability improved, but complementary infrastructure is needed to use it
Current productivity must already have risen by the full value of the deposit
items.feedback: The natural resource exists, but access requires produced infrastructure. A resource discovery is not itself measured production or guaranteed immediate productivity.

items.stem: A new production method raises output with the same workforce and machines. If the method is shared with a comparable second plant, what change could occur without more physical capital?
options: Only its number of machines could rise
Its output per worker must fall
Only its nominal selling price could change
Its output per worker could rise
items.feedback: Using a better method can raise productivity at unchanged inputs; technology is distinct from adding machines.

items.stem: Which policy pair is expansionary for aggregate demand?
options: Higher taxes and lower money supply
Lower taxes and higher money supply
Lower spending and higher taxes
Higher reserve requirements and lower spending
items.feedback: Lower taxes and higher money supply both tend to shift AD right.

items.stem: A recession begins, but Congress passes stimulus after the economy has already recovered. This illustrates:
options: Policy lag risk
Monetary neutrality
A reserve multiplier
Commodity money
items.feedback: Policy lags can make stabilization arrive after conditions have changed.

items.stem: If the economy is in a liquidity trap, a traditional money-supply increase may fail because:
options: Interest rates cannot fall much further
LRAS slopes downward
Taxes must rise automatically
M1 no longer includes currency
items.feedback: When rates are near zero, traditional monetary policy may not lower rates enough to boost spending.

items.stem: If a negative demand shock pushes output below its natural level, stabilization policy would most likely try to
options: shift aggregate demand right
shift aggregate demand left
reduce output further
raise unemployment intentionally
items.feedback: A negative demand shock reduces output, so stabilization policy would typically try to shift AD right.

items.stem: If aggregate demand is too high and inflation pressure is building, stabilization policy would most likely try to
options: shift aggregate demand left
shift aggregate demand right
increase government spending
lower interest rates
items.feedback: If AD is too strong, contractionary policy can shift AD left and reduce inflation pressure.

items.stem: A key argument for active stabilization policy is that policymakers can
options: counteract short-run aggregate demand shocks
eliminate scarcity permanently
make all real variables nominal
force velocity to equal zero
items.feedback: Supporters argue that active policy can reduce the damage caused by short-run AD shocks.

items.stem: A key argument against aggressive stabilization policy is that
options: policy lags can cause poorly timed interventions
AD never changes
the Fed cannot affect interest rates
government spending is not part of aggregate demand
items.feedback: Policy lags can cause interventions to arrive after conditions have already changed.

items.stem: If policymakers misread a temporary shock as a lasting recession, they risk
options: overstimulating aggregate demand
making aggregate demand vanish
ending the money multiplier
turning fiat money into commodity money
items.feedback: If policymakers stimulate after the economy is already recovering, they may push AD too far.

items.stem: A pandemic reduces production and also weakens spending. Why is stabilization policy harder here than with a simple demand shock?
options: Because both supply and demand may be affected.
Because monetary policy cannot affect interest rates in any economy.
Because fiscal policy cannot affect aggregate demand.
Because money demand must be zero during pandemics.
items.feedback: A mixed shock is harder because policy may support demand, but it cannot instantly fix lost production capacity.

items.stem: Congress cuts spending to reduce deficits during a recession. What policy concern is most direct?
options: AD may fall further before recovery
SRAS must shift right instantly
Inflation must rise immediately
LRPC must become horizontal
items.feedback: Cutting spending during a recession can reduce AD further and deepen the downturn.

items.stem: If interest rates are near zero and output is below potential, why may monetary policy struggle?
options: Rates have little room to fall
Money demand becomes vertical forever
LRAS shifts left automatically
Taxes cannot change AD
items.feedback: At near-zero nominal rates, standard rate-cut channels have little room to stimulate spending.

items.stem: A policy takes six months to pass and another year to affect spending. The main risk is:
options: The shock may reverse before policy hits
The money multiplier must equal zero
LRAS becomes horizontal
M2 stops including near money
items.feedback: Inside and outside lags can make policy arrive after conditions have changed.

items.stem: Which policy mix is most expansionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed buys bonds and Congress increases government spending.
Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed sells bonds and Congress cuts spending.
Fed raises interest rates and Congress raises taxes.
items.feedback: Fed bond purchases are expansionary monetary policy, and higher government spending is expansionary fiscal policy.

items.stem: Which policy mix is most contractionary for aggregate demand?
options: Fed sells bonds and Congress raises taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress cuts taxes.
Fed buys bonds and Congress increases spending.
Fed lowers interest rates and Congress increases transfers.
items.feedback: Fed bond sales reduce money supply, and tax increases reduce consumption. Both push AD left.

items.stem: A recession is already ending, but expansionary fiscal policy passed months earlier now takes effect. What is the risk?
options: AD may be pushed too far right, creating inflation pressure.
AD must shift left automatically.
Interest rates must fall to zero forever.
The money multiplier becomes zero.
items.feedback: Late stimulus can overstimulate demand after recovery is already underway.

items.stem: A government passes stimulus after a recession has ended, and the economy is already above potential. What is the risk?
options: The stimulus may worsen inflation pressure
The stimulus must lower output below potential
The stimulus shifts SRAS right automatically
The stimulus lowers expected prices instantly
items.feedback: Because of lags, stimulus can hit after recovery and add excess demand.

items.stem: If the economy is already near full employment and fiscal policy shifts AD right through the multiplier, what risk becomes more important?
options: Inflation pressure from excessive AD
Deflation from collapsing AD
A lower price level from higher government spending
A smaller price level because MPC is positive
items.feedback: If the economy is already near capacity, more AD can create inflation pressure instead of useful output gains.

items.stem: If the economy initially needed AD to fall by $300 billion and the MS1 to MS2 movement reduces AD by $200 billion, what remains?
options: $100 billion of excess AD remains.
The overheating gap closes exactly.
AD overshoots by $100 billion.
Output rises from Y2 to Y1.
items.feedback: The graph shows AD shifting left. If AD needed to fall $300 billion but falls $200 billion, $100 billion of excess AD remains.

items.stem: The MS1 to MS2 movement causes AD to shift left by $180 billion. A separate fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $60 billion. What is the net AD change?
options: AD falls by $120 billion.
AD falls by $240 billion.
AD rises by $120 billion.
AD rises by $60 billion.
items.feedback: The graph's monetary policy lowers AD by $180 billion. Fiscal policy raises AD by $60 billion. Net AD falls by $120 billion.

items.stem: The monetary-policy movement shifts AD left by $160 billion. Fiscal expansion shifts AD right by $160 billion. What is the net AD effect?
options: Zero—equal and opposite shifts.
AD falls $160 billion.
AD rises $160 billion.
AD falls $320 billion.
items.feedback: The graph shows monetary policy shifting AD left. A fiscal expansion of the same size shifts AD right by the same amount, so the net AD effect is zero.

items.stem: An adverse supply shock reduces output by 110 and raises inflation. Which policy comparison recognizes the constraint facing demand management?
options: Support: output rises, inflation falls; restraint: output falls, inflation rises.
Support: output and inflation rise; restraint: output and inflation fall.
Support: output and inflation fall; restraint: output and inflation rise.
Support: potential output rises; restraint: potential output falls by reversing the disruption.
items.feedback: An adverse supply shock worsens the inflation-output tradeoff. Demand management changes the position on that tradeoff; it does not directly repair the supply cause.

items.stem: An economy has returned to potential output. At the current price level, a delayed purchases program would raise aggregate demand by $60 billion after all multiplier effects. Automatic stabilizers would reduce it by $20 billion, with no other changes. Does their response fully offset the program?
options: AD rises $40 billion; the program is only partly offset.
AD rises $80 billion; both changes add to demand.
AD is unchanged; automatic stabilizers fully offset the program.
AD falls $40 billion; automatic stabilizers more than offset the program.
items.feedback: The stated total effects give a net AD increase of $60 billion − $20 billion = $40 billion. Automatic stabilizers offset only part of the delayed program, so it can still add demand pressure after output has returned to potential.

items.stem: Monetary restraint reduces AD by a total $390, while an already-enacted fiscal program adds a total $260. Output initially equals potential and supply is fixed. Which net effect and coordination issue follow?
options: AD rises $130; fiscal policy must dominate any monetary action
AD is unchanged because the two policy directions oppose
AD falls $650; add the magnitudes as though both were restraint
AD falls $130; the opposing fiscal action partly offsets, rather than reverses, monetary restraint
items.feedback: The stated total effects sum to −390+260=−130. Opposing instruments do not necessarily cancel; compare their magnitudes and the starting output position.

items.stem: After a demand recession, falling wages are already shifting SRAS right toward recovery. A stimulus takes a year to arrive. What fact is most relevant to whether it will stabilize output at arrival?
options: Only the size of the gap when the recession began
Whether the original shock was measured in dollars
Whether the economy has ever used fiscal policy before
The expected remaining gap when the stimulus arrives
items.feedback: Compare the intervention with conditions at implementation. Existing self-correction can reduce or eliminate the gap before delayed stimulus arrives.

items.stem: A stimulus approved during recession arrives after output has returned to potential. With no new negative shock, which risk follows from the implementation lag?
options: It lowers potential output by changing the approval date
It can push demand above capacity
It automatically reverses direction and contracts demand
It is costless because the initial recession justified it
items.feedback: The demand addition arrives after its original gap has closed and can create excess demand.

items.stem: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers pay most of the burden. What explains this?
options: Legal assignment does not determine economic burden
Sellers always avoid all taxes
Buyers became legally responsible for the tax after prices adjusted.
The market must have a price ceiling
items.feedback: Tax burden depends on market responses, not just who is legally assigned to pay.

items.stem: Buyers legally pay the tax shown. Compared with the original equilibrium price, how much of the tax is borne by buyers and how much by sellers?
options: Buyers bear $3 per unit and sellers bear $3 per unit.
Buyers bear $4.50 per unit and sellers bear $1.50 per unit.
Buyers bear $1.50 per unit and sellers bear $4.50 per unit.
Buyers bear $6 per unit and sellers bear $0 per unit.
items.feedback: Buyers pay $3 more than the original $10.50 price, while sellers receive $3 less. The legal placement on buyers does not make buyers bear the entire tax.

items.stem: A tax is legally imposed on sellers, but buyers end up paying most of the burden. What does this show?
options: Economic incidence does not depend only on legal assignment
Sellers never pay taxes
Buyers must have become the statutory taxpayers when the market price changed.
The tax must be a price ceiling
items.feedback: Who legally pays the tax does not determine who bears the economic burden.

items.stem: A policy analyst says a tax legally placed on sellers will be paid entirely by sellers. What is wrong with this claim?
options: Legal assignment does not determine economic incidence
Sellers always pass the entire tax to buyers
Buyers always avoid taxes completely
A seller tax is the same as a price floor
items.feedback: Economic tax burden depends on market responses and elasticities, not only on who legally sends payment.

items.stem: A tax causes buyers to pay more, sellers to receive less, and quantity to fall. Which statement is false?
options: The side legally assigned the tax must bear the entire burden
The tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices
The market quantity falls after the tax
Buyers and sellers can both be worse off per unit traded
items.feedback: The legal assignment does not determine the entire burden. Market elasticities matter.

items.stem: The price of a good falls, and sellers produce less of it. What happened?
options: Quantity supplied decreased
Supply decreased
Demand increased
Supply shifted right
items.feedback: A change in the good's own price changes quantity supplied, not supply.

items.stem: A new machine lowers the cost of producing shoes. What happens to the supply of shoes?
options: Supply increases
Supply decreases
Demand decreases
Quantity demanded decreases
items.feedback: Lower production costs from better technology shift supply right.

items.stem: Several sellers leave the market. What happens to market supply?
options: Supply decreases
Supply increases
Demand decreases
Quantity supplied rises
items.feedback: Fewer sellers means less market supply at each price.

items.stem: An input used to make pizza becomes more expensive. What is the likely effect in the pizza market?
options: Supply decreases and price rises
Supply increases and price falls
Demand increases and price rises
Quantity demanded increases because cost rose
items.feedback: Higher input costs decrease supply, which tends to raise price.

items.stem: Refer to the supply and demand graph. Which curve shift is shown when equilibrium moves from Price P2, Quantity Q1 to Price P1, Quantity Q2?
options: A rightward shift in supply
A rightward shift in demand
A leftward shift in demand
A leftward shift in supply
items.feedback: The move from D1 with S1 to D1 with S2 lowers price and raises quantity, which matches an increase in supply.

items.stem: The government begins paying producers a subsidy for every unit sold. What happens to market supply, other things equal?
options: Supply shifts left because the subsidy increases firms’ effective production cost.
Supply shifts right because the subsidy lowers the effective marginal cost of selling output.
Quantity supplied rises along the original curve because only the market price changed.
Demand shifts right because the payment is received directly by buyers.
items.feedback: A per-unit producer subsidy raises the return from supplying each unit and shifts supply right.

items.stem: What economic change does the move from A to B in the coffee graph represent?
options: Price rises $5; quantity supplied increases by 100 thousand along the existing curve.
Price rises $5; supply increases by 125 thousand because the curve shifts right.
Price rises $5; supply increases by 100 thousand because the curve shifts right.
Price rises $5; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
items.feedback: A is at $6 and 100 thousand units; B is at $11 and 225 thousand. Price rises $5 and quantity supplied rises 125 thousand along the same supply curve. This is an increase in quantity supplied, not a rightward shift of supply.

items.stem: Moving from point A to point B on the displayed supply curve changes quantity supplied by:
options: An increase of 125 thousand units
A decrease of 125 thousand units
An increase of 5 thousand units
An increase of 225 thousand units
items.feedback: Quantity supplied rises from 100 thousand at A to 225 thousand at B, an increase of 125 thousand.

items.stem: At a price of $9 on the displayed hamburger graph, how does quantity supplied change when supply shifts from S0 to S1?
options: It increases from 100 thousand to 200 thousand
It decreases from 200 thousand to 100 thousand
It decreases from 300 thousand to 200 thousand
It stays at 200 thousand
items.feedback: At $9, S0 shows 200 thousand units while S1 shows 100 thousand, a decrease of 100 thousand at the same price.

items.stem: Which event is consistent with the shift from S0 to S1 shown in the hamburger market?
options: The price of hamburgers rises and firms move up S0
A new cost-saving grill technology is adopted
The price of a major meat input rises
More hamburger restaurants enter the market
items.feedback: Higher input costs reduce supply, shifting the supply curve left.

items.stem: What economic change does the move from A to B in the tacos graph represent?
options: Price rises $1; quantity supplied increases by 100 thousand along the existing curve.
Price rises $1; supply increases by 125 thousand because the curve shifts right.
Price rises $1; supply increases by 100 thousand because the curve shifts right.
Price rises $1; quantity supplied increases by 125 thousand along the existing curve.
items.feedback: A is at $3 and 100 thousand tacos; B is at $4 and 225 thousand. Price rises $1 and quantity supplied rises 125 thousand along S0. The higher quantity supplied reflects movement along the curve, not an increase in supply.

items.stem: At a price of $3, the shift from S0 to S1 changes quantity supplied from 100 thousand to approximately:
options: 225 thousand
125 thousand
200 thousand
325 thousand
items.feedback: At $3, point A on S0 is 100 thousand, while S1 crosses the $3 line at about 225 thousand. Supply therefore increases by about 125 thousand units at that price.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What market change is shown from A to B?
options: Supply increases, lowering price and raising quantity
Demand increases, raising price and quantity
Supply decreases, raising price and reducing quantity
Demand decreases, lowering price and quantity
items.feedback: Supply shifts left; price rises from 10 to 12 and quantity falls from 200 to 150 thousand.

items.stem: Use the graph. Which explanation of the move from A to B is supported by comparing what sellers offer at the price marked at A?
options: Supply decreases: at that same price, sellers offer 100 thousand fewer tickets on S1 than on S0.
Supply decreases: at that same price, sellers offer 50 thousand fewer tickets on S1 than on S0.
Only quantity supplied decreases: a lower ticket price moves sellers along S0 by 100 thousand tickets.
Only quantity supplied decreases: a lower ticket price moves sellers along S0 by 50 thousand tickets.
items.feedback: At A’s $10 price, S0 offers 200 thousand tickets and S1 offers 100 thousand. Offering 100 thousand fewer tickets at the same price is a decrease in supply. A movement along S0 would instead be a change in quantity supplied caused by a price change. In the graph, the A-to-B price actually rises.

items.stem: The price of handmade tables rises, and sellers produce more tables. What happened?
options: Quantity supplied increased
Supply increased
Demand increased
Supply shifted right
items.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along supply, so quantity supplied changes.

items.stem: At a market price of $8, approximately how many units does the displayed coffee supply curve show producers are willing to sell?
options: 100 thousand units
175 thousand units
150 thousand units
225 thousand units
items.feedback: The supply line passes through quantity 150 thousand at a price of $8.

items.stem: A producer says the movement from A to B shows an increase in supply. How much does quantity change, and does this movement shift the supply curve?
options: An increase of 100 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
An increase of 125 thousand units; any rise in quantity is an increase in the whole supply schedule.
An increase of 100 thousand units; any rise in quantity is an increase in the whole supply schedule.
An increase of 125 thousand units; this is a change in quantity supplied along the existing curve.
items.feedback: A is at 100 thousand units and B at 225 thousand, an increase of 125 thousand. Both lie on the same supply curve. The higher own price changes quantity supplied; an increase in supply would shift the entire schedule.

items.stem: According to the law of supply, how are price and quantity supplied related, other things equal?
options: As price rises, quantity supplied rises
As price rises, supply shifts left
As price falls, quantity supplied rises
As demand rises, supply must rise
items.feedback: The law of supply says price and quantity supplied move in the same direction.

items.stem: The price of handmade tables rises, and sellers offer more tables for sale. What is the most precise statement?
options: Quantity supplied increases
Supply increases
Demand increases
Supply shifts right
items.feedback: A change in the good's own price causes movement along the supply curve, so quantity supplied changes.

items.stem: Steel becomes more expensive for car producers. What happens to the supply of cars?
options: Supply decreases
Quantity supplied increases because car price changed
Demand decreases
Supply increases
items.feedback: More expensive steel raises the cost of producing cars at every output level, shifting car supply left rather than changing demand.

items.stem: If demand is very inelastic and supply is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear exactly zero
The side with more firms always bears it
items.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the tax burden. Here, that is buyers.

items.stem: If supply is very inelastic and demand is elastic, who likely bears more of a tax?
options: Sellers
Buyers
Only the government
No one because demand is elastic
items.feedback: The less elastic side bears more of the burden. Here, that is sellers.

items.stem: Why does the more elastic side of a market tend to bear less of a tax?
options: It can adjust its behavior more easily in response to the tax.
A binding price floor absorbs part of the tax.
Elasticity affects only the legal assignment of the tax.
The more elastic side cannot change quantity when price changes.
items.feedback: The more elastic side can respond more easily, so it bears less of the tax burden.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. Who bears more of the tax burden?
options: Buyers and sellers share the burden equally
Buyers bear all of the burden
Sellers bear all of the burden
No one bears the burden
items.feedback: Buyers pay $3 more and sellers receive $3 less, so the burden is split equally.

items.stem: A tax on cigarettes causes only a small drop in smoking even though buyers face a noticeably higher price. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Demand is relatively inelastic
Demand is perfectly elastic
Supply increased after the tax
The tax created a price floor
items.feedback: If quantity falls only a little after a tax, demand is likely relatively inelastic.

items.stem: A tax is imposed on a market where demand is perfectly inelastic. Who bears the tax burden?
options: Buyers bear the burden because quantity demanded does not respond
Sellers bear the burden because they collect the money
The government bears the burden
No one bears the burden because quantity does not change
items.feedback: If buyers do not change quantity demanded at all, buyers bear the tax burden.

items.stem: A $6 tax causes buyers to pay $4 more than before and sellers to receive $2 less than before. Who bears more of the tax burden?
options: Buyers
Sellers
Both sides bear zero burden
Only the government
items.feedback: Buyers bear $4 of the $6 tax, while sellers bear $2, so buyers bear more.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by buyers?
items.feedback: Buyers paid $15 before the tax and pay $18 after the tax, so their burden is $3.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. How much of the tax burden is paid by sellers?
items.feedback: Sellers received $15 before the tax and receive $12 after the tax, so their burden is $3.

items.stem: A tax on sellers shifts the supply curve upward because:
options: The tax raises the cost of selling each unit
The tax increases buyers' income
The tax makes demand perfectly elastic
The tax eliminates opportunity cost
items.feedback: A tax on sellers raises the cost of selling each unit, shifting supply upward.

items.stem: A tax reduces the quantity sold from 100 units to 75 units. What is the best interpretation?
options: The tax shrinks the size of the market
The tax eliminates scarcity
The tax increases both supply and demand
The tax causes quantity sold to rise
items.feedback: A tax raises the cost of exchange and reduces the quantity traded.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the original equilibrium price and quantity before the tax?
options: $15 and 100 units
$18 and 80 units
$12 and 80 units
$20 and 65 units
items.feedback: Before the tax, demand and the original supply curve intersect at $15 and 100 units.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. After the tax, what price do buyers pay?
items.feedback: After the tax, the price buyers pay is read from the demand curve at the new quantity, which is $18.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. After the tax, what price do sellers receive?
items.feedback: After the tax, sellers receive $12 per unit after the tax is accounted for.

items.stem: Refer to the tax graph. Which before-and-after quantities describe the change in sales, and why does the tax affect sales?
options: From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
From 100 to 65 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
From 100 to 80 units; the 20 units no longer sold become tax revenue.
From 100 to 80 units; all buyer payments become a social loss rather than a payment to sellers or government.
items.feedback: The tax lowers sales from 100 to 80. Buyers pay $18 and sellers receive $12, leaving a $6 wedge that prevents mutually beneficial trades. Lost units are not tax revenue; revenue is the tax times units still traded.

items.stem: Refer to the tax graph. Which quantity change accompanies the wedge between the price buyers pay and the amount sellers receive?
options: From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
From 100 to 65 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
From 100 to 80 units; the buyer’s $3 price increase is the entire wedge because the seller’s loss does not count.
From 80 to 100 units; using the untaxed intersection as the after-tax quantity measures the sales response.
items.feedback: The original quantity is 100 and the taxed quantity 80. The wedge is $18 − $12 = $6, including the $3 rise in buyer price and the $3 fall in seller receipt from the original $15.

items.stem: After the seller-side tax shown, quantity falls to 100 thousand movies. What prices do buyers pay and sellers receive?
options: Buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $12
Buyers pay $14 and sellers receive $10
Buyers pay $10 and sellers receive $14
Buyers pay $14 and sellers receive $12
items.feedback: At the post-tax quantity of 100 thousand, demand gives the buyer price of $14 while the original supply curve gives the seller receipt of $10.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. After the tax is imposed, by how much does quantity traded fall?
options: 20 thousand movies
100 thousand movies
40 thousand movies
240 thousand movies
items.feedback: Read the pre-tax and post-tax quantities from the graph: 140 thousand − 100 thousand = 40 thousand movies.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the per-trip tax wedge?
options: 2 dollars
4 dollars
8 dollars
20 dollars
items.feedback: Buyers pay 12 and sellers receive 8.

items.stem: Refer to the graph. What is the post-tax quantity?
options: 150 thousand tickets
50 thousand tickets
200 thousand tickets
350 thousand tickets
items.feedback: Taxed supply intersects demand at 150 thousand.

items.stem: A $10 tax is imposed. Before the tax, price is $50. After the tax, buyers pay $56 and sellers receive $46. What happened to quantity sold?
options: It likely decreased because the tax created a wedge
It must have increased because buyers pay more
It stayed exactly the same because the tax is split
It became zero because all taxes eliminate trade
items.feedback: A tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices and usually reduces the quantity traded.

items.stem: A tax on gasoline raises the price paid by drivers, lowers the price received by sellers, and reduces gallons sold. Which concept chain is correct?
options: Tax wedge → shared burden → lower quantity traded
Price ceiling → shortage → higher quantity traded
Demand increase → higher price → higher quantity
PPF shift → economic growth → lower price
items.feedback: A tax creates a wedge between buyer and seller prices, splits the burden, and reduces the quantity traded.

items.stem: Compare the quantities sold before and after the tax. How does the gap between buyer and seller prices explain the lost sales?
options: From 100 to 80 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
From 100 to 65 units; the wedge between buyer payment and seller receipt removes some mutually beneficial trades.
From 100 to 80 units; the tax leaves buyer and seller prices identical, so it creates no wedge.
From 100 to 65 units; the tax leaves buyer and seller prices identical, so it creates no wedge.
items.feedback: Original supply meets demand at Q = 100. Supply plus tax meets demand at Q 80. Buyers pay 18 and sellers receive 12 at the taxed quantity, so the wedge prevents trades that would occur without tax.

items.stem: At Q = 80 in the tax graph, how much higher is Supply + tax than Supply, and what does this vertical distance mean?
options: $6; sellers need a buyer price $6 above their net supply price to cover the per-unit tax.
$4; sellers need a buyer price $4 above their net supply price to cover the per-unit tax.
$6; the tax makes sellers willing to receive $6 less net of tax at every quantity.
$4; the tax makes sellers willing to receive $4 less net of tax at every quantity.
items.feedback: At Q 80 the original supply price is 12 and supply-plus-tax price 18. The vertical gap 6 is the tax. The shifted curve expresses the required buyer price inclusive of tax; it does not change the underlying net-of-tax supply schedule.

items.stem: A $7 tax reduces quantity from 500 to 420 units. What does this show beyond tax revenue?
options: The tax shrinks the market by discouraging mutually beneficial trades
The tax increases market size because government collects revenue
The tax leaves buyers and sellers unaffected if revenue is spent
The tax creates a surplus because quantity falls
items.feedback: A tax reduces quantity traded, meaning some mutually beneficial exchanges no longer happen.

items.stem: Before tax, price is $20 and quantity is 1,000. After a $6 tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity is 850. What is tax revenue?
items.feedback: Tax revenue equals tax per unit times after-tax quantity: $6 × 850 = $5,100.

items.stem: A city taxes ride-share trips. Riders pay higher prices, drivers receive less per trip, and fewer trips occur. What is the best synthesis?
options: The tax wedge is shared and shrinks the number of exchanges
The tax affects only riders if they see the fee at checkout
The tax affects only drivers if the platform remits it
The tax increases quantity because government revenue rises
items.feedback: A tax creates a wedge shared by market participants and reduces the quantity traded.

items.stem: A student uses the original quantity to calculate tax revenue. Calculate the correct revenue and explain which transactions are taxed.
options: $6 × 80 = $480; collect the full wedge on units actually traded after tax.
$6 × 65 = $390; collect the full wedge on units actually traded after tax.
$6 × 80 = $480; apply the tax to the original untaxed transactions even if some no longer occur.
$6 × 65 = $390; apply the tax to the original untaxed transactions even if some no longer occur.
items.feedback: The wedge is 18−12 = $6 and the taxed quantity 80, so receipts are $480. The original 100 includes 20 transactions prevented by the tax; revenue cannot be collected on those missing trades.

items.stem: Before a tax, buyers pay $30 and sellers receive $30. After a tax, buyers pay $34 and sellers receive $27. What is the tax per unit?
items.feedback: The tax wedge is the buyer price minus the seller price: $34 - $27 = $7.

items.stem: A tax reduces quantity sold from 500 to 420 units. If the tax is $8 per unit, how much tax revenue is collected?
items.feedback: Tax revenue uses the quantity sold after the tax: $8 × 420 = $3,360.

items.stem: Calculate tax revenue. Which quantity should be multiplied by the full tax per unit?
options: $6 × 80 = $480; collect the full wedge on units actually traded after tax.
$6 × 65 = $390; collect the full wedge on units actually traded after tax.
$6 × 80 = $480; apply the tax to the original untaxed transactions even if some no longer occur.
$6 × 65 = $390; apply the tax to the original untaxed transactions even if some no longer occur.
items.feedback: The wedge is 18−12 = $6 and the taxed quantity 80, so receipts are $480. The original 100 includes 20 transactions prevented by the tax; revenue cannot be collected on those missing trades.

items.stem: Before a tax, buyers pay $10 and sellers receive $10. After the tax, buyers pay $12 and sellers receive $8. What is the tax wedge?
items.feedback: The wedge is the price buyers pay minus the price sellers receive: $12 - $8 = $4.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. What is the amount of the tax per unit?
items.feedback: The tax wedge is the difference between what buyers pay and what sellers receive: $18 - $12 = $6.

items.stem: Refer to the tax incidence graph. By how many units does the tax reduce the quantity sold?
options: 20 units
80 units
100 units
180 units
items.feedback: Quantity falls from 100 to 80, so the tax reduces quantity sold by 20 units.

items.stem: If 2 million unemployed workers become discouraged and stop looking for work, what happens immediately to the measured unemployment rate?
options: It rises because discouraged workers become unemployed
It falls because they leave the labor force
It is unchanged because employment rises
It becomes 100%
items.feedback: Discouraged workers leave the labor force, which can lower the measured unemployment rate.

items.stem: A parent who stays home full-time and is not seeking paid work is classified as:
options: Employed
Unemployed
Not in the labor force
Structurally unemployed
items.feedback: Someone not working and not looking for paid work is not in the labor force.

items.stem: A person works one hour for pay during the survey week while looking for full-time work. How is the person classified?
options: Unemployed
Employed
Not in the labor force
Discouraged worker
items.feedback: A person who does any paid work during the survey period is counted as employed.

items.stem: A worker without a job sends out applications during the last four weeks. How is the worker classified?
options: Employed
Unemployed
Not in the labor force
Retired
items.feedback: Actively looking for work while jobless means the person is unemployed.

items.stem: A discouraged worker wants a job but stopped searching because they believe no jobs are available. How is this worker classified in official unemployment statistics?
options: Employed
Unemployed
Not in the labor force
Part of investment
items.feedback: Discouraged workers are not in the labor force because they are not actively searching.

items.stem: Which classification is most likely to make the unemployment rate understate labor market weakness?
options: Counting discouraged workers as not in the labor force
Counting active job seekers as unemployed
Counting paid workers as employed
Counting unemployed workers in the labor force
items.feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from unemployment, which can hide labor market weakness.

items.stem: Which case creates the biggest problem for interpreting the official unemployment rate?
options: A large increase in discouraged workers
A worker voluntarily switches jobs and searches for one week
A student works part time by choice
A retiree remains retired
items.feedback: Discouraged workers are excluded from measured unemployment, hiding some labor market distress.

items.stem: A person works 5 hours per week for pay but wants 40 hours. How is this person treated in the headline unemployment rate?
options: Counted as employed, even though underemployment is present
Counted as unemployed because they want more hours
Counted as not in the labor force
Counted as discouraged
items.feedback: The official unemployment rate counts part-time workers as employed, even if they want full-time work.

items.stem: Which change would reduce the unemployment rate without improving the number of people employed?
options: Unemployed workers become discouraged and stop searching
Part-time workers become full-time workers
Discouraged workers begin looking for jobs
New firms hire unemployed workers
items.feedback: When unemployed workers stop searching, they leave the labor force and measured unemployment can fall.

items.stem: A survey classifies people as employed, unemployed, or not in the labor force. Whose difficulty finding enough work is least likely to be captured by the official unemployment rate?
options: A part-time worker who wants full-time work
A full-time worker satisfied with their job
A retiree who does not want work
A student not seeking employment
items.feedback: Involuntary part-time workers are counted as employed, even though their labor situation is weak.

items.stem: Which case makes the headline unemployment rate look better than the actual labor market experience?
options: A rise in discouraged workers and involuntary part-time workers
A rise in full-time employment
More unemployed workers actively searching
More job openings filled
items.feedback: Discouraged and involuntary part-time workers are not fully captured by the headline unemployment rate.

items.stem: An economy has 140 million employed people, 10 million unemployed people, and 50 million people not in the labor force. What is the labor force?
options: 140 million
150 million
190 million
200 million
items.feedback: Labor force = employed + unemployed = 140 + 10 = 150 million.

items.stem: Using 140 million employed and 10 million unemployed, what is the unemployment rate?
items.feedback: Unemployment rate = 10 / 150 x 100 = 6.7%.

items.stem: The labor force is 150 million and the adult population is 200 million. What is the labor-force participation rate, and what does the remaining share represent?
options: 75%; the remaining 25% are all unemployed.
50%; the remaining 50% are outside the labor force.
75%; the remaining 25% are outside the labor force.
66.7%; the remaining 33.3% are all unemployed.
items.feedback: LFPR = 150/200 × 100 = 75%. The remaining 50 million adults are outside the labor force. Unemployed people who are actively seeking work belong to the labor force.

items.stem: An economy has 90 employed, 10 unemployed, and 50 not in the labor force. If 5 unemployed workers stop looking, what is the new unemployment rate?
items.feedback: New unemployed = 5 and new labor force = 95, so unemployment = 5/95 = 5.3%.

items.stem: Of 280 employed workers, ten full-time workers lose half their hours but retain paid jobs. No one enters or leaves the labor force. Which observation would reveal the deterioration that the official unemployment rate misses?
options: Employment falls by five; two half-time jobs equal one employed person.
Unemployment rises by ten; each loss of full-time hours counts as joblessness.
Hours fall; employment, unemployment and participation remain unchanged.
Participation falls by ten; paid part-time workers leave the labor force.
items.feedback: A paid part-time worker is employed. Head-count employment, UR and LFPR can stay constant while hours and underemployment worsen; hours-based evidence supplies the missing margin.

items.stem: Initially 290 adults are employed and 29 unemployed. A recession causes 14 employed workers to lose jobs and actively search, while an equal number of previously unemployed people stop searching. Which joint result can occur?
options: Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls
Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles
Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed
items.feedback: Layoffs move employed people to unemployment; discouraged exits remove an equal number from unemployment. U is unchanged, E and the labor force fall, so U/LF rises. Equal flows do not cancel employment or participation effects.

items.stem: An economy has 300 employed and 30 unemployed people. Thirty employed people lose their jobs and immediately begin actively seeking work. No one enters or leaves the labor force. What happens to the unemployment rate?
options: It rises from about 9.1% to about 18.2%.
It stays at about 9.1% because the labor force is unchanged.
It rises from 10% to 20% because employment is the denominator.
It falls from about 9.1% to about 8.3% because the labor force grows.
items.feedback: Initially, UR = 30/(300+30) ≈ 9.1%. Job losses move 30 people from employment to unemployment without changing the labor force: UR = 60/330 ≈ 18.2%.

items.stem: Initially 140 adults are employed and 14 unemployed. A recession causes 7 employed workers to lose jobs and actively search, while an equal number of previously unemployed people stop searching. Which joint result can occur?
options: Employment is fixed because layoffs and exits cancel; the unemployment rate is fixed
Employment falls and unemployment head count falls; the unemployment rate necessarily falls
Employment and labor-force participation fall; unemployment head count stays fixed and its rate rises
Employment falls but participation is fixed; unemployment head count doubles
items.feedback: Layoffs move employed people to unemployment; discouraged exits remove an equal number from unemployment. U is unchanged, E and the labor force fall, so U/LF rises. Equal flows do not cancel employment or participation effects.

items.stem: Of 300 adults, 150 are employed and 15 are unemployed and actively looking for work. A survey also finds 15 people who want work but have stopped searching. What are the unemployment rate and labor-force participation rate?
options: Include discouraged workers only in the labor force; UR is about 8.3% and LFPR is 60%
Exclude discouraged workers but divide unemployment by adult population; UR is 5% and LFPR is 50%
Exclude discouraged workers from unemployment and the labor force; UR is about 9.1% and LFPR is 55%
Include discouraged workers in unemployment; UR is about 16.7% and LFPR is 60%
items.feedback: The labor force is 150+15 = 165. The discouraged are not active searchers. UR = 0.1/1.1 ≈ 9.1%; LFPR = 1.1/2 = 55%.

items.stem: Employment is 160 and unemployment is 16. Then 8 previously inactive adults begin actively searching; nobody finds or loses a job. Which interpretation reconciles the rate change with employment?
options: Employment is unchanged and both rates are unchanged; inactive adults cannot affect the denominator
Employment is unchanged while unemployment and participation rise; the rate increase does not show job destruction
Employment falls while unemployment rises; every new searcher must have left a job
Employment rises and unemployment falls; entering the labor force counts as finding work
items.feedback: Active searchers without jobs enter both unemployment and the labor force. Employment is unchanged; unemployment rises relative to the larger labor force, and participation rises. A higher unemployment rate need not mean jobs were lost.

items.stem: A survey has 90 employed and 10 unemployed. One employed person cuts paid work to one hour while seeking full-time work. How do measured employment and unemployment change?
options: Employment: falls 1; unemployment: rises 1.
Employment: rises 1; unemployment: falls 1.
Employment: unchanged; unemployment: unchanged.
Employment: falls 1; unemployment: unchanged.
items.feedback: One paid hour still counts as employed under the stated status rule. Underemployment changes without changing these measured counts.

items.stem: There are 90 employed and 10 unemployed. Four unemployed people stop searching; nobody else changes status. What is the new labor force?
items.feedback: The four move from unemployed to outside the labor force.90+6=96; employment stays 90.

items.stem: A college graduate takes two months to find a first job that matches their skills. This is most likely:
options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Not in the labor force
items.feedback: Job search while matching workers and firms is frictional unemployment.

items.stem: A coal miner loses work because the economy shifts permanently toward other energy sources and the miner lacks transferable skills. This is:
options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Seasonal inflation
items.feedback: A long-term mismatch between skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.

items.stem: A hotel lays off workers because a recession reduces travel demand. This is:
options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Natural unemployment only
items.feedback: Layoffs from weak demand during a recession are cyclical unemployment.

items.stem: Which type of unemployment would still exist even when the economy is healthy?
options: Frictional unemployment
Only cyclical unemployment
Only recession unemployment
No unemployment
items.feedback: Frictional unemployment exists because workers and firms take time to match.

items.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes structural from frictional unemployment?
options: Structural means mismatch; frictional means normal job search
Frictional unemployment is always permanent, while structural unemployment lasts one day
Structural unemployment is caused only by inflation
They are the same thing
items.feedback: Structural unemployment is about mismatch; frictional unemployment is about normal search.

items.stem: A worker leaves a job to move to another city and spends six weeks searching for a similar position while local demand remains strong. Which type of unemployment best fits the case?
options: Frictional unemployment
Structural unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
The worker is outside the labor force
items.feedback: Frictional unemployment comes from normal search and matching as workers move between jobs or enter the labor market.

items.stem: A city loses manufacturing jobs permanently, but health care jobs expand and require different credentials. Which unemployment type dominates?
options: Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment
Cyclical unemployment
Seasonal unemployment only
items.feedback: A mismatch between worker skills and available jobs is structural unemployment.

items.stem: Which example is most clearly frictional rather than structural unemployment?
options: An accountant leaves a job and searches for another locally
A miner cannot find work after mines permanently close
A worker is laid off because recession reduces demand
A cashier loses work because all stores automate checkout permanently
items.feedback: Short-term search between similar jobs is frictional unemployment.

items.stem: A software worker is unemployed for three weeks while comparing offers. A former textile worker is unemployed for two years because local factories closed. What is the best classification?
options: Software worker: frictional; textile worker: structural
Both are cyclically unemployed
Both are frictionally unemployed
The software worker is not in the labor force
items.feedback: Short job search is frictional; long-term mismatch after industry decline is structural.

items.stem: A recession closes restaurants temporarily, while automation permanently reduces demand for cashiers. Which unemployment types are present?
options: Cyclical and structural
Only frictional
Only cyclical
Only natural
items.feedback: Recession-related layoffs are cyclical; permanent automation mismatch is structural.

items.stem: A worker leaves a job voluntarily to search for a better match during a strong economy. A different worker loses a job because their industry permanently shrinks. Which pairing is correct?
options: Frictional; structural
Structural; frictional
Cyclical; frictional
Natural; cyclical
items.feedback: Voluntary job search is frictional; long-term industry decline creates structural unemployment.

items.stem: A worker has the right skills but needs time to find the right employer. Another has obsolete skills and needs retraining. What separates the two cases?
options: Search time versus skill mismatch
Nominal versus real wages
CPI versus GDP deflator
Imports versus exports
items.feedback: Frictional unemployment is search time; structural unemployment is mismatch.

items.stem: A worker is unemployed because moving to available jobs is too costly, even though jobs exist elsewhere. Which type is most likely?
options: Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment only
Cyclical unemployment only
Not in the labor force
items.feedback: Geographic mismatch is a form of structural unemployment.

items.stem: A recession causes restaurants to lay off workers. At the same time, some workers quit jobs to search for better matches. Which types of unemployment are present?
options: Cyclical and frictional
Only structural
Only frictional
Only natural unemployment from unions
items.feedback: Recession layoffs are cyclical; voluntary job search is frictional.

items.stem: Job vacancies and active job seekers both remain high in a region with 320 displaced workers, even after aggregate sales return to normal. Which added evidence best distinguishes persistent mismatch from ordinary search?
options: Whether every unemployed worker has zero current earnings
Whether the statistical agency counts the employed in the labor force
Whether the workers' skills and locations fit the available vacancies
Whether job seekers want higher real incomes than before
items.feedback: Vacancies alongside unemployment can reflect search or mismatch. Evidence about skill/location fit addresses that distinction; the other facts do not identify its source.

items.stem: Successful retraining reduces a qualification mismatch, but workers spend longer comparing offers before accepting jobs. What evidence is needed to determine the change in natural unemployment?
options: Neither component; natural unemployment is fixed regardless of matching and skills.
The structural reduction and frictional increase; their relative sizes determine the net change.
The structural reduction alone; longer search is excluded from natural unemployment.
The frictional increase alone; retraining affects only cyclical unemployment.
items.feedback: Retraining reduces structural unemployment while longer job search can increase frictional unemployment. Both belong to the natural rate; without their sizes, the net natural-rate change is ambiguous.

items.stem: A matching service shortens unemployment spells among otherwise qualified job seekers. At the same time, an industry closes permanently and displaced workers need new qualifications. Which conclusion is defensible?
options: Frictional falls, structural is unchanged; their net natural-rate effect is downward.
Frictional is unchanged, structural rises; their net natural-rate effect is upward.
Frictional falls, structural rises; their net natural-rate effect is uncertain.
Both components fall; faster matching also removes the new qualification mismatch.
items.feedback: Better matching reduces search friction, while a durable skills mismatch raises structural unemployment. Natural unemployment includes both, so opposing changes do not determine the net effect.

items.stem: Sales fall economy-wide during recession and trained workers are laid off. If demand returns with skills still suitable, which unemployment component should most directly shrink?
options: Cyclical unemployment
Structural unemployment from obsolete skills
Frictional unemployment from voluntary job changes
Natural unemployment caused by permanent skill mismatch
items.feedback: The unemployment arose from weak aggregate demand rather than an enduring mismatch; recovery can reduce its cyclical component.

items.stem: Two workers are unemployed: A is briefly between suitable jobs; B’s old occupation has disappeared and employers require skills B lacks. Which worker is more directly helped by retraining?
options: A, because all job search is structural mismatch
Both equally, because duration alone defines unemployment type
Neither, because training can affect only cyclical unemployment
B, because the problem is structural mismatch
items.feedback: B lacks the skills demanded in available jobs. A’s short search between suitable jobs is frictional; faster matching may help without retraining.

items.stem: Automation removes jobs whose workers lack skills for new vacancies. A policy only boosts demand for output without changing skills. Which limit follows?
options: The skill mismatch may persist despite stronger demand
All mismatch disappears as soon as spending increases
Unemployment becomes frictional solely because demand rises
The workers leave the labor force automatically
items.feedback: More demand need not give displaced workers the skills needed for existing vacancies. A structural problem can require retraining or mobility.
